abstract: Networks of simple analog processors having neuron-like properties have been employed to compute good solutions to a variety of optimization prob(cid:173) lems. This paper presents a neural-net solution to a resource allocation prob(cid:173) lem that arises in providing local access to the backbone of a wide-area com(cid:173) munication network. The problem is described in terms of an energy function that can be mapped onto an analog computational network. Simulation results characterizing the performance of the neural computation are also presented.

paragraphs: This paper applies an analog neural network to a resource allocation problem in communications: assigning local access to the backbone of a wide-area network. The task concerns how communication resources should be allocated, making it an optimization problem rather than a problem of recognizing patterns or learning labels.

The central step is to express the assignment problem as an energy function that can be represented by a network of simple, neuron-like analog processors. This creates a connection between an allocation decision and the behavior of a physical computational system. The energy formulation supplies the objective that the network is intended to optimize.

The paper also presents simulations that characterize the resulting neural computation. Its contribution is therefore both a formulation of the application and an examination of how the proposed computation performs. The significance is the use of neural hardware principles for a concrete communications problem, with the energy function providing the link between the practical assignment task and the analog network.
summary.tldr: The paper translates a communications resource allocation problem into an energy function for an analog neural network and evaluates its behavior through simulation.

title: A Neural-Network Solution to the Concentrator Assignment Problem
Teaching Artificial Neural Systems to Drive: Manual Training Techniques for Autonomous Systems

abstract: We present an algorithm based on reinforcement and state recurrence learning techniques to solve control scheduling problems. In particular, we have devised a simple learning scheme called "handicapped learning", in which the weights of the associative search element are reinforced, either positively or negatively, such that the system is forced to move towards the desired setpoint in the shortest possible trajectory. To improve the learning rate, a variable reinforcement scheme is employed: negative reinforcement values are varied depending on whether the failure occurs in handicapped or normal mode of operation. Furthermore, to realize a simulated annealing scheme for accelerated learning, if the system visits the same failed state successively, the negative reinforcement value is increased. In examples studied, these learning schemes have demonstrated high learning rates, and therefore may prove useful for in-situ learning.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a reinforcement learning method for control scheduling, where a system must choose actions that move it toward a desired operating point. Its central idea is called handicapped learning. Positive and negative reinforcement adjust the weights of an associative search element so that the system is pushed toward the target along the shortest possible trajectory.

The learning signal also changes with the circumstances of failure. A failure during handicapped operation receives different negative reinforcement from one during normal operation. This makes the feedback sensitive to the operating mode rather than assigning the same penalty to every unsuccessful outcome.

The method additionally tracks repeated visits to unsuccessful states. When the system successively returns to the same failed state, the negative reinforcement increases, implementing what the authors describe as a simulated annealing scheme. In the examples studied, these combined mechanisms produce rapid learning. That result motivates the suggestion that the method could support learning directly within an operating control system.
summary.tldr: A control learning method adjusts penalties by operating mode and repeated failure to accelerate movement toward a target.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Variant for Control Scheduling

abstract: This paper deals with an application of Neural Networks to satellite remote sensing observations. Because of the complexity of the application and the large amount of data, the problem cannot be solved by using a single method. The solution we propose is to build multi(cid:173) modules NN architectures where several NN cooperate together. Such system suffer from generic problem for whom we propose solutions. They allow to reach accurate performances for multi-valued function approximations and probability estimations. The results are compared with six other methods which have been used for this problem. We show that the methodology we have developed is general and can be used for a large variety of applications.

paragraphs: This paper applies neural networks to satellite remote sensing observations. The authors describe an application whose complexity and data volume make a single method insufficient. Their proposed response is a multimodule architecture in which several neural networks cooperate, making the organization of the overall system part of the solution.

The work addresses generic problems that arise when combining multiple neural modules. The resulting system supports both multivalued function approximation and probability estimation. These capabilities matter because the architecture must do more than produce one simple prediction: it must accommodate the different forms of modeling required by the remote sensing application.

The authors report accurate performance and compare their results with six other methods previously used for the problem. They also argue that the methodology extends to a broad range of applications. The contribution is therefore a cooperative modeling strategy, illustrated through remote sensing, in which solutions to shared architectural problems help several networks function together as a useful estimation system.
summary.tldr: A cooperative architecture of neural modules tackles complex satellite remote sensing tasks involving function approximation and probability estimation.

title: Multimodular Architecture for Remote Sensing Operations.

abstract: We present a theory of cortico-hippocampal interaction in discrimination learning. The hippocampal region is presumed to form new stimulus representations which facilitate learning by enhancing the discriminability of predictive stimuli and compressing stimulus-stimulus redundancies. The cortical and cerebellar regions, which are the sites of long-term memory. may acquire these new representations but are not assumed to be capable of forming new representations themselves. Instantiated as a connectionist model. this theory accounts for a wide range of trial-level classical conditioning phenomena in normal (intact) and hippocampal-Iesioned animals. It also makes several novel predictions which remain to be investigated empirically. The theory implies that the hippocampal region is involved in even the simplest learning tasks; although hippocampal-Iesioned animals may be able to use other strategies to learn these tasks. the theory predicts that they will show consistently different patterns of transfer and generalization when the task demands change.

paragraphs: The paper proposes that the hippocampal region helps learning by changing how stimuli are represented. It makes predictive stimuli easier to distinguish while compressing redundant relationships among stimuli. Under this theory, learning depends partly on constructing a more useful description of experience, rather than only changing responses to an existing description.

The model assigns different roles to interacting brain regions. The hippocampal region forms new representations, while cortical and cerebellar regions store long-term memories and may acquire those representations. These latter regions are not assumed to create new representations themselves. Implemented as a connectionist model, this division of labor accounts for many trial-level classical-conditioning phenomena in intact animals and animals with hippocampal lesions.

The theory predicts hippocampal involvement even in simple tasks. Animals with lesions may still learn through other strategies, but should show different transfer and generalization when demands change. That distinction matters because successful initial learning need not imply the same underlying representation. The paper also offers novel predictions that remain to be tested empirically.
summary.tldr: A connectionist theory assigns the hippocampus a role in reshaping stimulus representations, explaining conditioning patterns and predicting altered transfer after lesions.

title: Adaptive Stimulus Representations: A Computational Theory of Hippocampal-Region Function

abstract: We use statistical mechanics to study generalization in large com(cid:173) mittee machines. For an architecture with nonoverlapping recep(cid:173) tive fields a replica calculation yields the generalization error in the limit of a large number of hidden units. For continuous weights the generalization error falls off asymptotically inversely proportional to Q, the number of training examples per weight. For binary weights we find a discontinuous transition from poor to perfect generalization followed by a wide region of metastability. Broken replica symmetry is found within this region at low temperatures. For a fully connected architecture the generalization error is cal(cid:173) culated within the annealed approximation. For both binary and continuous weights we find transitions from a symmetric state to one with specialized hidden units, accompanied by discontinuous drops in the generalization error.

paragraphs: This paper uses statistical mechanics to analyze generalization in large committee machines, neural architectures that combine hidden-unit responses. It studies how prediction error changes with training data, weight constraints, and connectivity. The analysis distinguishes networks whose hidden units receive nonoverlapping inputs from fully connected networks.

For nonoverlapping receptive fields, a replica calculation gives the generalization error in the limit of many hidden units. With continuous weights, error eventually decreases inversely with the number of training examples per weight. With binary weights, the analysis instead finds an abrupt transition from poor to perfect generalization, followed by a broad metastable region. Broken replica symmetry appears within that region at low temperatures.

For fully connected networks, the authors use an annealed approximation. Both binary and continuous weights exhibit transitions from a symmetric state to one in which hidden units specialize, accompanied by sudden error reductions. The results show that learning can involve qualitative changes in internal organization, and that weight constraints and connectivity affect whether improvement is gradual or abrupt.
summary.tldr: Statistical-mechanics calculations reveal gradual error scaling and abrupt specialization transitions in committee machines, depending on weights and connectivity.

title: Statistical Mechanics of Learning in a Large Committee Machine

abstract: Data clustering amounts to a combinatorial optimization problem to re(cid:173) duce the complexity of a data representation and to increase its precision. Central and pairwise data clustering are studied in the maximum en(cid:173) tropy framework. For central clustering we derive a set of reestimation equations and a minimization procedure which yields an optimal num(cid:173) ber of clusters, their centers and their cluster probabilities. A meanfield approximation for pairwise clustering is used to estimate assignment probabilities. A se1fconsistent solution to multidimensional scaling and pairwise clustering is derived which yields an optimal embedding and clustering of data points in a d-dimensional Euclidian space.

paragraphs: This paper treats clustering as an optimization problem: finding a grouping that makes a data representation simpler and more precise. It studies both central clustering, which represents groups through centers, and pairwise clustering, which works with relationships between data points. A maximum-entropy framework provides the common basis for the two treatments.

For central clustering, the authors derive equations for repeatedly updating estimates and a minimization procedure. The procedure determines the number of clusters, their centers, and their probabilities together. This makes the organization of the groups part of the optimization. For pairwise clustering, the authors use a mean-field approximation to estimate probabilities of assigning points to clusters.

The paper further combines pairwise clustering with multidimensional scaling, which places points in a Euclidean space. It derives a self-consistent solution in which the embedding and clustering are determined together. The stated result is an optimal arrangement and grouping in a space of specified dimension. The broader contribution is a connected probabilistic treatment of cluster structure, assignments, and spatial representation.
summary.tldr: A maximum-entropy framework jointly addresses cluster selection, probabilistic assignments, and embedding data in Euclidean space.

title: Central and Pairwise Data Clustering by Competitive Neural Networks

abstract: We describe the relationship between certain reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing (RL) methods based on dynamic programming (DP) and a class of unorthodox Monte Carlo methods for solving systems of linear equations proposed in the 1950's. These methods recast the solu(cid:173) tion of the linear system as the expected value of a statistic suitably defined over sample paths of a Markov chain. The significance of our observations lies in arguments (Curtiss, 1954) that these Monte Carlo methods scale better with respect to state-space size than do standard, iterative techniques for solving systems of linear equa(cid:173) tions. This analysis also establishes convergence rate estimates. Because methods used in RL systems for approximating the evalu(cid:173) ation function of a fixed control policy also approximate solutions to systems of linear equations, the connection to these Monte Carlo methods establishes that algorithms very similar to TD algorithms (Sutton, 1988) are asymptotically more efficient in a precise sense than other methods for evaluating policies. Further, all DP-based RL methods have some of the properties of these Monte Carlo al(cid:173) gorithms, which suggests that although RL is often perceived to be slow, for sufficiently large problems, it may in fact be more ef(cid:173) ficient than other known classes of methods capable of producing the same results.

paragraphs: The paper connects reinforcement learning based on dynamic programming to Monte Carlo methods for solving linear equations. These methods express a linear system's solution as an expected statistic over paths through a Markov chain. Sampling trajectories can therefore provide a route to a quantity that might otherwise be obtained through conventional equation-solving iterations.

The connection applies to evaluating a fixed control policy, where estimating its value also means approximating a solution to linear equations. Drawing on analyses of the Monte Carlo methods, the authors obtain convergence-rate estimates and establish a precise asymptotic efficiency advantage for algorithms closely resembling temporal-difference learning over other policy-evaluation methods.

The significance concerns how computation scales as the state space grows. Learning from sampled experience may appear slow while still comparing favorably with alternatives on sufficiently large problems. The authors further suggest that shared properties of dynamic-programming-based reinforcement learning extend this perspective more broadly. The stated advantage is asymptotic, making problem size central to the efficiency argument.
summary.tldr: A connection to Monte Carlo linear solvers establishes asymptotic efficiency advantages for methods resembling temporal-difference policy evaluation.

title: Monte Carlo Matrix Inversion and Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Radial Basis Function (RBF) Networks, also known as networks of locally-tuned processing units (see [6]) are well known for their ease of use. Most algorithms used to train these types of net(cid:173) works, however, require a fixed architecture, in which the number of units in the hidden layer must be determined before training starts. The RCE training algorithm, introduced by Reilly, Cooper and Elbaum (see [8]), and its probabilistic extension, the P-RCE algorithm, take advantage of a growing structure in which hidden units are only introduced when necessary. The nature of these al(cid:173) gorithms allows training to reach stability much faster than is the case for gradient-descent based methods. Unfortunately P-RCE networks do not adjust the standard deviation of their prototypes individually, using only one global value for this parameter. This paper introduces the Dynamic Decay Adjustment (DDA) al(cid:173) gorithm which utilizes the constructive nature of the P-RCE al(cid:173) gorithm together with independent adaptation of each prototype's decay factor. In addition, this radial adjustment is class dependent and distinguishes between different neighbours. It is shown that networks trained with the presented algorithm perform substan(cid:173) tially better than common RBF networks. 522 Michael R. Berthold, Jay Diamond

paragraphs: Radial basis function networks use locally responsive units, but many training methods require choosing the number of hidden units before learning begins. The paper builds on constructive methods that add units only when needed. These methods provide a growing architecture and, according to the abstract, reach training stability faster than gradient-descent approaches.

The specific starting point is P-RCE, which uses a single global setting for the spread of its prototypes. The proposed Dynamic Decay Adjustment algorithm retains the growing structure while adapting each prototype's decay factor independently. This factor controls how its response changes with distance. The adjustment also depends on class membership and distinguishes among different neighboring prototypes.

Giving each prototype its own decay setting lets the network tailor local responses instead of imposing one shared width throughout the model. The abstract reports substantially better performance than common radial basis function networks. The contribution brings together two forms of adaptation: deciding when additional units are needed and adjusting how broadly each existing unit responds to nearby inputs.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Decay Adjustment improves growing RBF networks by adapting each prototype's response width using class-dependent neighborhood information.

title: Boosting the Performance of RBF Networks with Dynamic Decay Adjustment

paragraphs: This paper develops a policy-iteration algorithm for improving a motion controller built from harmonic functions. The user specifies the performance criterion to optimize. The task is therefore to adapt the controller toward a chosen objective while preserving the safety properties of its motion guidance.

The method represents value functions as potential distributions over the problem domain and control policies as gradient fields over that same domain. This gives both evaluation and action selection a spatial representation. A central stated property is that every intermediate policy remains intrinsically safe: the adaptation process does not promote collisions.

The algorithm is suitable for efficient implementation on parallel SIMD architectures. Travel-distance minimization illustrates how a user-defined objective can guide its optimization. The contribution brings together three considerations that matter for adaptive motion control: improving a specified performance measure, retaining collision-related safety during the updates themselves, and organizing the computation so it can be carried out efficiently in parallel.
summary.tldr: A parallel policy-iteration method optimizes harmonic-function motion controllers while keeping intermediate policies intrinsically safe.

title: Parallel Optimization of Motion Controllers via Policy Iteration

paragraphs: The paper studies neural networks for classifying airborne particles from laser-generated images. It contrasts this goal with environmental monitoring systems that assume particles are spherical and do not classify them. The proposed sensing approach produces two-dimensional scattering profiles, giving the classifier a pattern of measured light to analyze.

The authors compare template matching with two neural-network approaches, HyperNet and semi-linear units. All are evaluated as image classifiers for the scattering profiles. Template matching bases recognition on comparison with reference patterns; the neural-network alternatives learn a classification mapping. The comparison asks whether learned classifiers can provide useful recognition within this particle-monitoring setting.

The abstract reports that neural networks achieve recognition performance comparable to template matching while offering additional advantages. The central finding is therefore that the neural approach preserves useful classification capability in this application. By treating scattering profiles as images to recognize, the work connects laser-based particle sensing with learned pattern classification and moves beyond monitoring that relies only on a spherical-particle assumption.
summary.tldr: Neural networks classify laser scattering images of airborne particles with recognition performance comparable to template matching.

title: High-Speed Airborne Particle Monitoring Using Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: Binaural coincidence detection is essential for the localization of external sounds and requires auditory signal processing with high temporal precision. We present an integrate-and-fire model of spike processing in the auditory pathway of the barn owl. It is shown that a temporal precision in the microsecond range can be achieved with neuronal time constants which are at least one magnitude longer. paragraphs: Locating a sound requires comparing signals arriving through the two ears with very high temporal precision. This paper models spike processing in the barn owl auditory pathway, focusing on coincidence detection. The central question is how a neural system can distinguish extremely fine timing relationships despite the slower time scales of its component neurons.

The authors use an integrate-and-fire model and show that it can achieve microsecond-scale precision even when neuronal time constants are at least an order of magnitude longer. The result separates the precision of the system's timing computation from the characteristic response time of an individual modeled neuron.

A key component is an unsupervised Hebbian learning rule that fine-tunes the timing properties of neuronal connections. Learning therefore helps organize the connections needed for precise spike processing. The model offers an explanation for how auditory timing can become much sharper than neuronal time constants alone might suggest, linking connection-level adaptation to the temporal accuracy required for binaural sound localization.
summary.tldr: An integrate-and-fire auditory model uses Hebbian connection tuning to achieve timing precision much finer than neuronal time constants.

title: Temporal coding in the sub-millisecond range: Model of barn owl auditory pathway

abstract: We propose to train trading systems by optimizing financial objective functions via reinforcement learning. The performance functions that we consider are profit or wealth, the Sharpe ratio and our recently proposed differential Sharpe ratio for online learning. In Moody & Wu (1997), we presented empirical results that demonstrate the advantages of reinforcement learning relative to supervised learning . Here we extend our previous work to compare Q-Learning to our Recurrent Reinforcement Learning (RRL) algorithm. We provide new simulation results that demonstrate the presence of predictability in the monthly S&P 500 Stock Index for the 25 year period 1970 through 1994, as well as a sensitivity analysis that provides economic insight into the trader's structure.

paragraphs: The paper proposes training trading systems by directly optimizing financial objectives through reinforcement learning. The objectives include profit or wealth, the Sharpe ratio, and a differential Sharpe ratio designed for online learning. This makes the chosen financial measure part of the learning target rather than leaving trading performance separate from training.

The work extends an earlier comparison with supervised learning by comparing Q-learning with the authors' Recurrent Reinforcement Learning algorithm. The comparison examines alternative reinforcement-learning approaches within the same trading problem. Including several financial objectives also makes clear that the desired behavior depends on what measure the system is trained to improve.

New simulations report predictability in monthly S&P 500 index data over the 25-year period from 1970 through 1994. The authors also use sensitivity analysis to obtain economic insight into the trader's structure. Together, these contributions connect direct financial optimization, algorithm comparison, and interpretation of the learned trader within the historical simulation setting studied.
summary.tldr: Trading systems learn directly from financial objectives, with Q-learning and recurrent reinforcement learning compared in historical market simulations.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Trading

abstract: The problem of constructing weak classifiers for boosting algo(cid:173) rithms is studied. We present an algorithm that produces a linear classifier that is guaranteed to achieve an error better than random guessing for any distribution on the data. While this weak learner is not useful for learning in general, we show that under reasonable conditions on the distribution it yields an effective weak learner for one-dimensional problems. Preliminary simulations suggest that similar behavior can be expected in higher dimensions, a result which is corroborated by some recent theoretical bounds. Addi(cid:173) tionally, we provide improved convergence rate bounds for the gen(cid:173) eralization error in situations where the empirical error can be made small, which is exactly the situation that occurs if weak learners with guaranteed performance that is better than random guessing can be established.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to construct weak classifiers for boosting. It presents an algorithm producing a linear classifier with error guaranteed to be better than random guessing for any distribution on the data. The authors also state that this weak learner is not useful for learning in general, separating the stated guarantee from broader practical effectiveness.

Under reasonable conditions on the distribution, the construction becomes an effective weak learner for one-dimensional problems. Preliminary simulations suggest similar behavior in higher dimensions, and the abstract says recent theoretical bounds corroborate that suggestion. The higher-dimensional evidence is therefore presented more cautiously than the conditional result for one dimension.

The paper additionally improves convergence-rate bounds for generalization error in settings where empirical error can be made small. The authors connect this condition to the availability of weak learners whose performance is guaranteed to exceed random guessing. The contribution joins a classifier construction with an analysis of how such weak-learning guarantees support conclusions about boosting's generalization behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs a weak linear learner with conditional effectiveness and improves boosting generalization bounds when empirical error can be small.

title: Weak Learners and Improved Rates of Convergence in Boosting

abstract: Natural sounds are structured on many time-scales. A typical segment of speech, for example, contains features that span four orders of magnitude: Sentences (~1s); phonemes (~0.1s); glottal pulses (~0.01s); and formants (<0.001s). The auditory system uses information from each of these time-scales to solve complicated tasks such as auditory scene analysis. One route toward understanding how auditory processing accomplishes this analysis is to build neuroscience-inspired algorithms which solve similar tasks and to compare the properties of these algorithms with properties of auditory processing. There is however a discord: Current machine-audition algorithms largely concentrate on the shorter time-scale structures in sounds, and the longer structures are ignored. The reason for this is two-fold. Firstly, it is a difficult technical problem to construct an algorithm that utilises both sorts of information. Secondly, it is computationally demanding to simultaneously process data both at high resolution (to extract short temporal information) and for long duration (to extract long temporal information). The contribution of this work is to develop a new statistical model for natural sounds that captures structure across a wide range of time-scales, and to provide efficient learning and inference algorithms. We demonstrate the success of this approach on a missing data task.

A typical segment of speech, for example, contains features that span four orders of magnitude: Sentences (~1s); phonemes (~0.1s); glottal pulses (~0.01s); and formants (<0.001s). The auditory system uses information from each of these time-scales to solve complicated tasks such as auditory scene analysis. One route toward understanding how auditory processing accomplishes this analysis is to build neuroscience-inspired algorithms which solve similar tasks and to compare the properties of these algorithms with properties of auditory processing. There is however a discord: Current machine-audition algorithms largely concentrate on the shorter time-scale structures in sounds, and the longer structures are ignored. The reason for this is two-fold. Firstly, it is a difficult technical problem to construct an algorithm that utilises both sorts of information. Secondly, it is computationally demanding to simultaneously process data both at high resolution (to extract short temporal information) and for long duration (to extract long temporal information). The contribution of this work is to develop a new statistical model for natural sounds that captures structure across a wide range of time-scales, and to provide efficient learning and inference algorithms. We demonstrate the success of this approach on a missing data task.

paragraphs: Natural sounds contain meaningful structure at very different timescales. In speech, broad sentence structure coexists with much shorter phonemes, glottal pulses, and formants. The paper argues that understanding auditory processing benefits from algorithms that can use this range of structure, since the auditory system draws on information across these scales.

The authors identify two obstacles to doing so computationally. Combining short and long temporal information is technically difficult, and processing long recordings at sufficiently fine resolution is expensive. These pressures help explain why machine-audition algorithms have concentrated largely on shorter structures while leaving longer ones underused.

The contribution is a statistical model for natural sounds that captures structure across a wide range of timescales, together with efficient learning and inference algorithms. The authors demonstrate the approach on a missing-data task. This provides evidence that the model’s representation can be useful for reasoning about incomplete sounds, while the efficient algorithms address the computational difficulty that motivates the work. The stated demonstration concerns that task rather than every auditory-processing problem.
summary.tldr: A statistical sound model captures structure across multiple timescales with efficient learning and inference, demonstrated on a missing-data task.

title: Modeling Natural Sounds with Modulation Cascade Processes

abstract: In recent work Long and Servedio LS05short presented a ``martingale boosting'' algorithm that works by constructing a branching program over weak classifiers and has a simple analysis based on elementary properties of random walks. LS05short showed that this martingale booster can tolerate random classification noise when it is run with a noise-tolerant weak learner; however, a drawback of the algorithm is that it is not adaptive, i.e. it cannot effectively take advantage of variation in the quality of the weak classifiers it receives. In this paper we present a variant of the original martingale boosting algorithm and prove that it is adaptive. This adaptiveness is achieved by modifying the original algorithm so that the random walks that arise in its analysis have different step size depending on the quality of the weak learner at each stage. The new algorithm inherits the desirable properties of the original LS05short algorithm, such as random classification noise tolerance, and has several other advantages besides adaptiveness: it requires polynomially fewer calls to the weak learner than the original algorithm, and it can be used with confidence-rated weak hypotheses that output real values rather than Boolean predictions.

In this paper we present a variant of the original martingale boosting algorithm and prove that it is adaptive. The new algorithm inherits the desirable properties of the original LS05short algorithm, such as random classification noise tolerance, and has several other advantages besides adaptiveness: it requires polynomially fewer calls to the weak learner than the original algorithm, and it can be used with confidence-rated weak hypotheses that output real values rather than Boolean predictions.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak classifiers into a stronger decision procedure. The paper revisits a martingale boosting method that organizes weak classifiers into a branching program and can be analyzed through random walks. The earlier method could tolerate random classification noise when paired with a noise-tolerant weak learner, but did not effectively exploit differences in classifier quality.

The proposed variant makes that quality variation part of the algorithm’s behavior. In its random-walk analysis, the step size changes according to the quality of the weak learner at each stage. This provides the mechanism for adaptiveness: stronger and weaker contributions need not be treated as though they offer the same amount of progress.

The authors prove that the resulting booster is adaptive and requires polynomially fewer weak-learner calls than its predecessor. It also accepts confidence-rated hypotheses with real-valued outputs, extending beyond Boolean predictions. The method retains the earlier noise-tolerance property in the setting involving a noise-tolerant weak learner. Together, these results improve how the booster uses both the quality and the expressive form of its inputs.
summary.tldr: An adaptive martingale booster adjusts to weak-learner quality while reducing learner calls and retaining conditional noise tolerance.

title: Adaptive Martingale Boosting

abstract: A principled mechanism for identifying conditional dependencies in time-series data is provided through structure learning of dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). An important assumption of DBN structure learning is that the data are generated by a stationary processâan assumption that is not true in many important settings. In this paper, we introduce a new class of graphical models called non-stationary dynamic Bayesian networks, in which the conditional dependence structure of the underlying data-generation process is permitted to change over time. Non-stationary dynamic Bayesian networks represent a new framework for studying problems in which the structure of a network is evolving over time. We define the non-stationary DBN model, present an MCMC sampling algorithm for learning the structure of the model from time-series data under different assumptions, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm on both simulated and biological data.

paragraphs: Dynamic Bayesian networks provide a way to learn conditional dependencies from time-series data. Their usual structure-learning formulation assumes a stationary generating process. The paper addresses situations where that assumption fails because the relationships among variables themselves evolve over time, making one unchanging network structure inadequate for the intended description.

The authors introduce non-stationary dynamic Bayesian networks, which explicitly permit the conditional dependence structure to change. The model therefore concerns changes in which variables depend on which others, extending the role of the network beyond describing a fixed set of relationships through a sequence of observations.

The paper defines this model class and develops an MCMC sampling algorithm to learn its structure under different assumptions. Demonstrations on simulated and biological data show the algorithm's effectiveness in the studied settings. The resulting framework offers a principled way to investigate evolving networks from time-series measurements, with structural change incorporated into the model rather than ruled out by a stationarity assumption.
summary.tldr: Non-stationary dynamic Bayesian networks learn time-varying dependency structures from time-series data.

title: Non-stationary dynamic Bayesian networks

abstract: We propose a new sketch recognition framework that combines a rich representation of low level visual appearance with a graphical model for capturing high level relationships between symbols. This joint model of appearance and context allows our framework to be less sensitive to noise and drawing variations, improving accuracy and robustness. The result is a recognizer that is better able to handle the wide range of drawing styles found in messy freehand sketches. We evaluate our work on two real-world domains, molecular diagrams and electrical circuit diagrams, and show that our combined approach significantly improves recognition performance.

This joint model of appearance and context allows our framework to be less sensitive to noise and drawing variations, improving accuracy and robustness. The result is a recognizer that is better able to handle the wide range of drawing styles found in messy freehand sketches. We evaluate our work on two real-world domains, molecular diagrams and electrical circuit diagrams, and show that our combined approach significantly improves recognition performance.

paragraphs: Freehand sketch recognition must cope with messy marks and differences in how people draw the same symbol. This paper proposes a framework that uses both the visual appearance of a symbol and its relationships with surrounding symbols. The aim is to make recognition more reliable when local drawing quality or style makes appearance alone difficult to interpret.

The framework combines a rich representation of low-level visual information with a graphical model of higher-level relationships. These components form a joint model of appearance and context. This allows evidence about neighboring symbols to contribute to recognition alongside the marks themselves, connecting local visual interpretation with the organization of the diagram.

The authors evaluate the method on molecular diagrams and electrical circuit diagrams, reporting significantly improved recognition performance. They attribute greater accuracy and robustness to reduced sensitivity to noise and drawing variation. The two application domains demonstrate the usefulness of the combined approach across different kinds of structured sketches. The main contribution is the integration of detailed appearance information and contextual relationships within one recognition framework.
summary.tldr: Combining symbol appearance with graphical context improves recognition of messy molecular and electrical circuit sketches.

title: Learning from Neighboring Strokes: Combining Appearance and Context for Multi-Domain Sketch Recognition

abstract: We propose a class of sparse coding models that utilizes a Laplacian Scale Mixture (LSM) prior to model dependencies among coefficients. Each coefficient is modeled as a Laplacian distribution with a variable scale parameter, with a Gamma distribution prior over the scale parameter. We show that, due to the conjugacy of the Gamma prior, it is possible to derive efficient inference procedures for both the coefficients and the scale parameter. When the scale parameters of a group of coefficients are combined into a single variable, it is possible to describe the dependencies that occur due to common amplitude fluctuations among coefficients, which have been shown to constitute a large fraction of the redundancy in natural images. We show that, as a consequence of this group sparse coding, the resulting inference of the coefficients follows a divisive normalization rule, and that this may be efficiently implemented a network architecture similar to that which has been proposed to occur in primary visual cortex. We also demonstrate improvements in image coding and compressive sensing recovery using the LSM model.

paragraphs: This paper develops sparse coding models that represent dependencies among coefficients through a Laplacian Scale Mixture prior. Each coefficient has a Laplacian distribution with an adjustable scale, and that scale has a Gamma prior. The mathematical compatibility of these distributions allows efficient inference for both coefficient values and their scale parameter.

To model groups, the authors replace separate scale parameters with one shared variable. This captures cases where several coefficients fluctuate together in amplitude. Such shared fluctuations are described as accounting for a large portion of redundancy in natural images, giving the grouping a direct connection to the structure of image data.

The resulting coefficient inference follows a divisive normalization rule. The authors show that this computation may be implemented efficiently in a network architecture resembling one proposed for primary visual cortex. They also demonstrate improvements in image coding and compressive sensing recovery. The model therefore connects an explicit probabilistic account of coefficient dependence with a structured inference computation and practical image-processing results.
summary.tldr: Sharing scale variables across sparse coefficients models common amplitude changes, yields divisive normalization, and improves image coding and compressive sensing recovery.

title: Group Sparse Coding with a Laplacian Scale Mixture Prior

abstract: There is no generally accepted way to define wavelets on permutations. We address this issue by introducing the notion of coset based multiresolution analysis (CMRA) on the symmetric group; find the corresponding wavelet functions; and describe a fast wavelet transform of O(n^p) complexity with small p for sparse signals (in contrast to the O(n^q n!) complexity typical of FFTs). We discuss potential applications in ranking, sparse approximation, and multi-object tracking.
originalAbstract: There is no generally accepted way to define wavelets on permutations. We address this issue by introducing the notion of coset based multiresolution analysis (CMRA) on the symmetric group; find the corresponding wavelet functions; and describe a fast wavelet transform of O(n^p) complexity with small p for sparse signals (in contrast to the O(n^q n!) complexity typical of FFTs). We discuss potential applications in ranking, sparse approximation, and multi-object tracking.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to define wavelets for signals on permutations. Permutations describe different arrangements of a collection, and the symmetric group contains all such arrangements. A multiresolution representation aims to organize information at different levels of detail, but the authors note that no generally accepted wavelet construction existed for this setting.

Their construction is called coset-based multiresolution analysis. It uses the structure of the symmetric group to define the resolution hierarchy and derives corresponding wavelet functions. The authors also describe a fast transform for sparse signals with complexity O(n^p), where p is small. The sparsity qualification is part of this computational claim.

That complexity contrasts with the O(n^q n!) cost the abstract associates with typical fast Fourier transforms in this setting. Removing the factorial factor for the stated sparse-signal case is the key computational attraction. Ranking, sparse approximation, and multi-object tracking are discussed as potential applications, giving possible uses for the representation beyond the mathematical construction itself.
summary.tldr: Coset-based multiresolution analysis defines wavelets on permutations and supports a polynomial-time transform for sparse signals.

title: Multiresolution analysis on the symmetric group

abstract: In this work, we propose a general method for recovering low-rank three-order tensors, in which the data can be deformed by some unknown transformation and corrupted by arbitrary sparse errors. Since the unfolding matrices of a tensor are interdependent, we introduce auxiliary variables and relax the hard equality constraints by the augmented Lagrange multiplier method. To improve the computational efficiency, we introduce a proximal gradient step to the alternating direction minimization method. We have provided proof for the convergence of the linearized version of the problem which is the inner loop of the overall algorithm. Both simulations and experiments show that our methods are more efficient and effective than previous work. The proposed method can be easily applied to simultaneously rectify and align multiple images or videos frames. In this context, the state-of-the-art algorithms RASL'' and "TILT'' can be viewed as two special cases of our work, and yet each only performs part of the function of our method."

Since the unfolding matrices of a tensor are interdependent, we introduce auxiliary variables and relax the hard equality constraints by the augmented Lagrange multiplier method. To improve the computational efficiency, we introduce a proximal gradient step to the alternating direction minimization method. We have provided proof for the convergence of the linearized version of the problem which is the inner loop of the overall algorithm. paragraphs: This paper addresses recovery of low-rank three-way tensors when the data have undergone unknown transformations and contain sparse errors of arbitrary values. In image applications, the formulation supports correcting geometric distortion and aligning multiple images or video frames together. It combines these tasks with recovery of the underlying low-rank structure.

The optimization must handle dependencies among the different matrix unfoldings of a tensor. The authors introduce auxiliary variables and use an augmented Lagrange multiplier method to relax hard equality constraints. They further add a proximal gradient step to alternating direction minimization to improve efficiency. Their convergence proof applies to the linearized problem solved in the algorithm's inner loop.

Simulations and experiments show greater efficiency and effectiveness than previous work. The framework also contains RASL and TILT as special cases, while combining functions that those methods each address only in part. This unification is the practical significance of the tensor formulation: rectification and alignment can be treated together despite sparse corruption and unknown transformations.
summary.tldr: Robust low-rank tensor recovery jointly rectifies and aligns transformed, sparsely corrupted images, with convergence proved for its linearized inner loop.

title: Simultaneous Rectification and Alignment via Robust Recovery of Low-rank Tensors

abstract: In past few years, several techniques have been proposed for training of linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) in limited-memory setting, where a dual block-coordinate descent (dual-BCD) method was used to balance cost spent on I/O and computation. In this paper, we consider the more general setting of regularized \emph{Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM)} when data cannot fit into memory. In particular, we generalize the existing block minimization framework based on strong duality and \emph{Augmented Lagrangian} technique to achieve global convergence for ERM with arbitrary convex loss function and regularizer. The block minimization framework is flexible in the sense that, given a solver working under sufficient memory, one can integrate it with the framework to obtain a solver globally convergent under limited-memory condition. We conduct experiments on L1-regularized classification and regression problems to corroborate our convergence theory and compare the proposed framework to algorithms adopted from online and distributed settings, which shows superiority of the proposed approach on data of size ten times larger than the memory capacity.

paragraphs: Training becomes a different computational problem when the dataset cannot fit into memory: the learner must manage both optimization and the cost of accessing data. Earlier work addressed this setting for linear support vector machines using updates to blocks of variables. This paper extends that strategy to regularized empirical risk minimization, a broader formulation that combines a data-fitting loss with a regularization term.

The framework uses strong duality and an augmented Lagrangian technique to establish global convergence for convex losses and convex regularizers. Its practical attraction is flexibility: a solver designed for data that fits in memory can be incorporated into the framework to produce a solver with convergence guarantees under limited memory.

Experiments cover classification and regression with L1 regularization. They support the convergence theory and show better performance than the compared methods adapted from online and distributed learning on datasets ten times larger than available memory. The contribution connects a general convex optimization guarantee with an approach designed around the realities of data access.
summary.tldr: A flexible block optimization framework extends convex learning algorithms to datasets larger than memory while retaining global convergence guarantees.

title: A Dual Augmented Block Minimization Framework for Learning with Limited Memory

abstract: We define and study the problem of predicting the solution to a linear program (LP) given only partial information about its objective and constraints. This generalizes the problem of learning to predict the purchasing behavior of a rational agent who has an unknown objective function, that has been studied under the name “Learning from Revealed Preferences". We give mistake bound learning algorithms in two settings: in the first, the objective of the LP is known to the learner but there is an arbitrary, fixed set of constraints which are unknown. Each example is defined by an additional known constraint and the goal of the learner is to predict the optimal solution of the LP given the union of the known and unknown constraints. This models the problem of predicting the behavior of a rational agent whose goals are known, but whose resources are unknown. In the second setting, the objective of the LP is unknown, and changing in a controlled way. The constraints of the LP may also change every day, but are known. An example is given by a set of constraints and partial information about the objective, and the task of the learner is again to predict the optimal solution of the partially known LP.

paragraphs: A rational decision can be modeled as the solution to an optimization problem, but an observer may know only part of that problem. This paper studies predicting the solution of a linear program when some objectives or constraints are unknown. It generalizes learning from revealed preferences, where observed choices provide information about an agent’s unknown goals.

In the first setting, the learner knows the objective but does not know an arbitrary, fixed collection of constraints. Each example adds a known constraint, and the learner predicts the optimum under both the hidden and visible constraints. This represents an agent whose goals are understood but whose available resources are hidden.

In the second setting, the objective is unknown and changes in a controlled way. Constraints can also change each day, but they are known, and each example supplies partial information about the objective. The authors give mistake-bound learning algorithms for both settings. These results frame prediction under incomplete optimization knowledge as a learning problem with guarantees on accumulated prediction errors.
summary.tldr: Mistake-bound algorithms predict linear-program solutions when constraints are hidden or an unknown objective changes in a controlled way.

title: Learning from Rational Behavior: Predicting Solutions to Unknown Linear Programs

abstract: Currently, deep neural networks are deployed on low-power portable devices by first training a full-precision model using powerful hardware, and then deriving a corresponding low-precision model for efficient inference on such systems. However, training models directly with coarsely quantized weights is a key step towards learning on embedded platforms that have limited computing resources, memory capacity, and power consumption. Numerous recent publications have studied methods for training quantized networks, but these studies have mostly been empirical. In this work, we investigate training methods for quantized neural networks from a theoretical viewpoint. We first explore accuracy guarantees for training methods under convexity assumptions. We then look at the behavior of these algorithms for non-convex problems, and show that training algorithms that exploit high-precision representations have an important greedy search phase that purely quantized training methods lack, which explains the difficulty of training using low-precision arithmetic.

However, training models directly with coarsely quantized weights is a key step towards learning on embedded platforms that have limited computing resources, memory capacity, and power consumption. Numerous recent publications have studied methods for training quantized networks, but these studies have mostly been empirical. We then look at the behavior of these algorithms for non-convex problems, and show that training algorithms that exploit high-precision representations have an important greedy search phase that purely quantized training methods lack, which explains the difficulty of training using low-precision arithmetic.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the theory of training neural networks with coarsely quantized weights. Direct low-precision training matters for embedded systems with limited computation, memory, and power. The authors distinguish this goal from the common workflow of training a full-precision model on powerful hardware and then deriving a low-precision version for inference.

They first examine accuracy guarantees under convexity assumptions. These assumptions define the setting of that part of the analysis and should not be carried over automatically to general neural-network training. The paper then studies algorithm behavior on nonconvex problems, where the role of higher-precision representations becomes central.

The authors show that training methods using high-precision representations have an important greedy search phase that purely quantized methods lack. This difference provides an explanation for the difficulty of training with low-precision arithmetic. The contribution moves beyond empirical comparisons by identifying an algorithmic behavior associated with higher precision and relating it to the challenges of direct quantized learning.
summary.tldr: Theoretical analysis links the difficulty of purely quantized training to a greedy search phase available to methods retaining high-precision representations.

title: Training Quantized Nets: A Deeper Understanding

abstract: Rich experimental evidences show that one can better estimate users' unknown ratings with the aid of graph side information such as social graphs. However, the gain is not theoretically quantified. In this work, we study the binary rating estimation problem to understand the fundamental value of graph side information. Considering a simple correlation model between a rating matrix and a graph, we characterize the sharp threshold on the number of observed entries required to recover the rating matrix (called the optimal sample complexity) as a function of the quality of graph side information (to be detailed). To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to reveal how much the graph side information reduces sample complexity. Further, we propose a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the limit. Our experimental results demonstrate that the algorithm performs well even with real-world graphs.

paragraphs: Graphs such as social networks can help estimate users' missing ratings, but empirical improvements leave a theoretical question unanswered: how many rating observations does a useful graph actually save? This paper studies that question for binary ratings. It focuses on recovering a rating matrix using both observed entries and a related graph.

Under a simple model connecting the graph and rating matrix, the authors characterize a sharp threshold for the number of observed entries needed for recovery. The threshold depends on the quality of the graph information. This turns the graph's value into a sample-complexity statement, describing how much direct rating evidence is needed when the additional structure is available.

The authors also propose a computationally efficient algorithm that reaches this theoretical limit. Experiments show that the algorithm performs well with real-world graphs, extending its empirical appeal beyond the model used for analysis. The recovery threshold remains a result within the stated correlation model, while the experiments provide separate evidence of practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies how graph information reduces the ratings needed for recovery and gives an efficient algorithm attaining that limit.

title: Binary Rating Estimation with Graph Side Information

abstract: In a number of disciplines, the data (e.g., graphs, manifolds) to be analyzed are non-Euclidean in nature. Geometric deep learning corresponds to techniques that generalize deep neural network models to such non-Euclidean spaces. Several recent papers have shown how convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can be extended to learn with graph-based data. In this work, we study the setting where the data (or measurements) are ordered, longitudinal or temporal in nature and live on a Riemannian manifold -- this setting is common in a variety of problems in statistical machine learning, vision and medical imaging. We show how recurrent statistical recurrent network models can be defined in such spaces. We give an efficient algorithm and conduct a rigorous analysis of its statistical properties. We perform extensive numerical experiments demonstrating competitive performance with state of the art methods but with significantly less number of parameters. We also show applications to a statistical analysis task in brain imaging, a regime where deep neural network models have only been utilized in limited ways.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequences whose measurements live in a curved mathematical space rather than an ordinary space of numerical vectors. Its focus is symmetric positive definite matrices. When such measurements arrive over time, a model needs to capture both their sequential relationships and the geometry of the space they inhabit.

The authors develop a statistical recurrent network for this setting. Recurrence provides a way to connect successive observations, while the manifold formulation accommodates their non-Euclidean structure. The contribution includes an efficient algorithm and a rigorous study of its statistical properties, connecting the proposed network architecture with an analysis of how it behaves.

Numerical experiments show performance competitive with leading methods while using substantially fewer parameters. That finding suggests the geometric structure can support a compact model without giving up competitive results in the evaluated settings. The paper also applies the approach to statistical analysis in brain imaging, illustrating its relevance to a domain where these structured measurements arise.
summary.tldr: A recurrent statistical model handles manifold-valued sequences and achieves competitive experimental results with substantially fewer parameters.

title: A Statistical Recurrent Model on the Manifold of Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices

abstract: The large majority of differentially private algorithms focus on the static setting, where queries are made on an unchanging database. This is unsuitable for the myriad applications involving databases that grow over time. To address this gap in the literature, we consider the dynamic setting, in which new data arrive over time. Previous results in this setting have been limited to answering a single non-adaptive query repeatedly as the database grows. In contrast, we provide tools for richer and more adaptive analysis of growing databases. Our first contribution is a novel modification of the private multiplicative weights algorithm, which provides accurate analysis of exponentially many adaptive linear queries (an expressive query class including all counting queries) for a static database. Our modification maintains the accuracy guarantee of the static setting even as the database grows without bound. Our second contribution is a set of general results which show that many other private and accurate algorithms can be immediately extended to the dynamic setting by rerunning them at appropriate points of data growth with minimal loss of accuracy, even when data growth is unbounded.

Previous results in this setting have been limited to answering a single non-adaptive query repeatedly as the database grows. In contrast, we provide tools for richer and more adaptive analysis of growing databases. Our first contribution is a novel modification of the private multiplicative weights algorithm, which provides accurate analysis of exponentially many adaptive linear queries (an expressive query class including all counting queries) for a static database. Our modification maintains the accuracy guarantee of the static setting even as the database grows without bound. Our second contribution is a set of general results which show that many other private and accurate algorithms can be immediately extended to the dynamic setting by rerunning them at appropriate points of data growth with minimal loss of accuracy, even when data growth is unbounded.

paragraphs: Many private data-analysis algorithms assume that the database stays fixed. That assumption does not fit applications where new records continually arrive and analysts ask new questions as they learn from earlier answers. The paper addresses this growing-database setting, moving beyond earlier results that repeatedly answered a single query chosen in advance.

Its first contribution modifies private multiplicative weights, an algorithm that supports exponentially many adaptive linear queries on a static database. Linear queries include counting questions, so the supported analysis is broad. The modified algorithm retains the static setting’s accuracy guarantee even when database growth has no fixed endpoint, allowing privacy-preserving analysis to continue as records accumulate.

The second contribution provides general results for extending many other private, accurate algorithms to growing data. The strategy reruns an algorithm at appropriately chosen stages of database growth, with only a small loss of accuracy. Together, these results offer both a specialized adaptive-query method and a broader route for reusing existing private algorithms in an indefinitely expanding database.
summary.tldr: The paper extends private analysis to indefinitely growing databases while preserving strong accuracy guarantees for adaptive queries.

title: Differential Privacy for Growing Databases

abstract: We propose Ephemeral Value Adjusments (EVA): a means of allowing deep reinforcement learning agents to rapidly adapt to experience in their replay buffer. EVA shifts the value predicted by a neural network with an estimate of the value function found by prioritised sweeping over experience tuples from the replay buffer near the current state. EVA combines a number of recent ideas around combining episodic memory-like structures into reinforcement learning agents: slot-based storage, content-based retrieval, and memory-based planning. We show that EVA is performant on a demonstration task and Atari games.

EVA combines a number of recent ideas around combining episodic memory-like structures into reinforcement learning agents: slot-based storage, content-based retrieval, and memory-based planning. We show that EVA is performant on a demonstration task and Atari games.

paragraphs: Ephemeral Value Adjustments, or EVA, gives a deep reinforcement learning agent a way to adapt rapidly using experiences already stored in its replay buffer. The method focuses on value estimates, which assess the usefulness of states or decisions. It combines a neural network's prediction with an additional estimate obtained from remembered experience.

For the current state, EVA retrieves nearby experience tuples from the replay buffer. It then applies prioritized sweeping over those experiences to estimate values and uses the result to shift the value predicted by the network. This makes local stored experience part of the agent's value computation rather than relying solely on the network prediction.

The approach brings together three memory-related ideas: storage in slots, retrieval based on content, and planning with retrieved memories. Their combination connects the current situation to relevant past experience and uses that experience to adjust estimates online. The authors report good performance on a demonstration task and Atari games, supporting this combination as a workable mechanism for incorporating memory-based adaptation into deep reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: EVA adjusts neural value predictions using planning over nearby replay-buffer experiences to support rapid adaptation.

title: Fast deep reinforcement learning using online adjustments from the past

abstract: Social bias in machine learning has drawn significant attention, with work ranging from demonstrations of bias in a multitude of applications, curating definitions of fairness for different contexts, to developing algorithms to mitigate bias. In natural language processing, gender bias has been shown to exist in context-free word embeddings. Recently, contextual word representations have outperformed word embeddings in several downstream NLP tasks. These word representations are conditioned on their context within a sentence, and can also be used to encode the entire sentence. In this paper, we analyze the extent to which state-of-the-art models for contextual word representations, such as BERT and GPT-2, encode biases with respect to gender, race, and intersectional identities. Towards this, we propose assessing bias at the contextual word level. This novel approach captures the contextual effects of bias missing in context-free word embeddings, yet avoids confounding effects that underestimate bias at the sentence encoding level. We demonstrate evidence of bias at the corpus level, find varying evidence of bias in embedding association tests, show in particular that racial bias is strongly encoded in contextual word models, and observe that bias effects for intersectional minorities are exacerbated beyond their constituent minority identities. Further, evaluating bias effects at the contextual word level captures biases that are not captured at the sentence level, confirming the need for our novel approach.

paragraphs: Contextual language models represent a word differently depending on its surrounding sentence. This paper investigates whether those representations encode social biases involving gender, race, and intersecting identities. It examines models including BERT and GPT-2, asking how bias should be measured when a word’s representation changes with context.

The authors propose measuring bias at the contextual word level. This preserves information about how a particular context affects a word, while avoiding confounding effects that can make whole-sentence representations underestimate bias. The choice of measurement level therefore matters: combining information into a sentence representation can conceal associations visible in individual contextualized words.

The study finds corpus-level evidence of bias and varying evidence across embedding association tests. It reports strong encoding of racial bias and amplified bias for intersectional minorities beyond their constituent minority identities. Contextual word measurements also reveal biases missed at the sentence level. These findings support evaluating contextual representations directly, rather than assuming improved language-task performance or sentence-level testing establishes their fairness.
summary.tldr: Measuring bias in contextualized words reveals racial and intersectional biases that whole-sentence measurements can miss.

title: Assessing Social and Intersectional Biases in Contextualized Word Representations

abstract: This paper considers the problem of estimating the distribution of returns in reinforcement learning (i.e., distributional RL problem). It presents a new representational framework to maintain the uncertainty of returns and provides mathematical tools to compute it. We show that instead of representing a probability distribution function of returns, one can represent their characteristic function instead, the Fourier transform of their distribution. We call the new representation Characteristic Value Function (CVF), which can be interpreted as the frequency domain representation of the probability distribution of returns. We show that the CVF satisfies a Bellman-like equation, and its corresponding Bellman operator is contraction with respect to certain metrics. The contraction property allows us to devise an iterative procedure to compute the CVF, which we call Characteristic Value Iteration (CVI). We analyze CVI and its approximate variant and show how approximation errors affect the quality of computed CVF.

We show that the CVF satisfies a Bellman-like equation, and its corresponding Bellman operator is contraction with respect to certain metrics. paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning estimates the distribution of possible returns, preserving information about uncertainty in outcomes. This paper proposes representing that distribution through its characteristic function, its Fourier-transform representation. The authors call this object the Characteristic Value Function, or CVF, and develop tools for computing it.

They show that the CVF obeys a Bellman-like equation. Its associated operator is a contraction under certain metrics, meaning that applying it brings representations closer together according to those measures. This mathematical property supports an iterative computation method called Characteristic Value Iteration, or CVI.

The paper analyzes both CVI and an approximate version, including how approximation errors influence the quality of the resulting characteristic value function. This connects the exact mathematical representation with the consequences of computing it approximately. The contribution is a frequency-domain framework for return uncertainty, together with an iterative algorithm whose behavior can be studied through contraction and error analysis. The contraction claim applies to the specified metrics rather than every possible comparison between distributions.
summary.tldr: Characteristic Value Iteration computes return distributions through their Fourier representation, with contraction and approximation-error analyses.

title: Value Function in Frequency Domain and the Characteristic Value Iteration Algorithm

abstract: Stochastic classifiers arise in a number of machine learning problems, and have become especially prominent of late, as they often result from constrained optimization problems, e.g. for fairness, churn, or custom losses. Despite their utility, the inherent randomness of stochastic classifiers may cause them to be problematic to use in practice for a variety of practical reasons. In this paper, we attempt to answer the theoretical question of how well a stochastic classifier can be approximated by a deterministic one, and compare several different approaches, proving lower and upper bounds. We also experimentally investigate the pros and cons of these methods, not only in regard to how successfully each deterministic classifier approximates the original stochastic classifier, but also in terms of how well each addresses the other issues that can make stochastic classifiers undesirable.
originalAbstract: Stochastic classifiers arise in a number of machine learning problems, and have become especially prominent of late, as they often result from constrained optimization problems, e.g. for fairness, churn, or custom losses. Despite their utility, the inherent randomness of stochastic classifiers may cause them to be problematic to use in practice for a variety of practical reasons. In this paper, we attempt to answer the theoretical question of how well a stochastic classifier can be approximated by a deterministic one, and compare several different approaches, proving lower and upper bounds. We also experimentally investigate the pros and cons of these methods, not only in regard to how successfully each deterministic classifier approximates the original stochastic classifier, but also in terms of how well each addresses the other issues that can make stochastic classifiers undesirable.

paragraphs: Some classification methods deliberately produce randomized decisions. Such classifiers can arise when training must satisfy constraints involving fairness, churn, or custom losses. Although the randomness can be useful for constructing a solution, it can also make that solution difficult to use in practice. This paper asks how closely a deterministic classifier can approximate a stochastic one.

The authors compare several approaches to removing prediction randomness and establish both lower and upper bounds. These bounds address complementary questions: what approximation quality a method can achieve, and what limits constrain the task. The theoretical focus is therefore the relationship between the original randomized classifier and a replacement that makes deterministic decisions.

The experimental study considers more than approximation quality alone. It also examines how well each approach handles the practical issues that made randomness undesirable in the first place. This distinction matters because faithfully matching a stochastic classifier and providing a useful deterministic replacement are related but separate goals. The paper evaluates the advantages and disadvantages of the methods through both perspectives.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds and empirically compares ways to replace randomized classifiers with deterministic approximations.

title: On Making Stochastic Classifiers Deterministic

abstract: We consider a collaborative learning scenario in which multiple data-owners wish to jointly train a logistic regression model, while keeping their individual datasets private from the other parties. We propose COPML, a fully-decentralized training framework that achieves scalability and privacy-protection simultaneously. The key idea of COPML is to securely encode the individual datasets to distribute the computation load effectively across many parties and to perform the training computations as well as the model updates in a distributed manner on the securely encoded data. We provide the privacy analysis of COPML and prove its convergence. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate that COPML can achieve significant speedup in training over the benchmark protocols. Our protocol provides strong statistical privacy guarantees against colluding parties (adversaries) with unbounded computational power, while achieving up to $16\times$ speedup in the training time against the benchmark protocols.
