paragraphs: COPML addresses a collaborative learning problem: several data owners want to train one logistic regression model while keeping their individual datasets private from one another. The paper aims to make this collaboration scalable as well as private, so distributing work across additional participants can help with the computational burden.

The framework securely encodes each owner's data and distributes computation across the participating parties. Both training calculations and model updates operate on those encoded data in a fully decentralized arrangement. This makes secure encoding part of the computational organization of training, rather than merely a way to protect data during transfer.

The authors analyze privacy and prove convergence of the training procedure. Their protocol provides statistical privacy guarantees against colluding adversaries even when those adversaries have unbounded computing power. Experiments report training speedups of up to sixteen times over the benchmark protocols. These results support the possibility of combining privacy protection with substantial computational gains in the collaborative logistic regression setting studied.
summary.tldr: COPML distributes logistic regression training over securely encoded data, providing statistical privacy guarantees and reported speedups of up to sixteen times.

title: A Scalable Approach for Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Machine Learning

abstract: We present Cycle-Contrastive Learning (CCL), a novel self-supervised method for learning video representation. Following a nature that there is a belong and inclusion relation of video and its frames, CCL is designed to find correspondences across frames and videos considering the contrastive representation in their domains respectively. It is different from recent approaches that merely learn correspondences across frames or clips. In our method, the frame and video representations are learned from a single network based on an R3D network, with a shared non-linear transformation for embedding both frame and video features before the cycle-contrastive loss. We demonstrate that the video representation learned by CCL can be transferred well to downstream tasks of video understanding, outperforming previous methods in nearest neighbour retrieval and action recognition tasks on UCF101, HMDB51 and MMAct.

It is different from recent approaches that merely learn correspondences across frames or clips. In our method, the frame and video representations are learned from a single network based on an R3D network, with a shared non-linear transformation for embedding both frame and video features before the cycle-contrastive loss. We demonstrate that the video representation learned by CCL can be transferred well to downstream tasks of video understanding, outperforming previous methods in nearest neighbour retrieval and action recognition tasks on UCF101, HMDB51 and MMAct.

paragraphs: Cycle-Contrastive Learning learns video representations through self-supervision by connecting individual frames with the videos containing them. Its starting point is the relationship between a whole video and its constituent frames. The method uses that relationship to learn correspondences across both levels, extending the focus beyond matching frames or matching clips alone.

Frame and video representations come from a single network based on an R3D architecture. A shared nonlinear transformation embeds features from both levels before the cycle-contrastive loss is applied. The training design therefore connects frame-level and video-level learning while considering contrastive representations within their respective domains. This gives the model a way to use relationships between parts and wholes as a learning signal.

The authors evaluate whether the resulting representations transfer to video understanding tasks. They report better nearest-neighbor retrieval and action recognition performance than previous methods on UCF101, HMDB51, and MMAct. These findings support the usefulness of learning frame–video relationships for representations that can subsequently serve multiple downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: Cycle-Contrastive Learning uses relationships between frames and whole videos to learn representations that improve reported retrieval and action recognition results.

title: Cycle-Contrast for Self-Supervised Video Representation Learning

abstract: Gradient clipping is commonly used in training deep neural networks partly due to its practicability in relieving the exploding gradient problem. Recently, \citet{zhang2019gradient} show that clipped (stochastic) Gradient Descent (GD) converges faster than vanilla GD via introducing a new assumption called $(L_0, L_1)$-smoothness, which characterizes the violent fluctuation of gradients typically encountered in deep neural networks. However, their iteration complexities on the problem-dependent parameters are rather pessimistic, and theoretical justification of clipping combined with other crucial techniques, e.g. momentum acceleration, are still lacking. In this paper, we bridge the gap by presenting a general framework to study the clipping algorithms, which also takes momentum methods into consideration.We provide convergence analysis of the framework in both deterministic and stochastic setting, and demonstrate the tightness of our results by comparing them with existing lower bounds. Our results imply that the efficiency of clipping methods will not degenerate even in highly non-smooth regions of the landscape. Experiments confirm the superiority of clipping-based methods in deep learning tasks.

paragraphs: Gradient clipping is widely used to manage exploding gradients during neural-network training. Earlier theory showed advantages over ordinary gradient descent under an assumption called (L0, L1)-smoothness, designed to capture sharp changes in gradients. However, those bounds had pessimistic dependence on problem parameters and did not adequately explain clipping combined with momentum.

This paper develops a general framework that includes both clipping and momentum methods. It analyzes convergence in deterministic and stochastic settings, covering computations with exact gradients and those using noisy estimates. The authors assess the tightness of their results by comparing the guarantees with existing lower bounds.

Within the analyzed framework, the results imply that clipping methods retain their efficiency even in regions where the landscape behaves highly nonsmoothly. Deep-learning experiments also favor clipping-based methods. The contribution strengthens the mathematical explanation for a practical training technique and extends that explanation to its interaction with momentum, rather than analyzing clipping only as an isolated modification.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis strengthens convergence guarantees for gradient clipping and incorporates momentum in deterministic and stochastic optimization.

title: Improved Analysis of Clipping Algorithms for Non-convex Optimization

abstract: We study dropout in two-layer neural networks with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations. Under mild overparametrization and assuming that the limiting kernel can separate the data distribution with a positive margin, we show that the dropout training with logistic loss achieves $\epsilon$-suboptimality in the test error in $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations.
originalAbstract: We study dropout in two-layer neural networks with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations. Under mild overparametrization and assuming that the limiting kernel can separate the data distribution with a positive margin, we show that the dropout training with logistic loss achieves $\epsilon$-suboptimality in the test error in $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations.

paragraphs: This paper gives a theoretical guarantee for dropout training in a specific neural-network setting. The networks have two layers and use rectified linear unit activations, and training uses logistic loss. The result concerns test error, linking the training procedure to performance on the data distribution beyond the training examples.

The guarantee requires mild overparameterization and a positive-margin separation assumption on the limiting kernel. In plain terms, the kernel associated with the limiting model must be able to distinguish the distribution's classes with some separation to spare. These conditions specify the setting in which the claimed convergence behavior holds.

Under those assumptions, dropout training reaches epsilon-suboptimal test error in a number of iterations proportional to one over epsilon. Thus the theorem quantifies how the iteration requirement scales as the desired error tolerance becomes smaller. Its significance is the joint treatment of optimization progress and generalization for dropout, with a concrete accuracy dependence established for the stated architecture, loss, and separation conditions.
summary.tldr: For mildly overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks with a separating limiting kernel, dropout reaches epsilon-suboptimal test error in O(1/epsilon) iterations.

title: On Convergence and Generalization of Dropout Training

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation aims to align a labeled source domain and an unlabeled target domain, but it requires to access the source data which often raises concerns in data privacy, data portability and data transmission efficiency. We study unsupervised model adaptation (UMA), or called Unsupervised Domain Adaptation without Source Data, an alternative setting that aims to adapt source-trained models towards target distributions without accessing source data. To this end, we design an innovative historical contrastive learning (HCL) technique that exploits historical source hypothesis to make up for the absence of source data in UMA. HCL addresses the UMA challenge from two perspectives. First, it introduces historical contrastive instance discrimination (HCID) that learns from target samples by contrasting their embeddings which are generated by the currently adapted model and the historical models. With the historical models, HCID encourages UMA to learn instance-discriminative target representations while preserving the source hypothesis. Second, it introduces historical contrastive category discrimination (HCCD) that pseudo-labels target samples to learn category-discriminative target representations. Specifically, HCCD re-weights pseudo labels according to their prediction consistency across the current and historical models. Extensive experiments show that HCL outperforms and state-of-the-art methods consistently across a variety of visual tasks and setups.

paragraphs: Adapting a trained model to an unlabelled target domain often assumes access to the original source data. That access can be difficult because of privacy, portability, or transmission concerns. This paper instead studies adaptation using a source-trained model without the source dataset, drawing on historical models to retain useful information during adaptation.

Historical contrastive learning has two components. The first contrasts target-image embeddings produced by the current model and historical models. It encourages representations that distinguish individual target examples while preserving the source hypothesis. The second assigns pseudo-labels to target samples and adjusts their weights according to prediction consistency across current and historical models.

These components support complementary goals: keeping individual examples distinguishable and learning representations that separate categories. Historical predictions provide a reference throughout both processes, compensating for the absence of source observations. The authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods across several visual tasks and setups. The results support model history as a useful resource for adapting to an unlabelled domain.
summary.tldr: Historical contrastive learning uses current and past models to adapt to unlabelled target data without accessing source data.

title: Model Adaptation: Historical Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation without Source Data

abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is the problem of finding a reward function which describes observed/known expert behavior. The IRL setting is remarkably useful for automated control, in situations where the reward function is difficult to specify manually or as a means to extract agent preference. In this work, we provide a new IRL algorithm for the continuous state space setting with unknown transition dynamics by modeling the system using a basis of orthonormal functions. Moreover, we provide a proof of correctness and formal guarantees on the sample and time complexity of our algorithm. Finally, we present synthetic experiments to corroborate our theoretical guarantees.
originalAbstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is the problem of finding a reward function which describes observed/known expert behavior. The IRL setting is remarkably useful for automated control, in situations where the reward function is difficult to specify manually or as a means to extract agent preference. In this work, we provide a new IRL algorithm for the continuous state space setting with unknown transition dynamics by modeling the system using a basis of orthonormal functions. Moreover, we provide a proof of correctness and formal guarantees on the sample and time complexity of our algorithm. Finally, we present synthetic experiments to corroborate our theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning starts with expert behavior and seeks a reward function that describes it. This can help when a useful reward is difficult to write manually, or when the aim is to infer an agent's preferences. The paper develops an algorithm for continuous state spaces where the transition dynamics are unknown.

A continuous state space allows states to vary across a continuum, rather than belonging to a finite list. Unknown dynamics mean that the algorithm is not given the system's transition behavior in advance. The authors model the system through a basis of orthonormal functions, providing a mathematical representation for addressing both aspects of this learning setting.

The contribution includes a correctness proof and formal bounds on sample requirements and running time. These guarantees address whether the algorithm works and how much data and computation it requires within its analyzed setting. Synthetic experiments corroborate the theoretical results. The paper thus connects reward inference from expert behavior with an explicitly analyzed algorithm for continuous systems, supported by controlled experimental evidence.
summary.tldr: An inverse reinforcement-learning algorithm infers rewards in continuous state spaces with unknown dynamics and provides correctness and complexity guarantees.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning in a Continuous State Space with Formal Guarantees

abstract: Temporal-difference learning with gradient correction (TDC) is a two time-scale algorithm for policy evaluation in reinforcement learning. This algorithm was initially proposed with linear function approximation, and was later extended to the one with general smooth function approximation. The asymptotic convergence for the on-policy setting with general smooth function approximation was established in [Bhatnagar et al., 2009], however, the non-asymptotic convergence analysis remains unsolved due to challenges in the non-linear and two-time-scale update structure, non-convex objective function and the projection onto a time-varying tangent plane. In this paper, we develop novel techniques to address the above challenges and explicitly characterize the non-asymptotic error bound for the general off-policy setting with i.i.d. or Markovian samples, and show that it converges as fast as $\mathcal O(1/\sqrt T)$ (up to a factor of $\mathcal O(\log T)$). Our approach can be applied to a wide range of value-based reinforcement learning algorithms with general smooth function approximation.

In this paper, we develop novel techniques to address the above challenges and explicitly characterize the non-asymptotic error bound for the general off-policy setting with i.i.d. or Markovian samples, and show that it converges as fast as $\mathcal O(1/\sqrt T)$ (up to a factor of $\mathcal O(\log T)$). Our approach can be applied to a wide range of value-based reinforcement learning algorithms with general smooth function approximation.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning with gradient correction, or TDC, estimates the value of a policy using two coupled updates that operate at different time scales. Although it began with linear function approximation, it was extended to general smooth approximators. Existing asymptotic convergence results did not establish how much error remains after a finite number of updates.

This paper develops a finite-time analysis for the more general off-policy setting, where the data-generating policy can differ from the policy being evaluated. The analysis covers both independent samples and Markovian samples. Its technical challenges include nonlinear updates, a nonconvex objective, and projection onto a tangent plane that changes over time.

The authors explicitly bound the error and obtain convergence as fast as order one over the square root of the iteration count, up to a logarithmic factor. This turns a long-run convergence question into a quantitative statement about progress with finite data and computation. They also state that their analytical approach applies to a broad range of value-based reinforcement learning algorithms using smooth function approximation.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes finite-time error bounds for off-policy TDC with smooth nonlinear approximation and independent or Markovian samples.

title: Non-Asymptotic Analysis for Two Time-scale TDC with General Smooth Function Approximation

abstract: Combining discrete probability distributions and combinatorial optimization problems with neural network components has numerous applications but poses several challenges. We propose Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (I-MLE), a framework for end-to-end learning of models combining discrete exponential family distributions and differentiable neural components. I-MLE is widely applicable as it only requires the ability to compute the most probable states and does not rely on smooth relaxations. The framework encompasses several approaches such as perturbation-based implicit differentiation and recent methods to differentiate through black-box combinatorial solvers. We introduce a novel class of noise distributions for approximating marginals via perturb-and-MAP. Moreover, we show that I-MLE simplifies to maximum likelihood estimation when used in some recently studied learning settings that involve combinatorial solvers. Experiments on several datasets suggest that I-MLE is competitive with and often outperforms existing approaches which rely on problem-specific relaxations.

We propose Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (I-MLE), a framework for end-to-end learning of models combining discrete exponential family distributions and differentiable neural components. I-MLE is widely applicable as it only requires the ability to compute the most probable states and does not rely on smooth relaxations. The framework encompasses several approaches such as perturbation-based implicit differentiation and recent methods to differentiate through black-box combinatorial solvers. We introduce a novel class of noise distributions for approximating marginals via perturb-and-MAP. Moreover, we show that I-MLE simplifies to maximum likelihood estimation when used in some recently studied learning settings that involve combinatorial solvers. Experiments on several datasets suggest that I-MLE is competitive with and often outperforms existing approaches which rely on problem-specific relaxations.

paragraphs: Combining neural networks with discrete choices or combinatorial solvers creates a training challenge: ordinary gradient methods do not pass straightforwardly through discrete computations. Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or I-MLE, provides a framework for learning such combined models end to end. Its scope includes discrete exponential-family distributions alongside differentiable neural components.

The framework requires the ability to find the most probable discrete states and does not depend on replacing the problem with a smooth relaxation. It encompasses perturbation-based implicit differentiation and approaches for differentiating through black-box combinatorial solvers. The authors also introduce noise distributions for approximating marginal probabilities by perturbing a problem and finding its most probable state.

In some previously studied learning settings involving combinatorial solvers, the authors show that I-MLE reduces to ordinary maximum likelihood estimation. Experiments across several datasets suggest performance that is competitive with, and often better than, methods using problem-specific relaxations. The contribution is both a shared perspective on existing techniques and a broadly applicable route to training models with discrete internal computations.
summary.tldr: I-MLE enables end-to-end learning through discrete distributions and combinatorial solvers using most-probable-state computations without smooth relaxations.

title: Implicit MLE: Backpropagating Through Discrete Exponential Family Distributions

abstract: Datasets for training machine learning models tend to be biased unless the data is collected with complete care. In such a biased dataset, models are susceptible to making predictions based on the biased features of the data. The biased model fails to generalize to the case where correlations between biases and targets are shifted. To mitigate this, we propose Bias-Contrastive (BiasCon) loss based on the contrastive learning framework, which effectively leverages the knowledge of bias labels. We further suggest Bias-Balanced (BiasBal) regression which trains the classification model toward the data distribution with balanced target-bias correlation. Furthermore, we propose Soft Bias-Contrastive (SoftCon) loss which handles the dataset without bias labels by softening the pair assignment of the BiasCon loss based on the distance in the feature space of the bias-capturing model. Our experiments show that our proposed methods significantly improve previous debiasing methods in various realistic datasets.

paragraphs: When a training dataset links a target label to a biased feature, a classifier can learn to rely on that association. Its predictions can then fail when the association changes. This paper proposes training methods aimed at reducing that reliance, covering datasets both with and without explicit bias labels.

Bias-Contrastive loss uses known bias labels within a contrastive-learning framework. Bias-Balanced regression trains the classifier toward a distribution with balanced relationships between targets and biases. These approaches use information about the bias to change the learning objective, addressing the correlation that could otherwise become a shortcut for prediction.

It derives these from distances in the feature space of a model that captures bias. Experiments report significant improvements over previous debiasing methods on several realistic datasets. The contribution provides related training objectives for different levels of available bias information, with empirical evidence that they improve classification under the evaluated conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces contrastive and balancing objectives that reduce classifiers' reliance on biased correlations, with or without bias labels.

title: Unbiased Classification through Bias-Contrastive and Bias-Balanced Learning

abstract: Time is an important dimension in our physical world. Lots of facts can evolve with respect to time. For example, the U.S. President might change every four years. Therefore, it is important to consider the time dimension and empower the existing QA models to reason over time. However, the existing QA datasets contain rather few time-sensitive questions, hence not suitable for diagnosing or benchmarking the model's temporal reasoning capability. In order to promote research in this direction, we propose to construct a time-sensitive QA dataset. The dataset is constructed by 1) mining time-evolving facts from WikiData and aligning them to their corresponding Wikipedia page, 2) employing crowd workers to verify and calibrate these noisy facts, 3) generating question-answer pairs based on the annotated time-sensitive facts. Our dataset poses challenges in the aspect of both temporal understanding and temporal reasoning. We evaluate different SoTA long-document QA systems like BigBird and FiD on our dataset. The best-performing model FiD can only achieve 46\% accuracy, still far behind the human performance of 87\%. We demonstrate that these models are still lacking the ability to perform consistent temporal reasoning. Therefore, we believe that our dataset could serve as a benchmark to develop NLP models more sensitive to temporal shifts.

This paper introduces a question-answering dataset designed to test that dependence on time. Its motivation is that existing datasets contain too few time-sensitive questions to give a useful picture of a model’s temporal understanding and reasoning.

The authors build the dataset by extracting facts that change over time from WikiData and linking them to corresponding Wikipedia pages. The verified annotations become the basis for question-answer pairs, connecting the questions to information whose timing affects the correct answer.

The authors’ analysis also finds inconsistent temporal reasoning. These results make the dataset useful for studying whether systems can reason about temporal changes, beyond simply finding relevant text.
summary.tldr: A time-sensitive question-answering dataset exposes a substantial gap between tested language models and human temporal reasoning.

title: A Dataset for Answering Time-Sensitive Questions

abstract: We introduce Argoverse 2 (AV2) — a collection of three datasets for perception and forecasting research in the self-driving domain. The annotated Sensor Dataset contains 1,000 sequences of multimodal data, encompassing high-resolution imagery from seven ring cameras, and two stereo cameras in addition to lidar point clouds, and 6-DOF map-aligned pose. Sequences contain 3D cuboid annotations for 26 object categories, all of which are sufficiently-sampled to support training and evaluation of 3D perception models. The Lidar Dataset contains 20,000 sequences of unlabeled lidar point clouds and map-aligned pose. This dataset is the largest ever collection of lidar sensor data and supports self-supervised learning and the emerging task of point cloud forecasting. Finally, the Motion Forecasting Dataset contains 250,000 scenarios mined for interesting and challenging interactions be- tween the autonomous vehicle and other actors in each local scene. Models are tasked with the prediction of future motion for “scored actors" in each scenario and are provided with track histories that capture object location, heading, velocity, and category. In all three datasets, each scenario contains its own HD Map with 3D lane and crosswalk geometry — sourced from data captured in six distinct cities. We believe these datasets will support new and existing machine learning research problems in ways that existing datasets do not. All datasets are released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.

Its annotated Sensor Dataset contains 1,000 sequences combining imagery from seven ring cameras and two stereo cameras with lidar and map-aligned vehicle pose. Three-dimensional boxes identify objects in 26 categories, with samples supporting model training and evaluation.

The Lidar Dataset supplies 20,000 unlabeled sequences for self-supervised learning and point-cloud forecasting. The Motion Forecasting Dataset adds 250,000 scenarios selected for challenging interactions between the autonomous vehicle and other actors. Models receive histories describing location, heading, velocity, and category, and predict the future movement of designated actors.

Across all three datasets, each scenario includes a high-definition map with three-dimensional lane and crosswalk geometry. The data span six cities, connecting sensor observations and movement histories to local road structure. This collection supports multiple research tasks through related forms of driving data, and the datasets are released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.
summary.tldr: Argoverse 2 combines annotated sensors, unlabeled lidar, and motion scenarios with detailed maps for self-driving perception and forecasting research.

title: Argoverse 2: Next Generation Datasets for Self-Driving Perception and Forecasting

abstract: Existing top-performance 3D object detectors typically rely on the multi-modal fusion strategy. This design is however fundamentally restricted due to overlooking the modality-specific useful information and finally hampering the model performance. To address this limitation, in this work we introduce a novel modality interaction strategy where individual per-modality representations are learned and maintained throughout for enabling their unique characteristics to be exploited during object detection. To realize this proposed strategy, we design a DeepInteraction architecture characterized by a multi-modal representational interaction encoder and a multi-modal predictive interaction decoder. Experiments on the large-scale nuScenes dataset show that our proposed method surpasses all prior arts often by a large margin. Crucially, our method is ranked at the first position at the highly competitive nuScenes object detection leaderboard.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional object detectors often combine information from multiple modalities to improve their predictions. This paper argues that existing fusion strategies can overlook useful information specific to each modality. Combining inputs is therefore only part of the challenge: the detector also needs to retain the distinctive information each input provides.

DeepInteraction learns and maintains a separate representation for each modality throughout detection. Those representations interact through an architecture with two main components: an encoder for interaction between multimodal representations and a decoder for interaction during prediction. The design allows information to pass between modalities while preserving representations in which their individual characteristics remain available.

Experiments on nuScenes show that DeepInteraction surpasses prior methods, often by a large margin, and the paper reports first place on its object detection leaderboard. These results support modality interaction as an effective design for the evaluated detection setting. The broader architectural lesson is that maintaining distinct representations can matter alongside enabling information exchange between them.
summary.tldr: DeepInteraction improves 3D detection by letting modalities exchange information while maintaining their separate representations.

title: DeepInteraction: 3D Object Detection via Modality Interaction

abstract: Paraphrase Identification is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing. While much progress has been made in the field, the performance of many state-of- the-art models often suffer from distribution shift during inference time. We verify that a major source of this performance drop comes from biases introduced by negative examples. To overcome these biases, we propose in this paper to train two separate models, one that only utilizes the positive pairs and the other the negative pairs. This enables us the option of deciding how much to utilize the negative model, for which we introduce a perplexity based out-of-distribution metric that we show can effectively and automatically determine how much weight it should be given during inference. We support our findings with strong empirical results.

paragraphs: Paraphrase identification asks whether two pieces of text express the same meaning. Strong models can lose accuracy when the examples encountered during use differ from their training distribution. This paper identifies biases introduced by negative examples, pairs that are not paraphrases, as a major contributor to that performance drop.

GAPX separates the learning process into two models: one trained only on positive pairs and another trained only on negative pairs. This separation makes the influence of negative examples adjustable at prediction time. The authors introduce a perplexity-based measure of distribution shift that automatically determines how much weight to give the negative model.

The reported empirical results support both the diagnosis of negative-example bias and the proposed response. The approach matters because information learned from non-paraphrases need not have the same usefulness across different input distributions. Giving that information a separately controlled contribution lets the system adapt its reliance on it when making predictions on unfamiliar data.
summary.tldr: GAPX addresses distribution shift in paraphrase identification by separately learning from negative pairs and adapting their influence at inference.

title: GAPX: Generalized Autoregressive Paraphrase-Identification X

abstract: As the scope of machine learning broadens, we observe a recurring theme of *algorithmic monoculture*: the same systems, or systems that share components (e.g. datasets, models), are deployed by multiple decision-makers. While sharing offers advantages like amortizing effort, it also has risks. We introduce and formalize one such risk, *outcome homogenization*: the extent to which particular individuals or groups experience the same outcomes across different deployments. If the same individuals or groups exclusively experience undesirable outcomes, this may institutionalize systemic exclusion and reinscribe social hierarchy. We relate algorithmic monoculture and outcome homogenization by proposing the *component sharing hypothesis*: if algorithmic systems are increasingly built on the same data or models, then they will increasingly homogenize outcomes. We test this hypothesis on algorithmic fairness benchmarks, demonstrating that increased data-sharing reliably exacerbates homogenization and individual-level effects generally exceed group-level effects. Further, given the current regime in AI of foundation models, i.e. pretrained models that can be adapted to myriad downstream tasks, we test whether model-sharing homogenizes outcomes across tasks. We observe mixed results: we find that for both vision and language settings, the specific methods for adapting a foundation model significantly influence the degree of outcome homogenization. We also identify societal challenges that inhibit the measurement, diagnosis, and rectification of outcome homogenization in deployed machine learning systems.

paragraphs: When multiple decision-makers reuse datasets, models, or entire systems, the benefits of sharing may accompany a less visible risk: the same people repeatedly receive the same outcomes. This paper formalizes that risk as outcome homogenization. Repeatedly concentrating undesirable outcomes on particular individuals or groups may reinforce systemic exclusion.

The authors propose a component-sharing hypothesis: greater reuse of data or models will increase outcome similarity across deployments. Tests on algorithmic fairness benchmarks find that increased data sharing reliably worsens homogenization. Effects at the individual level generally exceed those measured at the group level, highlighting why tracking broad groups alone may give an incomplete view of repeated outcomes.

Results for shared foundation models are mixed. Across vision and language settings, the method used to adapt a pretrained model substantially influences the degree of homogenization across tasks. The findings therefore distinguish the observed effect of data sharing from the more conditional effect of model sharing. The paper also identifies societal obstacles to measuring, diagnosing, and correcting this phenomenon in deployed systems.
summary.tldr: Shared training data can concentrate repeated outcomes on the same people, while shared foundation models show effects that depend on adaptation methods.

title: Picking on the Same Person: Does Algorithmic Monoculture lead to Outcome Homogenization?

abstract: Nonnegative (linear) least square problems are a fundamental class of problems that is well-studied in statistical learning and for which solvers have been implemented in many of the standard programming languages used within the machine learning community. The existing off-the-shelf solvers view the non-negativity constraint in these problems as an obstacle and, compared to unconstrained least squares, perform additional effort to address it. However, in many of the typical applications, the data itself is nonnegative as well, and we show that the nonnegativity in this case makes the problem easier. In particular, while the worst-case dimension-independent oracle complexity of unconstrained least squares problems necessarily scales with one of the data matrix constants (typically the spectral norm) and these problems are solved to additive error, we show that nonnegative least squares problems with nonnegative data are solvable to multiplicative error and with complexity that is independent of any matrix constants. The algorithm we introduce is accelerated and based on a primal-dual perspective. We further show how to provably obtain linear convergence using adaptive restart coupled with our method and demonstrate its effectiveness on large-scale data via numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Nonnegative least squares fits a linear model while requiring its coefficients to stay nonnegative. Standard solvers typically treat that restriction as an extra complication. This paper asks what happens when the data are also nonnegative, and shows that the combination provides useful structure that an algorithm can exploit.

The authors introduce an accelerated algorithm based on a primal-dual formulation. Their central theoretical result concerns dimension-independent oracle complexity, a measure of the computational queries required to reach a desired accuracy. For nonnegative data, they obtain multiplicative accuracy with complexity independent of matrix constants. This differs from the stated worst-case behavior of unconstrained least squares, whose corresponding complexity necessarily depends on a matrix quantity and whose accuracy is additive.

The paper also establishes linear convergence by combining its method with adaptive restarting, and demonstrates effectiveness in numerical experiments on large datasets. The contribution is therefore both an algorithm and a sharper account of when nonnegativity helps: the favorable result specifically uses nonnegative data as well as nonnegative coefficients.
summary.tldr: An accelerated solver exploits nonnegative data to give nonnegative least squares multiplicative accuracy guarantees independent of matrix constants.

title: A Fast Scale-Invariant Algorithm for Non-negative Least Squares with Non-negative Data

abstract: Kernel matrix-vector multiplication (KMVM) is a foundational operation in machine learning and scientific computing. However, as KMVM tends to scale quadratically in both memory and time, applications are often limited by these computational constraints. In this paper, we propose a novel approximation procedure coined \textit{Faster-Fast and Free Memory Method} ($\text{F}^3$M) to address these scaling issues of KMVM for tall~($10^8\sim 10^9$) and skinny~($D\leq7$) data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $\text{F}^3$M has empirical \emph{linear time and memory} complexity with a relative error of order $10^{-3}$ and can compute a full KMVM for a billion points \emph{in under a minute} on a high-end GPU, leading to a significant speed-up in comparison to existing CPU methods. We demonstrate the utility of our procedure by applying it as a drop-in for the state-of-the-art GPU-based linear solver FALKON, \emph{improving speed 1.5-5.5 times} at the cost of $<1\%$ drop in accuracy. We further demonstrate competitive results on \emph{Gaussian Process regression} coupled with significant speedups on a variety of real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Kernel matrix-vector multiplication is a basic operation in machine learning and scientific computing, but its time and memory demands can grow quadratically with the number of points. The Faster-Fast and Free Memory Method, abbreviated F³M, approximates this operation for exceptionally large datasets with relatively few features: roughly one hundred million to one billion points, with dimension at most seven.

The reported experiments show empirical linear growth in time and memory, with relative error on the order of one thousandth. On a high-end GPU, the method performs a full approximate multiplication for a billion points in under a minute. These are experimental scaling and accuracy results for the targeted low-dimensional setting.

The authors also test whether the approximation helps complete learning systems. Used inside the GPU solver FALKON, it provides speedups of 1.5 to 5.5 times with less than a 1% accuracy drop. Gaussian process regression experiments show competitive results with substantial speedups, supporting the method's usefulness beyond an isolated computational benchmark.
summary.tldr: F³M approximates kernel matrix-vector products at billion-point scale on GPUs, showing empirical linear scaling for low-dimensional data.

title: Giga-scale Kernel Matrix-Vector Multiplication on GPU

abstract: Structured prediction of tree-shaped objects is heavily studied under the name of syntactic dependency parsing. Current practice based on maximum likelihood or margin is either agnostic to or inconsistent with the evaluation loss. Risk minimization alleviates the discrepancy between training and test objectives but typically induces a non-convex problem. These approaches adopt explicit regularization to combat overfitting without probabilistic interpretation. We propose a moment-based distributionally robust optimization approach for tree structured prediction, where the worst-case expected loss over a set of distributions within bounded moment divergence from the empirical distribution is minimized. We develop efficient algorithms for arborescences and other variants of trees. We derive Fisher consistency, convergence rates and generalization bounds for our proposed method. We evaluate its empirical effectiveness on dependency parsing benchmarks.

Risk minimization alleviates the discrepancy between training and test objectives but typically induces a non-convex problem. These approaches adopt explicit regularization to combat overfitting without probabilistic interpretation. We propose a moment-based distributionally robust optimization approach for tree structured prediction, where the worst-case expected loss over a set of distributions within bounded moment divergence from the empirical distribution is minimized. We develop efficient algorithms for arborescences and other variants of trees. We derive Fisher consistency, convergence rates and generalization bounds for our proposed method. paragraphs: Predicting a tree-shaped output arises in dependency parsing, where a model identifies relationships between words. Standard likelihood or margin objectives may not align with the loss used to evaluate those predictions. Directly minimizing risk addresses that mismatch but typically creates a non-convex optimization problem.

This paper proposes a distributionally robust objective based on moments. It considers a set of distributions whose moment divergence from the empirical distribution is bounded, then minimizes the worst-case expected loss within that set. This puts uncertainty about the data distribution directly into the learning objective and connects training to the evaluation loss.

The authors develop efficient algorithms for arborescences and other tree variants. They also derive Fisher consistency, convergence rates, and generalization bounds, supplying theoretical support for the proposed learning procedure. Empirical evaluation uses dependency parsing benchmarks. The contribution brings together a loss-aware objective, an explicit distributional uncertainty formulation, and algorithms specialized to tree outputs, providing a structured approach to the mismatch between training objectives and evaluation.
summary.tldr: The method learns tree predictions by minimizing worst-case expected loss over distributions constrained by their moment divergence from observed data.

title: Moment Distributionally Robust Tree Structured Prediction

abstract: In fair rent division, the problem is to assign rooms to roommates and fairly split the rent based on roommates' reported valuations for the rooms. Envy-free rent division is the most popular application on the fair division website Spliddit. The standard model assumes that agents can correctly report their valuations for each room. In practice, agents may be unsure about their valuations, for example because they have had only limited time to inspect the rooms. Our goal is to find a robust rent division that remains fair even if agent valuations are slightly different from the reported ones. We introduce the lexislack solution, which selects a rent division that remains envy-free for valuations within as large a radius as possible of the reported valuations. We also consider robustness notions for valuations that come from a probability distribution, and use results from learning theory to show how we can find rent divisions that (almost) maximize the probability of being envy-free, or that minimize the expected envy. We show that an almost optimal allocation can be identified based on polynomially many samples from the valuation distribution. Finding the best allocation given these samples is NP-hard, but in practice such an allocation can be found using integer linear programming.

paragraphs: Fair rent division assigns rooms and prices using roommates’ reported preferences. An envy-free outcome gives nobody a reason to prefer another roommate’s room-price combination. This paper questions the assumption that reported room values are exact: people may have inspected rooms only briefly and remain uncertain about how much they value them.

The proposed lexislack solution seeks an allocation that stays envy-free across as large a radius of valuation changes as possible around the reports. The authors also consider valuations drawn from a probability distribution. In that setting, they study allocations that nearly maximize the probability of envy-freeness or minimize expected envy.

Learning-theoretic results show that polynomially many samples from the valuation distribution suffice to identify an almost optimal allocation. Computing the best allocation for those samples is NP-hard, although integer linear programming can find such allocations in practice. The paper therefore distinguishes how much preference information is needed from how difficult the resulting optimization is, while making uncertainty in preferences central to fairness.
summary.tldr: Robust rent division seeks room assignments and prices that preserve fairness when reported preferences are uncertain.

title: Robust Rent Division

abstract: Molecular optimization is a fundamental goal in the chemical sciences and is of central interest to drug and material design. In recent years, significant progress has been made in solving challenging problems across various aspects of computational molecular optimizations, emphasizing high validity, diversity, and, most recently, synthesizability. Despite this progress, many papers report results on trivial or self-designed tasks, bringing additional challenges to directly assessing the performance of new methods. Moreover, the sample efficiency of the optimization---the number of molecules evaluated by the oracle---is rarely discussed, despite being an essential consideration for realistic discovery applications.To fill this gap, we have created an open-source benchmark for practical molecular optimization, PMO, to facilitate the transparent and reproducible evaluation of algorithmic advances in molecular optimization. This paper thoroughly investigates the performance of 25 molecular design algorithms on 23 single-objective (scalar) optimization tasks with a particular focus on sample efficiency. Our results show that most ``state-of-the-art'' methods fail to outperform their predecessors under a limited oracle budget allowing 10K queries and that no existing algorithm can efficiently solve certain molecular optimization problems in this setting. We analyze the influence of the optimization algorithm choices, molecular assembly strategies, and oracle landscapes on the optimization performance to inform future algorithm development and benchmarking. PMO provides a standardized experimental setup to comprehensively evaluate and compare new molecule optimization methods with existing ones. All code can be found at https://github.com/wenhao-gao/mol_opt.

In recent years, significant progress has been made in solving challenging problems across various aspects of computational molecular optimizations, emphasizing high validity, diversity, and, most recently, synthesizability. Despite this progress, many papers report results on trivial or self-designed tasks, bringing additional challenges to directly assessing the performance of new methods. Moreover, the sample efficiency of the optimization---the number of molecules evaluated by the oracle---is rarely discussed, despite being an essential consideration for realistic discovery applications.To fill this gap, we have created an open-source benchmark for practical molecular optimization, PMO, to facilitate the transparent and reproducible evaluation of algorithmic advances in molecular optimization. This paper thoroughly investigates the performance of 25 molecular design algorithms on 23 single-objective (scalar) optimization tasks with a particular focus on sample efficiency. Our results show that most ``state-of-the-art'' methods fail to outperform their predecessors under a limited oracle budget allowing 10K queries and that no existing algorithm can efficiently solve certain molecular optimization problems in this setting. We analyze the influence of the optimization algorithm choices, molecular assembly strategies, and oracle landscapes on the optimization performance to inform future algorithm development and benchmarking. PMO provides a standardized experimental setup to comprehensively evaluate and compare new molecule optimization methods with existing ones. All code can be found at https://github.com/wenhao-gao/mol_opt.

paragraphs: Molecular optimization searches for molecules with desirable properties, but evaluating candidates consumes a limited resource. This paper emphasizes sample efficiency: how many molecules an algorithm must submit to the evaluation oracle. It argues that comparisons based on trivial or individually designed tasks make progress difficult to assess, especially when evaluation budgets are overlooked.

The authors introduce Practical Molecular Optimization, an open-source benchmark with a standardized experimental setup. They compare 25 molecular design algorithms across 23 tasks, each optimizing a single scalar objective. A central evaluation setting limits algorithms to 10,000 oracle queries, making the cost of finding good candidates explicit.

Under this budget, most methods described as state of the art fail to outperform their predecessors, and some benchmark problems remain unsolved efficiently by the evaluated algorithms. The study also examines optimization choices, molecule assembly strategies, and oracle landscapes. These results show why practical comparisons need to consider how quickly an algorithm improves, alongside the quality of molecules it eventually finds.
summary.tldr: PMO compares molecular optimization under limited evaluation budgets and finds that many newer methods do not outperform earlier ones.

title: Sample Efficiency Matters: A Benchmark for Practical Molecular Optimization

abstract: Data augmentation is a critical contributing factor to the success of deep learning but heavily relies on prior domain knowledge which is not always available. Recent works on automatic data augmentation learn a policy to form a sequence of augmentation operations, which are still pre-defined and restricted to limited options. In this paper, we show that a prior-free autonomous data augmentation's objective can be derived from a representation learning principle that aims to preserve the minimum sufficient information of the labels. Given an example, the objective aims at creating a distant ``hard positive example'' as the augmentation, while still preserving the original label. We then propose a practical surrogate to the objective that can be optimized efficiently and integrated seamlessly into existing methods for a broad class of machine learning tasks, e.g., supervised, semi-supervised, and noisy-label learning. Unlike previous works, our method does not require training an extra generative model but instead leverages the intermediate layer representations of the end-task model for generating data augmentations. In experiments, we show that our method consistently brings non-trivial improvements to the three aforementioned learning tasks from both efficiency and final performance, either or not combined with pre-defined augmentations, e.g., on medical images when domain knowledge is unavailable and the existing augmentation techniques perform poorly. Code will be released publicly.

paragraphs: Data augmentation creates additional training examples, but choosing appropriate transformations often requires domain knowledge. Even automatic augmentation methods can depend on a predefined menu of operations. This paper derives an augmentation objective from a representation-learning principle: retain the minimum information sufficient to determine the label while allowing other aspects of an example to change.

The resulting goal is to produce a hard positive example: an augmentation that is distant from the original while preserving its label. The authors introduce a practical surrogate objective that can be optimized efficiently. Their method uses intermediate representations from the model being trained to generate augmentations, avoiding the need to train an additional generative model.

The approach can be integrated into supervised, semi-supervised, and noisy-label learning. In the reported experiments, it improves efficiency and final performance across these three settings, both with and without predefined augmentations. The experiments include medical images where domain knowledge is unavailable and existing augmentation methods perform poorly. The results support deriving useful transformations from the learning objective and model representations themselves.
summary.tldr: A label-preserving augmentation objective uses a model’s internal representations to create challenging examples and improve several learning settings.

title: Adversarial Auto-Augment with Label Preservation: A Representation Learning Principle Guided Approach

abstract: For common notions of correlated equilibrium in extensive-form games, computing an optimal (e.g., welfare-maximizing) equilibrium is NP-hard. Other equilibrium notions---communication and certification equilibria---augment the game with a mediator that has the power to both send and receive messages to and from the players---and, in particular, to remember the messages. In this paper, we investigate both notions in extensive-form games from a computational lens. We show that optimal equilibria in both notions can be computed in polynomial time, the latter under a natural additional assumption known in the literature. Our proof works by constructing a {\em mediator-augmented game} of polynomial size that explicitly represents the mediator's decisions and actions. Our framework allows us to define an entire family of equilibria by varying the mediator's information partition, the players' ability to lie, and the players' ability to deviate. From this perspective, we show that other notions of equilibrium, such as extensive-form correlated equilibrium, correspond to the mediator having imperfect recall. This shows that, at least among all these equilibrium notions, the hardness of computation is driven by the mediator's imperfect recall. As special cases of our general construction, we recover the polynomial-time algorithm of Conitzer & Sandholm [2004] for automated mechanism design in Bayes-Nash equilibria, and the correlation DAG algorithm of Zhang et al [2022] for optimal correlation. Our algorithm is especially scalable when the equilibrium notion is what we define as the full-certification equilibrium, where players cannot lie about their information but they can be silent. We back up our theoretical claims with experiments on a suite of standard benchmark games.

paragraphs: Finding an optimal correlated equilibrium in a sequential game can be computationally hard. This paper examines communication and certification equilibria, where a mediator can send messages, receive messages, and remember them. It asks how these communication capabilities affect the difficulty of selecting an equilibrium that optimizes an objective such as welfare.

The analysis identifies that memory restriction as the driver of computational hardness among the notions considered. The construction also recovers earlier algorithms as special cases. A full-certification version, where players may remain silent but cannot lie about their information, is especially scalable, and experiments on standard benchmark games support the theoretical claims.
summary.tldr: Explicitly modeling a mediator yields polynomial-time optimal communication equilibria and, under an additional assumption, certification equilibria.

title: Polynomial-Time Optimal Equilibria with a Mediator in Extensive-Form Games

abstract: Neural networks are known to produce poor uncertainty estimations, and a variety of approaches have been proposed to remedy this issue. This includes deep ensemble, a simple and effective method that achieves state-of-the-art results for uncertainty-aware learning tasks. In this work, we explore a combinatorial generalization of deep ensemble called deep combinatorial aggregation (DCA). DCA creates multiple instances of network components and aggregates their combinations to produce diversified model proposals and predictions. DCA components can be defined at different levels of granularity. And we discovered that coarse-grain DCAs can outperform deep ensemble for uncertainty-aware learning both in terms of predictive performance and uncertainty estimation. For fine-grain DCAs, we discover that an average parameterization approach named deep combinatorial weight averaging (DCWA) can improve the baseline training. It is on par with stochastic weight averaging (SWA) but does not require any custom training schedule or adaptation of BatchNorm layers. Furthermore, we propose a consistency enforcing loss that helps the training of DCWA and modelwise DCA. We experiment on in-domain, distributional shift, and out-of-distribution image classification tasks, and empirically confirm the effectiveness of DCWA and DCA approaches.

paragraphs: Deep ensembles combine multiple neural networks to improve predictions and uncertainty estimates. Deep Combinatorial Aggregation extends this idea by creating multiple versions of network components and combining them in different ways. The resulting combinations supply diverse model proposals and predictions, making the choice of component size a central part of the approach.

The authors find that coarse component choices can outperform conventional deep ensembles in both predictive performance and uncertainty estimation. With finer components, they introduce Deep Combinatorial Weight Averaging, which averages parameterizations to improve baseline training. Its reported performance is comparable to stochastic weight averaging, while avoiding a custom training schedule or changes to BatchNorm layers.

The paper also introduces a loss that encourages consistency and helps train both the weight-averaging approach and modelwise DCA. Experiments cover image classification within the training domain, under distribution shifts, and on out-of-distribution inputs. These results support component recombination as a useful extension of ensemble learning, with different benefits emerging depending on how finely the networks are divided.
summary.tldr: Combining alternative network components improves uncertainty-aware learning, while a related weight-averaging method improves ordinary training.

title: Deep Combinatorial Aggregation

abstract: We present a scalable approach for learning open-world object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) – the task of asking a virtual robot (agent) to find any instance of an object in an unexplored environment (e.g., “find a sink”). Our approach is entirely zero-shot – i.e., it does not require ObjectNav rewards or demonstrations of any kind. Instead, we train on the image-goal navigation (ImageNav) task, in which agents find the location where a picture (i.e., goal image) was captured. Specifically, we encode goal images into a multimodal, semantic embedding space to enable training semantic-goal navigation (SemanticNav) agents at scale in unannotated 3D environments (e.g., HM3D). After training, SemanticNav agents can be instructed to find objects described in free-form natural language (e.g., “sink,” “bathroom sink,” etc.) by projecting language goals into the same multimodal, semantic embedding space. As a result, our approach enables open-world ObjectNav. We extensively evaluate our agents on three ObjectNav datasets (Gibson, HM3D, and MP3D) and observe absolute improvements in success of 4.2% - 20.0% over existing zero-shot methods. For reference, these gains are similar or better than the 5% improvement in success between the Habitat 2020 and 2021 ObjectNav challenge winners. In an open-world setting, we discover that our agents can generalize to compound instructions with a room explicitly mentioned (e.g., “Find a kitchen sink”) and when the target room can be inferred (e.g., “Find a sink and a stove”).

Zero-shot here refers to transferring into object-goal navigation without task-specific rewards or demonstrations; the navigation behavior itself is learned through the image-goal task.

The authors also observe generalization to compound requests that either name a room or imply one through a combination of objects. These findings support shared image-language goal representations as a scalable route to open-world object navigation.
summary.tldr: ZSON transfers image-goal navigation to language-directed object search through shared multimodal goal embeddings, without object-navigation rewards or demonstrations.

title: ZSON: Zero-Shot Object-Goal Navigation using Multimodal Goal Embeddings

abstract: We focus on the problem of generating high-quality, private synthetic glucose traces, a task generalizable to many other time series sources. Existing methods for time series data synthesis, such as those using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), are not able to capture the innate characteristics of glucose data and cannot provide any formal privacy guarantees without severely degrading the utility of the synthetic data. In this paper we present GlucoSynth, a novel privacy-preserving GAN framework to generate synthetic glucose traces. The core intuition behind our approach is to conserve relationships amongst motifs (glucose events) within the traces, in addition to temporal dynamics. Our framework incorporates differential privacy mechanisms to provide strong formal privacy guarantees. We provide a comprehensive evaluation on the real-world utility of the data using 1.2 million glucose traces; GlucoSynth outperforms all previous methods in its ability to generate high-quality synthetic glucose traces with strong privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: Synthetic glucose traces need to reproduce useful characteristics of real measurements while protecting the people whose data informed them. The authors argue that existing time-series generators struggle with the distinctive structure of glucose data and lose substantial utility when formal privacy protection is added. GlucoSynth addresses these two requirements within a single generative framework.

The method uses a generative adversarial network designed to preserve more than temporal dynamics alone. It also aims to conserve relationships among motifs, meaning glucose events within a trace. This makes the connections between events an explicit part of the generation approach. Differential privacy mechanisms supply formal privacy guarantees.

The evaluation uses 1.2 million glucose traces to examine the real-world utility of the synthetic data. The authors report that GlucoSynth surpasses previous methods in generating high-quality glucose traces with strong privacy guarantees. The findings support modeling event relationships as part of private time-series synthesis, with glucose data serving as the demonstrated application and other time-series sources identified as potential extensions.
summary.tldr: GlucoSynth preserves glucose-event relationships and temporal dynamics to generate useful synthetic traces with differential privacy guarantees.

title: GlucoSynth: Generating Differentially-Private Synthetic Glucose Traces

abstract: Visual Reinforcement Learning (Visual RL), coupled with high-dimensional observations, has consistently confronted the long-standing challenge of out-of-distribution generalization. Despite the focus on algorithms aimed at resolving visual generalization problems, we argue that the devil is in the existing benchmarks as they are restricted to isolated tasks and generalization categories, undermining a comprehensive evaluation of agents' visual generalization capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce RL-ViGen: a novel **R**einforcement **L**earning Benchmark for **Vi**sual **Gen**eralization, which contains diverse tasks and a wide spectrum of generalization types, thereby facilitating the derivation of more reliable conclusions. Furthermore, RL-ViGen incorporates the latest generalization visual RL algorithms into a unified framework, under which the experiment results indicate that no single existing algorithm has prevailed universally across tasks. Our aspiration is that Rl-ViGen will serve as a catalyst in this area, and lay a foundation for the future creation of universal visual generalization RL agents suitable for real-world scenarios. Access to our code and implemented algorithms is provided at https://gemcollector.github.io/RL-ViGen/.

paragraphs: An agent that learns from images must cope with visual observations that differ from those encountered during training. Evaluating this ability is difficult when benchmarks cover only isolated tasks or a narrow category of change. RL-ViGen addresses that evaluation problem by bringing diverse tasks and a broad range of generalization types into one benchmark.

The paper also incorporates recent visual reinforcement-learning algorithms into a unified framework. This gives researchers a shared setting for comparing methods across multiple challenges. The purpose is to support conclusions about visual generalization that are less dependent on the particular task or category chosen for an evaluation.

The experiments find that no single evaluated algorithm dominates across all tasks. This result shows why strong performance on one benchmark setting should not be treated as evidence of universal visual robustness. RL-ViGen’s contribution is the broader testing foundation itself, together with implemented algorithms, intended to support research toward agents that generalize across more varied visual situations.
summary.tldr: RL-ViGen broadens visual reinforcement-learning evaluation and finds that no tested algorithm dominates across all tasks.

title: RL-ViGen: A Reinforcement Learning Benchmark for Visual Generalization

abstract: Subject-driven text-to-image generation models create novel renditions of an input subject based on text prompts. Existing models suffer from lengthy fine-tuning and difficulties preserving the subject fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we introduce BLIP-Diffusion, a new subject-driven image generation model that supports multimodal control which consumes inputs of subject images and text prompts. Unlike other subject-driven generation models, BLIP-Diffusion introduces a new multimodal encoder which is pre-trained to provide subject representation. We first pre-train the multimodal encoder following BLIP-2 to produce visual representation aligned with the text.Then we design a subject representation learning task which enables a diffusion model to leverage such visual representation and generates new subject renditions. Compared with previous methods such as DreamBooth, our model enables zero-shot subject-driven generation, and efficient fine-tuning for customized subject with up to 20x speedup. We also demonstrate that BLIP-Diffusion can be flexibly combined with existing techniques such as ControlNet and prompt-to-prompt to enable novel subject-driven generation and editing applications. Implementations are available at: https://github.com/salesforce/LAVIS/tree/main/projects/blip-diffusion.

paragraphs: BLIP-Diffusion addresses a practical difficulty in personalized image generation: producing new images of a particular subject while following a text prompt. Earlier approaches can require lengthy tuning for each subject and still struggle to preserve its appearance. This paper builds a model that accepts both subject images and text, giving the generator information about what to preserve and what to change.

The central contribution is a pretrained multimodal encoder that supplies a representation of the subject. Its training first follows BLIP-2 to align visual representations with text. A subsequent subject representation learning task teaches the diffusion model to use those representations when creating new renditions. This moves part of the personalization capability into shared pretraining.

The authors report generation for new subjects without subject-specific training, alongside customized fine-tuning with up to a twentyfold speedup over previous methods such as DreamBooth. They also demonstrate combinations with ControlNet and prompt-to-prompt. These results show how the learned representation can support both subject personalization and additional generation or editing controls.
summary.tldr: BLIP-Diffusion pretrains a subject representation that supports personalized image generation without subject-specific training and faster optional fine-tuning.

title: BLIP-Diffusion: Pre-trained Subject Representation for Controllable Text-to-Image Generation and Editing

abstract: Neurons can display highly variable dynamics. While such variability presumably supports the wide range of behaviors generated by the organism, their gene expressions are relatively stable in the adult brain. This suggests that neuronal activity is a combination of its time-invariant identity and the inputs the neuron receives from the rest of the circuit. Here, we propose a self-supervised learning based method to assign time-invariant representations to individual neurons based on permutation-, and population size-invariant summary of population recordings. We fit dynamical models to neuronal activity to learn a representation by considering the activity of both the individual and the neighboring population. Our self-supervised approach and use of implicit representations enable robust inference against imperfections such as partial overlap of neurons across sessions, trial-to-trial variability, and limited availability of molecular (transcriptomic) labels for downstream supervised tasks. We demonstrate our method on a public multimodal dataset of mouse cortical neuronal activity and transcriptomic labels. We report >35\% improvement in predicting the transcriptomic subclass identity and >20\% improvement in predicting class identity with respect to the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: A neuron's activity can change substantially while its gene expression remains relatively stable in the adult brain. This motivates separating a neuron's persistent identity from the changing inputs it receives. The paper learns a stable representation for each neuron using both its own activity and the dynamics of the surrounding population.

The method fits dynamical models through self-supervised learning. Its population summary is invariant to neuron ordering and population size, allowing the representation to use collective activity without depending on a fixed arrangement of recorded cells. Implicit representations and self-supervision support robust inference when recording sessions only partly overlap, activity varies across trials, or molecular labels for later supervised tasks are scarce.

The authors evaluate the approach on a public mouse cortical dataset containing activity recordings and transcriptomic labels. Relative to the state of the art, they report improvements exceeding 35% for transcriptomic subclass prediction and 20% for class prediction. These findings support the idea that activity interpreted in its population context contains useful information about relatively stable neuronal identity.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised modeling of individual and population activity learns stable neuron representations that improve transcriptomic identity prediction.

title: Learning Time-Invariant Representations for Individual Neurons from Population Dynamics

abstract: We introduce a two-stage probabilistic framework for statistical downscaling using unpaired data. Statistical downscaling seeks a probabilistic map to transform low-resolution data from a biased coarse-grained numerical scheme to high-resolution data that is consistent with a high-fidelity scheme. Our framework tackles the problem bycomposing two transformations: (i) a debiasing step via an optimal transport map, and (ii) an upsampling step achieved by a probabilistic diffusion model with a posteriori conditional sampling. This approach characterizes a conditional distribution without needing paired data, and faithfully recovers relevant physical statistics from biased samples. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed approach on one- and two-dimensional fluid flow problems, which are representative of the core difficulties present in numerical simulations of weather and climate. Our method produces realistic high-resolution outputs from low-resolution inputs, by upsampling resolutions of $8\times$ and $16\times$. Moreover, our procedure correctly matches the statistics of physical quantities, even when the low-frequency content of the inputs and outputs do not match, a crucial but difficult-to-satisfy assumption needed by current state-of-the-art alternatives. Code for this work is available at: https://github.com/google-research/swirl-dynamics/tree/main/swirl_dynamics/projects/probabilistic_diffusion.

paragraphs: Statistical downscaling converts coarse simulation outputs into plausible detailed outputs consistent with a higher-fidelity simulator. This paper addresses a setting where the coarse simulator is biased and matching low- and high-resolution training examples are unavailable. The objective is a conditional distribution of detailed outcomes, allowing more than one plausible refinement of an input.

The framework separates correction from refinement. An optimal transport map first debiases the coarse data. A probabilistic diffusion model then upsamples it using conditional sampling applied afterward. Combining these transformations lets the method learn from unpaired data while addressing both systematic discrepancies in the input and the need to generate finer detail.

Experiments on one- and two-dimensional fluid flows produce realistic outputs at 8× and 16× higher resolutions and recover relevant physical statistics. The procedure also matches these statistics when input and output low-frequency content differ. This matters because the alternatives discussed in the abstract depend on matching that coarse-scale content, an assumption that biased simulations can make difficult to satisfy.
summary.tldr: A two-stage method debiases coarse simulations and uses diffusion to generate statistically faithful high-resolution outputs from unpaired data.

title: Debias Coarsely, Sample Conditionally: Statistical Downscaling through Optimal Transport and Probabilistic Diffusion Models

abstract: Inverse problems describe the task of recovering an underlying signal of interest given observables. Typically, the observables are related via some non-linear forward model applied to the underlying unknown signal. Inverting the non-linear forward model can be computationally expensive, as it often involves computing and inverting a linearization at a series of estimates. Rather than inverting the physics-based model, we instead train a surrogate forward model (emulator) and leverage modern auto-grad libraries to solve for the input within a classical optimization framework. Current methods to train emulators are done in a black box supervised machine learning fashion and fail to take advantage of any existing knowledge of the forward model. In this article, we propose a simple learned weighted average model that embeds linearizations of the forward model around various reference points into the model itself, explicitly incorporating known physics. Grounding the learned model with physics based linearizations improves the forward modeling accuracy and provides richer physics based gradient information during the inversion process leading to more accurate signal recovery. We demonstrate the efficacy on an ocean acoustic tomography (OAT) example that aims to recover ocean sound speed profile (SSP) variations from acoustic observations (e.g. eigenray arrival times) within simulation of ocean dynamics in the Gulf of Mexico.
