The key intuition behind our approach is to use at each timestep a datapoint from the group that is worst off under the current model for updating the model. The ease of implementation and the generality of our robust formulation make it an attractive option for improving model performance on disadvantaged groups. For convex learning problems, such as linear or logistic regression, we provide a fine-grained analysis, proving the rate of convergence to a min-max fair solution.

paragraphs: A model can perform well overall while serving some groups poorly. This paper addresses that imbalance through min-max fairness: training with attention to the group that currently has the worst performance. The objective makes the weakest group’s outcome central to optimization, so improvements in aggregate performance do not define success on their own.

The proposed methods use active sampling and reweighting. Their central rule is straightforward: at each training step, update the model using a data point from the group currently doing worst. Because that group can change as training proceeds, the method repeatedly redirects attention according to the model’s present performance. The formulation applies to classification and regression models trained by minimizing a loss.

The paper also establishes convergence rates for convex learning problems, including linear and logistic regression. These results explain how quickly the proposed procedures approach a min-max fair solution in that setting. The broader practical appeal is the combination of a simple training intervention and compatibility with many loss-based models; the stated convergence guarantees specifically concern convex problems.
summary.tldr: Sampling from the currently worst-performing group provides a simple approach to min-max fairness, with convergence guarantees for convex learning problems.

title: Active Sampling for Min-Max Fairness

abstract: To leverage the power of big data from source domains and overcome the scarcity of target domain samples, representation learning based on multi-task pretraining has become a standard approach in many applications. However, large-scale pretraining is often computationally expensive and not affordable for small organizations. When there is only one target task, most source tasks can be irrelevant, and we can actively sample a subset of source data from the most To leverage the power of big data from source tasks and overcome the scarcity of the target task samples, representation learning based on multi-task pretraining has become a standard approach in many applications. However, up until now, choosing which source tasks to include in the multi-task learning has been more art than science. In this paper, we give the first formal study on resource task sampling by leveraging the techniques from active learning. We propose an algorithm that iteratively estimates the relevance of each source task to the target task and samples from each source task based on the estimated relevance. Theoretically, we show that for the linear representation class, to achieve the same error rate, our algorithm can save up to a textit{number of source tasks} factor in the source task sample complexity, compared with the naive uniform sampling from all source tasks. We also provide experiments on real-world computer vision datasets to illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method on both linear and convolutional neural network representation classes. We believe our paper serves as an important initial step to bring techniques from active learning to representation learning.

paragraphs: Multi-task pretraining learns a shared representation from several source tasks before applying it to a target task with limited data. The paper asks how to choose source examples when those tasks are not equally useful. Sampling uniformly can spend resources on tasks with little relevance to the particular target.

The proposed algorithm makes source selection an active learning problem. It repeatedly estimates how relevant each source task is to the target and uses those estimates to decide how much to sample from each task. This makes the allocation responsive to information gathered during learning, rather than fixing equal sampling rates at the outset.

For linear representations, the authors prove that reaching the same error can require fewer source samples than uniform sampling, with a possible saving as large as the number of source tasks. This is an upper-end improvement, not a guaranteed saving in every case. Experiments on computer vision datasets illustrate the method with both linear representations and convolutional neural networks, extending the empirical investigation beyond the class covered by the stated theoretical result.
summary.tldr: Actively estimating source-task relevance can reduce the data needed to learn a representation for a particular target task.

title: Active Multi-Task Representation Learning

abstract: Deep learning has shown great potential for modeling the physical dynamics of complex particle systems such as fluids. Existing approaches, however, require the supervision of consecutive particle properties, including positions and velocities. In this paper, we consider a partially observable scenario known as fluid dynamics grounding, that is, inferring the state transitions and interactions within the fluid particle systems from sequential visual observations of the fluid surface. We propose a differentiable two-stage network named NeuroFluid. Our approach consists of (i) a particle-driven neural renderer, which involves fluid physical properties into the volume rendering function, and (ii) a particle transition model optimized to reduce the differences between the rendered and the observed images. NeuroFluid provides the first solution to unsupervised learning of particle-based fluid dynamics by training these two models jointly. It is shown to reasonably estimate the underlying physics of fluids with different initial shapes, viscosity, and densities.

It is shown to reasonably estimate the underlying physics of fluids with different initial shapes, viscosity, and densities.

NeuroFluid tackles a partially observed setting in which the available evidence is a sequence of images of the fluid surface. The goal is to infer the hidden particle transitions and interactions that produce those visible changes.

The approach joins two differentiable components. A particle-driven neural renderer incorporates physical fluid properties into volume rendering, connecting particle descriptions to images. A particle transition model predicts changes in the particle system and is optimized to reduce discrepancies between rendered images and observed images. Training the two components jointly links visual agreement to learning the underlying dynamics.

The authors present this as the first solution for unsupervised learning of particle-based fluid dynamics. Their results show reasonable estimates of underlying fluid physics across different initial shapes, viscosities, and densities. The contribution demonstrates how surface observations can supervise a coupled rendering and dynamics model without requiring the consecutive particle-property supervision used by existing approaches.
summary.tldr: NeuroFluid jointly learns particle dynamics and rendering from fluid-surface images, producing reasonable estimates of hidden physical behavior.

title: NeuroFluid: Fluid Dynamics Grounding with Particle-Driven Neural Radiance Fields

abstract: Graph Neural Architecture Search (GNAS) has become a powerful method in automatically discovering suitable Graph Neural Network (GNN) architectures for different tasks. However, existing approaches fail to handle large-scale graphs because current performance estimation strategies in GNAS are computationally expensive for large-scale graphs and suffer from consistency collapse issues. To tackle these problems, we propose the Graph ArchitectUre Search at Scale (GAUSS) method that can handle large-scale graphs by designing an efficient light-weight supernet and the joint architecture-graph sampling. In particular, a graph sampling-based single-path one-shot supernet is proposed to reduce the computation burden. To address the consistency collapse issues, we further explicitly consider the joint architecture-graph sampling through a novel architecture peer learning mechanism on the sampled sub-graphs and an architecture importance sampling algorithm. Our proposed framework is able to smooth the highly non-convex optimization objective and stabilize the architecture sampling process. We provide theoretical analyses on GAUSS and empirically evaluate it on five datasets whose vertex sizes range from 10^4 to 10^8. The experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements of GAUSS over other GNAS baselines on all datasets. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed GAUSS method is the first graph neural architecture search framework that can handle graphs with billions of edges within 1 GPU day.

Existing search methods also encounter consistency collapse. This paper introduces GAUSS to address both the computational burden and the instability involved in estimating and comparing architecture performance.

Architecture peer learning on sampled subgraphs and architecture importance sampling help smooth the highly nonconvex objective and stabilize architecture sampling, connecting the search procedure to the data portions used for evaluation.

GAUSS shows substantial improvements over other graph architecture search baselines on every evaluated dataset. The authors also describe it, to their knowledge, as the first such framework to handle graphs with billions of edges within one GPU day.
summary.tldr: GAUSS combines an efficient supernet with joint architecture and graph sampling to scale graph architecture search to billions of edges.

title: Large-Scale Graph Neural Architecture Search

abstract: We consider the problem of predicting a protein sequence from its backbone atom coordinates. Machine learning approaches to this problem to date have been limited by the number of available experimentally determined protein structures. We augment training data by nearly three orders of magnitude by predicting structures for 12M protein sequences using AlphaFold2. Trained with this additional data, a sequence-to-sequence transformer with invariant geometric input processing layers achieves 51% native sequence recovery on structurally held-out backbones with 72% recovery for buried residues, an overall improvement of almost 10 percentage points over existing methods. The model generalizes to a variety of more complex tasks including design of protein complexes, partially masked structures, binding interfaces, and multiple states.

This paper expands the available training material by using AlphaFold2 to predict structures for 12 million sequences, increasing the training data by nearly three orders of magnitude.

The model is a sequence-to-sequence Transformer with invariant geometric layers for processing the structural input. Trained with the additional predicted structures, it achieves 51% native sequence recovery on structurally held-out backbones and 72% recovery for buried residues. The overall recovery result improves on existing methods by almost 10 percentage points.

The authors also report generalization to more complex settings, including protein complexes, partially masked structures, binding interfaces, and multiple states. These findings show the usefulness of predicted structures as training data for learning the structure-to-sequence relationship. The reported recovery figures describe agreement with native sequences, while the additional tasks demonstrate the breadth of structural inputs and design settings the model can handle.
summary.tldr: Training on millions of predicted protein structures improves inverse folding, reaching 51% native sequence recovery on structurally held-out backbones.

title: Learning inverse folding from millions of predicted structures

abstract: High-order interactions between multiple objects are common in real-world applications. Although tensor decomposition is a popular framework for high-order interaction analysis and prediction, most methods cannot well exploit the valuable timestamp information in data. The existent methods either discard the timestamps or convert them into discrete steps or use over-simplistic decomposition models. As a result, these methods might not be capable enough of capturing complex, fine-grained temporal dynamics or making accurate predictions for long-term interaction results. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel Temporal High-order Interaction decompoSition model based on Ordinary Differential Equations (THIS-ODE). We model the time-varying interaction result with a latent ODE. To capture the complex temporal dynamics, we use a neural network (NN) to learn the time derivative of the ODE state. We use the representation of the interaction objects to model the initial value of the ODE and to constitute a part of the NN input to compute the state. In this way, the temporal relationships of the participant objects can be estimated and encoded into their representations. For tractable and scalable inference, we use forward sensitivity analysis to efficiently compute the gradient of ODE state, based on which we use integral transform to develop a stochastic mini-batch learning algorithm. We demonstrate the advantage of our approach in simulation and four real-world applications.

Tensor decomposition is commonly used for such interactions, but many methods discard timestamps, group them into discrete steps, or impose simple temporal models. THIS-ODE represents the evolving interaction outcome through a latent ordinary differential equation. A neural network learns how the hidden state changes with time. Representations of the participating objects determine the initial state and supply part of the network’s input. This links each object’s representation to the temporal behavior of the interactions in which it participates.

Results from simulations and four real-world applications demonstrate advantages for the approach. The contribution combines a richer continuous-time interaction model with machinery for fitting it efficiently.
summary.tldr: THIS-ODE learns continuous-time dynamics of multi-object interactions using neural differential equations tied to object representations.

title: Decomposing Temporal High-Order Interactions via Latent ODEs

abstract: The optimization of multi-objective submodular systems appears in a wide variety of applications. However, there are currently very few techniques which are able to provide a robust allocation to such systems. In this work, we propose to design and analyse novel algorithms for the robust allocation of submodular systems through lens of quantile maximization. We start by observing that identifying an exact solution for this problem is computationally intractable. To tackle this issue, we propose a proxy for the quantile function using a softmax formulation, and show that this proxy is well suited to submodular optimization. Based on this relaxation, we propose a novel and simple algorithm called SOFTSAT. Theoretical properties are provided for this algorithm as well as novel approximation guarantees. Finally, we provide numerical experiments showing the efficiency of our algorithm with regards to state-of-the-art methods in a test bed of real-world applications, and show that SOFTSAT is particularly robust and well-suited to online scenarios.

This paper approaches that question through quantile maximization. A quantile-based objective makes a selected position in the distribution of outcomes part of the optimization target, giving robustness an explicit mathematical formulation.

The authors first show that finding an exact solution is computationally intractable. They then introduce a softmax-based proxy for the quantile function and show that it is suited to submodular optimization. This relaxation leads to SOFTSAT, a simple algorithm accompanied by theoretical properties and new approximation guarantees. The proxy is the bridge from the difficult exact problem to a tractable algorithmic approach.

Numerical experiments compare SOFTSAT with state-of-the-art methods across a collection of real-world applications. The reported results support its efficiency and robustness, particularly in online scenarios. The paper thus combines a formal treatment of the computational difficulty with an approximate solution and practical evidence. Its guarantees concern the proposed approximation approach, while the online suitability is supported by the numerical evaluations.
summary.tldr: SOFTSAT uses a softmax proxy for quantile maximization to obtain robust submodular allocations with approximation guarantees and promising online performance.

title: Robustness in Multi-Objective Submodular Optimization: a Quantile Approach

abstract: Neural networks are powerful function estimators, leading to their status as a paradigm of choice for modeling structured data. However, unlike other structured representations that emphasize the modularity of the problem {–} e.g., factor graphs {–} neural networks are usually monolithic mappings from inputs to outputs, with a fixed computation order. This limitation prevents them from capturing different directions of computation and interaction between the modeled variables. In this paper, we combine the representational strengths of factor graphs and of neural networks, proposing undirected neural networks (UNNs): a flexible framework for specifying computations that can be performed in any order. For particular choices, our proposed models subsume and extend many existing architectures: feed-forward, recurrent, self-attention networks, auto-encoders, and networks with implicit layers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of undirected neural architectures, both unstructured and structured, on a range of tasks: tree-constrained dependency parsing, convolutional image classification, and sequence completion with attention. By varying the computation order, we show how a single UNN can be used both as a classifier and a prototype generator, and how it can fill in missing parts of an input sequence, making them a promising field for further research.

paragraphs: Conventional neural networks usually map inputs to outputs through a fixed order of computation. That makes it difficult to express a structured problem in which variables can influence one another in different directions. This paper introduces undirected neural networks, combining the modular representation of factor graphs with the function-learning capabilities of neural networks.

The framework specifies computations that can be performed in different orders. With particular choices, it includes and extends feed-forward networks, recurrent networks, self-attention, auto-encoders, and architectures with implicit layers. This common formulation allows the authors to investigate how changing computation order changes what a single model can do.

The demonstrations cover tree-constrained dependency parsing, convolutional image classification, and sequence completion with attention. By varying computation order, a single undirected network can serve as both a classifier and a prototype generator, and the framework can fill missing portions of a sequence. These examples show how flexible interactions among variables can support several uses of a learned model within one architectural framework.
summary.tldr: Undirected neural networks combine factor-graph modularity with neural representations to support flexible computation orders and multiple model uses.

title: Modeling Structure with Undirected Neural Networks

abstract: Bootstrap is a principled and powerful frequentist statistical tool for uncertainty quantification. Unfortunately, standard bootstrap methods are computationally intensive due to the need of drawing a large i.i.d. bootstrap sample to approximate the ideal bootstrap distribution; this largely hinders their application in large-scale machine learning, especially deep learning problems. In this work, we propose an efficient method to explicitly optimize a small set of high quality “centroid” points to better approximate the ideal bootstrap distribution. We achieve this by minimizing a simple objective function that is asymptotically equivalent to the Wasserstein distance to the ideal bootstrap distribution. This allows us to provide an accurate estimation of uncertainty with a small number of bootstrap centroids, outperforming the naive i.i.d. sampling approach. Empirically, we show that our method can boost the performance of bootstrap in a variety of applications.

paragraphs: The bootstrap is a statistical approach to quantifying uncertainty, but approximating its ideal distribution can require many independently sampled bootstrap outcomes. That computational burden makes it difficult to use in large machine learning systems, particularly deep learning. This paper asks whether a smaller, deliberately optimized collection can represent the same target more effectively.

The authors construct a small set of representative points called centroids. Rather than relying on independent random sampling alone, they optimize these points using a simple objective. Asymptotically, that objective is equivalent to the Wasserstein distance from the ideal bootstrap distribution, connecting the optimization procedure to a measure of how closely one distribution approximates another.

This approach produces accurate uncertainty estimates with relatively few bootstrap centroids and outperforms naive independent sampling. Experiments show improvements across a variety of applications. The main idea is to improve the quality of the approximation points, rather than only increasing their number. The theoretical relationship is specifically asymptotic, while the practical benefits are supported by the reported empirical evaluations.
summary.tldr: Optimizing a small collection of bootstrap centroids improves uncertainty estimation compared with naive independent sampling.

title: Centroid Approximation for Bootstrap: Improving Particle Quality at Inference

abstract: Ensembling is among the most popular tools in machine learning (ML) due to its effectiveness in minimizing variance and thus improving generalization. Most ensembling methods for black-box base learners fall under the umbrella of "stacked generalization," namely training an ML algorithm that takes the inferences from the base learners as input. While stacking has been widely applied in practice, its theoretical properties are poorly understood. In this paper, we prove a novel result, showing that choosing the best stacked generalization from a (finite or finite-dimensional) family of stacked generalizations based on cross-validated performance does not perform "much worse" than the oracle best. Our result strengthens and significantly extends the results in Van der Laan et al. (2007). Inspired by the theoretical analysis, we further propose a particular family of stacked generalizations in the context of probabilistic forecasting, each one with a different sensitivity for how much the ensemble weights are allowed to vary across items, timestamps in the forecast horizon, and quantiles. Experimental results demonstrate the performance gain of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Stacking learns how to combine predictions from several base models by treating those predictions as inputs to another learner. Although widely used, the theoretical behavior of choosing a stacking strategy is less well understood. This paper studies whether cross-validation can reliably select among a family of such strategies.

The authors prove that selecting the best cross-validated strategy from a finite or finite-dimensional family does not perform much worse than the oracle-best choice in that family. The oracle is the comparison point representing the best available candidate. This supports selection within the specified family; it does not claim that every possible ensemble or unrestricted collection is covered.

Guided by the analysis, the authors propose a family of stacking methods for probabilistic forecasting. Members differ in how freely ensemble weights vary across forecasted items, future timestamps, and quantiles. This makes the flexibility of the combination itself a selectable property. Experiments demonstrate performance gains, linking the theoretical selection guarantee to a concrete forecasting approach with different degrees of weight variation.
summary.tldr: Cross-validation receives an oracle-comparison guarantee for selecting stacking strategies, motivating flexible ensembles for probabilistic forecasting.

title: Theoretical Guarantees of Learning Ensembling Strategies with Applications to Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Placement is a critical step in modern chip design, aiming to determine the positions of circuit modules on the chip canvas. Recent works have shown that reinforcement learning (RL) can improve human performance in chip placement. However, such an RL-based approach suffers from long training time and low transfer ability in unseen chip circuits. To resolve these challenges, we cast the chip placement as an offline RL formulation and present ChiPFormer that enables learning a transferable placement policy from fixed offline data. ChiPFormer has several advantages that prior arts do not have. First, ChiPFormer can exploit offline placement designs to learn transferable policies more efficiently in a multi-task setting. Second, ChiPFormer can promote effective finetuning for unseen chip circuits, reducing the placement runtime from hours to minutes. Third, extensive experiments on 32 chip circuits demonstrate that ChiPFormer achieves significantly better placement quality while reducing the runtime by 10x compared to recent state-of-the-art approaches in both public benchmarks and realistic industrial tasks. The deliverables are released at https://sites.google.com/view/chipformer/home.

paragraphs: Chip placement determines where circuit modules sit on a chip canvas. Reinforcement learning has shown promise for this task, but lengthy training and weak transfer to unfamiliar circuits can make it costly to use. ChiPFormer addresses both issues by learning from a fixed collection of existing placement designs.

The paper formulates placement as offline reinforcement learning and introduces a decision-transformer approach for learning a transferable placement policy. Its multi-task setting allows offline designs to contribute to learning across circuits. The resulting policy can then be fine-tuned for unseen circuits, making reuse of placement experience central to the approach.

Across experiments on 32 circuits, the authors report significantly better placement quality and a tenfold runtime reduction relative to recent state-of-the-art approaches. These evaluations include public benchmarks and realistic industrial tasks. They also report that effective fine-tuning reduces placement runtime from hours to minutes. The findings support offline policy learning as a way to improve both placement quality and the time needed to adapt to a new circuit.
summary.tldr: ChiPFormer learns transferable chip-placement policies from offline designs, improving placement quality and reducing runtime in experiments across 32 circuits.

title: ChiPFormer: Transferable Chip Placement via Offline Decision Transformer

abstract: Nyström low-rank approximation has shown great potential in processing large-scale kernel matrix and neural networks. However, there lacks a unified analysis for Nyström approximation, and the asymptotical minimax optimality for Nyström methods usually require a strict condition, assuming that the target regression lies exactly in the hypothesis space. In this paper, to tackle these problems, we provide a refined generalization analysis for Nyström approximation in the agnostic setting, where the target regression may be out of the hypothesis space. Specifically, we show Nyström approximation can still achieve the capacity-dependent optimal rates in the agnostic setting. To this end, we first prove the capacity-dependent optimal guarantees of Nyström approximation with the standard uniform sampling, which covers both loss functions and applies to some agnostic settings. Then, using data-dependent sampling, for example, leverage scores sampling, we derive the capacity-dependent optimal rates that apply to the whole range of the agnostic setting. To our best knowledge, the capacity-dependent optimality for the whole range of the agnostic setting is first achieved and novel in Nyström approximation.

paragraphs: Nyström approximation reduces a large kernel matrix to a lower-rank representation, making kernel methods more manageable at scale. However, earlier optimality analyses often assume that the target regression function belongs exactly to the learner’s hypothesis space. This paper studies the agnostic setting, which allows the target to fall outside that space.

The authors provide a refined generalization analysis showing that Nyström methods can still achieve optimal rates that depend on the hypothesis space’s capacity. With standard uniform sampling, they establish these guarantees for some agnostic settings. This demonstrates that a mismatch between the target and the hypothesis space does not automatically prevent optimal convergence.

Using data-dependent sampling, including leverage-score sampling, the analysis extends capacity-dependent optimal rates across the whole agnostic range considered. The authors identify this full-range result as a first for Nyström approximation. The distinction between sampling methods matters: uniform sampling supports part of the range, while data-dependent selection supports the broader guarantee. The contribution clarifies how approximation and sampling interact when the target is not exactly representable.
summary.tldr: Nyström kernel learning can achieve capacity-dependent optimal rates even outside the hypothesis space, with data-dependent sampling covering the full agnostic range analyzed.

title: Optimal Convergence Rates for Agnostic Nyström Kernel Learning

abstract: Based on binary inquiries, we developed an algorithm to estimate population quantiles under Local Differential Privacy (LDP). By self-normalizing, our algorithm provides asymptotically normal estimation with valid inference, resulting in tight confidence intervals without the need for nuisance parameters to be estimated. Our proposed method can be conducted fully online, leading to high computational efficiency and minimal storage requirements with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ space. We also proved an optimality result by an elegant application of one central limit theorem of Gaussian Differential Privacy (GDP) when targeting the frequently encountered median estimation problem. With mathematical proof and extensive numerical testing, we demonstrate the validity of our algorithm both theoretically and experimentally.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for estimating population quantiles under local differential privacy using binary inquiries. Its goal includes both producing an estimate and quantifying the uncertainty around it. This is useful when a private analysis needs a confidence interval, rather than only a single reported quantile.

The algorithm uses self-normalization to obtain asymptotically normal estimates and valid inference without separately estimating nuisance parameters. The authors report tight confidence intervals from this procedure. It operates fully online with constant space, so its storage requirement does not grow with the amount of data processed.

For median estimation, the paper additionally proves an optimality result using a central limit theorem from Gaussian differential privacy. That optimality claim is specifically associated with the median problem. Mathematical proofs and extensive numerical tests support the method’s validity, combining asymptotic inferential guarantees with an online implementation designed for computational efficiency and minimal storage.
summary.tldr: The paper gives an online, constant-space method for locally private quantile estimation with asymptotically valid confidence intervals.

title: Online Local Differential Private Quantile Inference via Self-normalization

abstract: We propose a hybrid neural network (NN) and PDE approach for learning generalizable PDE dynamics from motion observations. Many NN approaches learn an end-to-end model that implicitly models both the governing PDE and constitutive models (or material models). Without explicit PDE knowledge, these approaches cannot guarantee physical correctness and have limited generalizability. We argue that the governing PDEs are often well-known and should be explicitly enforced rather than learned. Instead, constitutive models are particularly suitable for learning due to their data-fitting nature. To this end, we introduce a new framework termed "Neural Constitutive Laws" (NCLaw), which utilizes a network architecture that strictly guarantees standard constitutive priors, including rotation equivariance and undeformed state equilibrium. We embed this network inside a differentiable simulation and train the model by minimizing a loss function based on the difference between the simulation and the motion observation. We validate NCLaw on various large-deformation dynamical systems, ranging from solids to fluids. After training on a single motion trajectory, our method generalizes to new geometries, initial/boundary conditions, temporal ranges, and even multi-physics systems. On these extremely out-of-distribution generalization tasks, NCLaw is orders-of-magnitude more accurate than previous NN approaches. Real-world experiments demonstrate our method’s ability to learn constitutive laws from videos.

paragraphs: Learning physical motion end to end can entangle two different things: governing equations and the material behavior those equations use. This paper argues that known governing PDEs should be enforced explicitly, while neural networks learn constitutive laws describing materials. The resulting framework is called Neural Constitutive Laws, or NCLaw.

NCLaw’s architecture strictly enforces standard constitutive properties, including rotation equivariance and equilibrium in an undeformed state. The network sits inside a differentiable simulator and is trained by comparing simulated motion with observed motion. This makes the learned material model accountable to the motion produced through the governing equations.

Evaluations cover large deformations in solids and fluids. After training on a single motion trajectory, the method generalizes to new geometries, initial and boundary conditions, time ranges, and even multiphysics systems. On the reported extreme distribution shifts, it is orders of magnitude more accurate than previous neural approaches. Real-world experiments also demonstrate learning constitutive laws from videos. These results support separating known physical structure from the material relationships that need to be learned.
summary.tldr: NCLaw learns material laws inside a physics simulator, enabling strong generalization from a single observed motion trajectory.

title: Learning Neural Constitutive Laws from Motion Observations for Generalizable PDE Dynamics

abstract: Large-scale multi-modal contrastive learning frameworks like CLIP typically require a large amount of image-text samples for training. However, these samples are always collected continuously in real scenarios. This paper discusses the feasibility of continual CLIP training using streaming data. Unlike continual learning based on self-supervised learning methods for pure images, which is empirically robust against catastrophic forgetting, CLIP’s performance degeneration in the continual setting is significant and non-neglectable. By analyzing the changes in the model’s representation space during continual CLIP training from a spatial geometry perspective, we explore and summarize these spatial variations as Spatial Disorder (SD) , which can be divided into Intra-modal Rotation and Inter-modal Deviation . Moreover, we empirically and theoretically demonstrate how SD leads to a performance decline for CLIP on cross-modal retrieval tasks. To alleviate SD, we propose a new continual vision-language representation learning framework Mod-X : M aintain o ff- d iagonal information-matri X . By selectively aligning the off-diagonal information distribution of contrastive matrices, the Mod-X improves the capability of the multi-modal model by maintaining the multi-modal representation space alignment on the old data domain during continuously fitting the new training data domain. Experiments on commonly used datasets with different scales and scopes have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Image-text datasets often arrive continuously, creating a need to update models such as CLIP as new examples become available. The paper finds substantial performance deterioration when CLIP is trained this way. This motivates studying how continual updates change the shared representation space used to connect images with text, especially for cross-modal retrieval.

This analysis identifies changes in the relationships among representations as a concrete mechanism behind the observed degradation.

Experiments on datasets with different sizes and scopes demonstrate effectiveness, supporting relational alignment as a way to improve continual vision-language learning.
summary.tldr: Mod-X improves continual vision-language learning by preserving relational information that helps keep image and text representations aligned.

title: Continual Vision-Language Representation Learning with Off-Diagonal Information

abstract: We provide an efficient implementation of the backpropagation algorithm, specialized to the case where the weights of the neural network being trained are sparse . Our algorithm is general, as it applies to arbitrary (unstructured) sparsity and common layer types (e.g., convolutional or linear). We provide a fast vectorized implementation on commodity CPUs, and show that it can yield speedups in end-to-end runtime experiments, both in transfer learning using already-sparsified networks, and in training sparse networks from scratch. Thus, our results provide the first support for sparse training on commodity hardware.

paragraphs: A neural network with sparse weights contains many zero-valued connections, but realizing a training-speed benefit requires an implementation that can exploit that structure. SparseProp provides a specialized implementation of backpropagation for sparse networks. Its focus is making sparsity useful for the computations performed during training on ordinary CPU hardware.

The method supports arbitrary, unstructured sparsity, so it does not require nonzero weights to follow a particular regular arrangement. It also applies to common layer types, including convolutional and linear layers. The authors provide a fast vectorized CPU implementation, connecting the general sparse-backpropagation algorithm to execution on widely available processors.

End-to-end runtime experiments show that the implementation can accelerate transfer learning with networks that have already been sparsified, as well as training sparse networks from scratch. These two settings demonstrate usefulness across different starting points for model training. The paper presents its findings as the first support for sparse training on commodity hardware, with the reported speedups establishing that sparse computation can translate into improvements in complete training runs.
summary.tldr: SparseProp exploits unstructured weight sparsity to accelerate end-to-end neural-network training on commodity CPUs.

title: SparseProp: Efficient Sparse Backpropagation for Faster Training of Neural Networks at the Edge

abstract: Evidential deep learning, built upon belief theory and subjective logic, offers a principled and computationally efficient way to turn a deterministic neural network uncertainty-aware. The resultant evidential models can quantify fine-grained uncertainty using the learned evidence. To ensure theoretically sound evidential models, the evidence needs to be non-negative, which requires special activation functions for model training and inference. This constraint often leads to inferior predictive performance compared to standard softmax models, making it challenging to extend them to many large-scale datasets. To unveil the real cause of this undesired behavior, we theoretically investigate evidential models and identify a fundamental limitation that explains the inferior performance: existing evidential activation functions create zero evidence regions , which prevent the model to learn from training samples falling into such regions. A deeper analysis of evidential activation functions based on our theoretical underpinning inspires the design of a novel regularizer that effectively alleviates this fundamental limitation. Extensive experiments over many challenging real-world datasets and settings confirm our theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: Evidential deep learning lets a deterministic neural network represent uncertainty through learned evidence. For the underlying theory to remain valid, that evidence must be non-negative, so the network uses special activation functions. Yet these models often predict less accurately than standard softmax models, making them harder to apply to large datasets.

The paper investigates why this performance gap occurs. Its theoretical analysis identifies regions created by existing evidential activations where the model produces zero evidence and cannot learn from training samples falling there. This connects the loss of predictive performance to a specific failure of the learning process: some examples fail to contribute useful learning because of how evidence is constrained.

Using that analysis, the authors design a regularizer that alleviates the zero-evidence limitation. Experiments across challenging real-world datasets and settings support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The work matters because it addresses a concrete obstacle inside evidential training, offering a route to better prediction while retaining the framework’s requirement that evidence remain non-negative.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies zero-evidence regions that block evidential learning and introduces a regularizer that alleviates the problem.

title: Learn to Accumulate Evidence from All Training Samples: Theory and Practice

abstract: In Reinforcement Learning (RL), an agent acts in an unknown environment to maximize the expected cumulative discounted sum of an external reward signal, i.e., the expected return. In practice, in many tasks of interest, such as policy optimization, the agent usually spends its interaction budget by collecting episodes of fixed length within a simulator (i.e., Monte Carlo simulation). However, given the discounted nature of the RL objective, this data collection strategy might not be the best option. Indeed, the rewards taken in early simulation steps weigh exponentially more than future rewards. Taking a cue from this intuition, in this paper, we design an a-priori budget allocation strategy that leads to the collection of trajectories of different lengths, i.e., truncated . The proposed approach provably minimizes the width of the confidence intervals around the empirical estimates of the expected return of a policy. After discussing the theoretical properties of our method, we make use of our trajectory truncation mechanism to extend Policy Optimization via Importance Sampling (POIS, Metelli et al., 2018) algorithm. Finally, we conduct a numerical comparison between our algorithm and POIS: the results are consistent with our theory and show that an appropriate truncation of the trajectories can succeed in improving performance.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo reinforcement learning often spends a fixed interaction budget on simulated episodes of equal length. This paper questions that allocation when the objective discounts future rewards. Earlier rewards contribute more heavily to discounted return, so collecting the same number of observations at every trajectory depth may use the budget inefficiently.

The authors design a budget-allocation strategy chosen in advance that collects trajectories of different lengths. Some simulations are truncated, changing how interaction effort is distributed across early and late steps. They prove that the proposed allocation minimizes the width of confidence intervals around empirical estimates of a policy's expected return.

The truncation mechanism is then incorporated into Policy Optimization via Importance Sampling, and the resulting algorithm is compared numerically with the original POIS method. The results agree with the theory and show that appropriate truncation can improve performance. The practical message is that trajectory length is a meaningful part of experimental design: allocating the same budget differently can improve return estimation and, in the reported comparisons, policy optimization.
summary.tldr: Allocating simulation budgets across unequal trajectory lengths tightens return-estimation confidence intervals and can improve policy optimization.

title: Truncating Trajectories in Monte Carlo Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the problem of learning mixtures of Gaussians with censored data. Statistical learning with censored data is a classical problem, with numerous practical applications, however, finite-sample guarantees for even simple latent variable models such as Gaussian mixtures are missing. Formally, we are given censored data from a mixture of univariate Gaussians $ \sum_{i=1}^k w_i \mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma^2), $ i.e. the sample is observed only if it lies inside a set $S$. The goal is to learn the weights $w_i$ and the means $\mu_i$. We propose an algorithm that takes only $\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{O(k)}}$ samples to estimate the weights $w_i$ and the means $\mu_i$ within $\varepsilon$ error.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a Gaussian mixture when only samples inside a set S are visible. The underlying distribution combines several one-dimensional Gaussian components, but censoring determines which observations reach the learner. The task is to recover the component means and mixture weights from this selectively observed data.

The formal model has k components sharing a common variance. Its weights describe how much each component contributes, while its means describe their locations. Recovering these quantities addresses the underlying mixture, rather than simply describing the distribution of the observations that pass the censoring rule. The stated learning targets are the weights and means.

The authors propose an algorithm requiring 1/ε^{O(k)} samples to estimate those targets within ε error. This provides a finite-sample guarantee for a latent-variable model under censoring, an area where such guarantees had been missing even for simple models. The bound makes the dependence on accuracy and component count explicit: the exponent depends on k, so the guarantee should be read with that dependence in view.
summary.tldr: An algorithm learns the means and weights of censored univariate Gaussian mixtures with a finite-sample accuracy guarantee.

title: Learning Mixtures of Gaussians with Censored Data

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful models for non-Euclidean data, but their training is often accentuated by massive unnecessary computation: on the one hand, training on non-Euclidean data has relatively high computational cost due to its irregular density properties; on the other hand, the class imbalance property often associated with non-Euclidean data cannot be alleviated by the massiveness of the data, thus hindering the generalisation of the models. To address the above issues, theoretically, we start with a hypothesis about the effectiveness of using a subset of training data for GNNs, which is guaranteed by the gradient distance between the subset and the full set. Empirically, we also observe that a subset of the data can provide informative gradients for model optimization and which changes over time dynamically. We name this phenomenon dynamic data sparsity. Additionally, we find that pruned sparse contrastive models may miss valuable information, leading to a large loss value on the informative subset. Motivated by the above findings, we develop a unified data model dynamic sparsity framework called Data Decantation (DataDec) to address the above challenges. The key idea of DataDec is to identify the informative subset dynamically during the training process by applying sparse graph contrastive learning. The effectiveness of DataDec is comprehensively evaluated on graph benchmark datasets and we also verify its generalizability on image data.

paragraphs: Training graph neural networks can involve substantial unnecessary computation, while simply using more graph data does not resolve class imbalance. This paper investigates whether a smaller, informative training subset can support effective learning. Its theoretical starting point relates subset effectiveness to how closely the subset’s gradients match those of the full dataset.

Empirically, the authors observe that informative subsets change during training, a phenomenon they call dynamic data sparsity. They also find that pruning a contrastive model can remove valuable information, causing large losses on informative examples. These observations link which data are used with what information the sparse model retains.

Data Decantation, or DataDec, combines dynamic sparsity in the data and model within one framework. It uses sparse graph contrastive learning to identify informative training subsets as optimization proceeds. The authors evaluate its effectiveness on graph benchmarks and verify generalizability to image data. The contribution is an adaptive approach to reducing training data and computation while addressing representation quality, supported by both gradient-based reasoning and empirical observations about changing data usefulness.
summary.tldr: DataDec dynamically selects informative data through sparse contrastive learning to address unnecessary computation and class-imbalanced representations.

title: When Sparsity Meets Contrastive Models: Less Graph Data Can Bring Better Class-Balanced Representations

abstract: We optimize pipeline parallelism for deep neural network (DNN) inference by partitioning model graphs into $k$ stages and minimizing the running time of the bottleneck stage, including communication. We give practical and effective algorithms for this NP-hard problem, but our emphasis is on tackling the practitioner’s dilemma of deciding when a solution is good enough. To this end, we design novel mixed integer programming (MIP) relaxations for proving lower bounds. Applying these methods to a diverse testbed of 369 production models, for $k \in \\{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\\}$, we empirically show that these lower bounds are strong enough to be useful in practice. Our lower bounds are substantially stronger than standard combinatorial bounds. For example, evaluated via geometric means across a production testbed with $k = 16$ pipeline stages, our MIP formulations raise the lower bound from 0.4598 to 0.9452, expressed as a fraction of the best partition found. In other words, our improved lower bounds close the optimality gap by a factor of 9.855x.

paragraphs: Splitting a neural network into pipeline stages is useful only if the slowest stage does not hold up the rest. This paper studies how to partition a model graph to minimize that bottleneck time, including communication. The optimization problem is NP-hard, so finding a good partition also raises a practical question: how close is it to the best possible one?

Alongside effective partitioning algorithms, the authors develop mixed integer programming relaxations that produce lower bounds on the optimal bottleneck time. Comparing such a bound with an actual partition gives evidence about how much improvement could still be possible. A stronger lower bound makes that assessment more informative.

The evaluation covers 369 production models and stage counts from two to 64. For 16 stages, geometric-mean lower bounds rise from 0.4598 to 0.9452 as fractions of the best partition found, closing the optimality gap by a factor of 9.855. This is an improvement in certifying solution quality, not a reported inference speedup of that magnitude. The findings show that these bounds can help practitioners decide when further partition optimization is unlikely to yield much.
summary.tldr: Stronger optimization lower bounds help practitioners assess how close a neural-network pipeline partition is to optimal.

title: Practical Performance Guarantees for Pipelined DNN Inference

abstract: Representing uncertainty in causal discovery is a crucial component for experimental design, and more broadly, for safe and reliable causal decision making. Bayesian Causal Discovery (BCD) offers a principled approach to encapsulating this uncertainty. Unlike non-Bayesian causal discovery, which relies on a single estimated causal graph and model parameters for assessment, evaluating BCD presents challenges due to the nature of its inferred quantity – the posterior distribution. As a result, the research community has proposed various metrics to assess the quality of the approximate posterior. However, there is, to date, no consensus on the most suitable metric(s) for evaluation. In this work, we reexamine this question by dissecting various metrics and understanding their limitations. Through extensive empirical evaluation, we find that many existing metrics fail to exhibit a strong correlation with the quality of approximation to the true posterior, especially in scenarios with low sample sizes where BCD is most desirable. We highlight the suitability (or lack thereof) of these metrics under two distinct factors: the identifiability of the underlying causal model and the quantity of available data. Both factors affect the entropy of the true posterior, indicating that the current metrics are less fitting in settings of higher entropy. Our findings underline the importance of a more nuanced evaluation of new methods by taking into account the nature of the true posterior, as well as guide and motivate the development of new evaluation procedures for this challenge.

paragraphs: Bayesian causal discovery represents uncertainty through a posterior distribution over causal explanations. Evaluating that distribution is more demanding than checking a single estimated graph: a method must represent which explanations remain plausible and how uncertainty is distributed among them. This paper investigates whether existing evaluation metrics capture the quality of that approximation.

The authors dissect several metrics and examine their behavior empirically. They find that many do not strongly track how well an approximate posterior matches the true posterior. The mismatch is especially pronounced when sample sizes are small, precisely a setting in which representing uncertainty can be particularly valuable.

The analysis highlights two factors: whether the underlying causal model is identifiable and how much data is available. Both influence posterior entropy, or how spread out the remaining uncertainty is. Existing metrics appear less suitable when that entropy is high. The paper therefore argues for evaluating methods in light of the posterior being approximated and motivates procedures that better reflect the uncertainty present in each setting.
summary.tldr: Common Bayesian causal discovery metrics can poorly reflect posterior approximation quality, particularly with limited data and high uncertainty.

title: Challenges and Considerations in the Evaluation of Bayesian Causal Discovery

abstract: When using an autoencoder to learn the low-dimensional manifold of high-dimensional data, it is crucial to find the latent representations that preserve the geometry of the data manifold. However, most existing studies assume a Euclidean nature for the high-dimensional data space, which is arbitrary and often does not precisely reflect the underlying semantic or domain-specific attributes of the data. In this paper, we propose a novel autoencoder regularization framework based on the premise that the geometry of the data manifold can often be better captured with a well-designed similarity graph associated with data points. Given such a graph, we utilize a Riemannian geometric distortion measure as a regularizer to preserve the geometry derived from the graph Laplacian and make it suitable for larger-scale autoencoder training. Through extensive experiments, we show that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art geometry-preserving and graph-based autoencoders with respect to learning accurate latent structures that preserve the graph geometry, and is particularly effective in learning dynamics in the latent space. Code is available at https://github.com/JungbinLim/GGAE-public.

paragraphs: An autoencoder compresses high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional representation, but preserving the meaningful relationships between data points requires choosing an appropriate geometry. This paper questions the common assumption that ordinary Euclidean geometry in the original data space captures those relationships. Semantic or domain-specific similarities may instead be expressed more accurately by a suitable graph.

Given a similarity graph over the data points, the authors derive geometry from its graph Laplacian. They use a Riemannian geometric distortion measure as a training regularizer, encouraging the latent representation to preserve that geometry. The framework also makes this regularization suitable for larger-scale autoencoder training.

Experiments show better preservation of graph geometry than existing state-of-the-art geometry-preserving and graph-based autoencoders. The method is particularly effective for learning dynamics in latent space. Its central premise is the availability of a well-designed similarity graph: that graph supplies the relationships the representation should retain. The results support using this supplied geometry to guide compression and subsequent learning of dynamics.
summary.tldr: A graph-derived geometric regularizer helps autoencoders preserve meaningful latent structure and learn dynamics in latent space.

title: Graph Geometry-Preserving Autoencoders

abstract: This work focuses on addressing two major challenges in the context of large-scale nonconvex Bi-Level Optimization (BLO) problems, which are increasingly applied in machine learning due to their ability to model nested structures. These challenges involve ensuring computational efficiency and providing theoretical guarantees. While recent advances in scalable BLO algorithms have primarily relied on lower-level convexity simplification, our work specifically tackles large-scale BLO problems involving nonconvexity in both the upper and lower levels. We simultaneously address computational and theoretical challenges by introducing an innovative single-loop gradient-based algorithm, utilizing the Moreau envelope-based reformulation, and providing non-asymptotic convergence analysis for general nonconvex BLO problems. Notably, our algorithm relies solely on first-order gradient information, enhancing its practicality and efficiency, especially for large-scale BLO learning tasks. We validate our approach’s effectiveness through experiments on various synthetic problems, two typical hyper-parameter learning tasks, and a real-world neural architecture search application, collectively demonstrating its superior performance.

paragraphs: Bi-level optimization models a nested decision problem: an upper-level objective depends on the outcome of a lower-level optimization problem. Such structures appear in machine learning, but making them computationally manageable while retaining theoretical guarantees is difficult. This paper addresses the case where both optimization levels can be nonconvex.

The authors introduce a reformulation based on the Moreau envelope and use it to construct a single-loop gradient-based algorithm. The method relies only on first-order gradient information, avoiding Hessian computations. These design choices target large-scale problems, where the computational demands of nested optimization and higher-order information can make an approach difficult to use.

The paper provides a non-asymptotic convergence analysis for the proposed treatment of general nonconvex bi-level problems. This accompanies the algorithmic contribution with a characterization of convergence before taking an infinite-iteration limit. Experiments cover synthetic problems, two hyperparameter-learning tasks, and a real-world neural architecture search application, reporting superior performance. Together, the analysis and evaluations support a practical strategy that addresses nonconvexity at both levels.
summary.tldr: A Moreau-envelope reformulation enables single-loop, first-order optimization when both levels of a bi-level problem are nonconvex.

title: Moreau Envelope for Nonconvex Bi-Level Optimization: A Single-Loop and Hessian-Free Solution Strategy

abstract: We propose the problem of conversational web navigation, where a digital agent controls a web browser and follows user instructions to solve real-world tasks in a multi-turn dialogue fashion. To support this problem, we introduce WEBLINX - a large-scale benchmark of 100K interactions across 2300 expert demonstrations of conversational web navigation. Our benchmark covers a broad range of patterns on over 150 real-world websites and can be used to train and evaluate agents in diverse scenarios. Due to the magnitude of information present, Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot process entire web pages in real-time. To solve this bottleneck, we design a retrieval-inspired model that efficiently prunes HTML pages by ranking relevant elements. We use the selected elements, along with screenshots and action history, to assess a variety of models for their ability to replicate human behavior when navigating the web. Our experiments span from small text-only to proprietary multimodal LLMs. We find that smaller finetuned decoders surpass the best zero-shot LLMs (including GPT-4V), but also larger finetuned multimodal models which were explicitly pretrained on screenshots. However, all finetuned models struggle to generalize to unseen websites. Our findings highlight the need for large multimodal models that can generalize to novel settings.

Our benchmark covers a broad range of patterns on over 150 real-world websites and can be used to train and evaluate agents in diverse scenarios. title: WebLINX: Real-World Website Navigation with Multi-Turn Dialogue

abstract: Existing Large Language Models (LLMs) usually remain static after deployment, which might make it hard to inject new knowledge into the model. We aim to build models containing a considerable portion of self-updatable parameters, enabling the model to integrate new knowledge effectively and efficiently. To this end, we introduce MEMORYLLM, a model that comprises a transformer and a fixed-size memory pool within the latent space of the transformer. MEMORYLLM can self-update with text knowledge and memorize the knowledge injected earlier. Our evaluations demonstrate the ability of MEMORYLLM to effectively incorporate new knowledge, as evidenced by its performance on model editing benchmarks. Meanwhile, the model exhibits long-term information retention capacity, which is validated through our custom-designed evaluations and long-context benchmarks. MEMORYLLM also shows operational integrity without any sign of performance degradation even after nearly a million memory updates. Our code and model are open-sourced at https://github.com/wangyu-ustc/MemoryLLM.

paragraphs: A deployed language model typically remains fixed, which can make adding new knowledge difficult. MEMORYLLM explores a model design with a substantial portion of self-updatable parameters. The aim is to incorporate incoming text knowledge efficiently while retaining information supplied through earlier updates.

The architecture combines a transformer with a fixed-size memory pool inside its latent space. This makes updateable memory part of the model's internal representation. The central challenge is twofold: new information must become usable, and repeated updates must preserve the ability to use older information. The paper evaluates both aspects rather than treating successful knowledge insertion as the whole problem.

Model-editing benchmarks support the model's ability to incorporate new knowledge. Custom evaluations and long-context benchmarks also support long-term information retention. In addition, the authors report no observed performance degradation after nearly a million memory updates. That endurance result provides evidence that repeated updates can remain operationally stable in their evaluations, making the architecture relevant to language models whose knowledge needs to change after deployment.
summary.tldr: MEMORYLLM embeds an updateable memory pool in a transformer, showing knowledge integration and retention without observed degradation across nearly a million updates.

title: MEMORYLLM: Towards Self-Updatable Large Language Models

abstract: A common approach for aligning language models to human preferences is to first learn a reward model from preference data, and then use this reward model to update the language model. We study two closely related problems that arise in this approach. First, any monotone transformation of the reward model preserves preference ranking; is there a choice that is "better" than others? Second, we often wish to align language models to multiple properties: how should we combine multiple reward models? Using a probabilistic interpretation of the alignment procedure, we identify a natural choice for transformation for (the common case of) rewards learned from Bradley-Terry preference models. The derived transformation is straightforward: we apply a log-sigmoid function to the centered rewards, a method we term "LSC-transformation" (log-sigmoid-centered transformation). This transformation has two important properties. First, it emphasizes improving poorly-performing outputs, rather than outputs that already score well. This mitigates both underfitting (where some prompts are not improved) and reward hacking (where the model learns to exploit misspecification of the reward model). Second, it enables principled aggregation of rewards by linking summation to logical conjunction: the sum of transformed rewards corresponds to the probability that the output is "good" in all measured properties, in a sense we make precise. Experiments aligning language models to be both helpful and harmless using RLHF show substantial improvements over the baseline (non-transformed) approach.

It derives an answer through a probabilistic interpretation of alignment with Bradley–Terry preference models.

The transformation also gives reward aggregation a logical interpretation: summing transformed rewards connects to the probability that an output is good on all measured properties, in the paper's precise formulation. Experiments using reinforcement learning from human feedback to improve helpfulness and harmlessness show substantial gains over untransformed rewards. The work therefore links reward scaling, optimization priorities, and multi-property alignment in one framework.
summary.tldr: LSC transforms preference rewards to emphasize weak outputs and gives their combination a probabilistic interpretation for satisfying multiple properties.

title: Transforming and Combining Rewards for Aligning Large Language Models

abstract: This paper describes a differentially private post-processing algorithm for learning fair regressors satisfying statistical parity, addressing privacy concerns of machine learning models trained on sensitive data, as well as fairness concerns of their potential to propagate historical biases. Our algorithm can be applied to post-process any given regressor to improve fairness by remapping its outputs. It consists of three steps: first, the output distributions are estimated privately via histogram density estimation and the Laplace mechanism, then their Wasserstein barycenter is computed, and the optimal transports to the barycenter are used for post-processing to satisfy fairness. We analyze the sample complexity of our algorithm and provide fairness guarantee, revealing a trade-off between the statistical bias and variance induced from the choice of the number of bins in the histogram, in which using less bins always favors fairness at the expense of error.

paragraphs: A regression model can produce different output distributions across groups, raising concerns about statistical parity. This paper develops a differentially private procedure that adjusts an existing regressor's outputs to improve fairness. Because it operates through output remapping, the procedure can be applied to any given regressor.

The algorithm first estimates output distributions using histograms, with the Laplace mechanism providing privacy for that estimation. It then computes a Wasserstein barycenter, a shared distribution defined through transport between distributions. Finally, it uses optimal transport maps to move the original outputs toward that common distribution. Aligning distributions in this way is the mechanism used to satisfy the fairness objective.

The authors analyze sample complexity and give a fairness guarantee. Their analysis also exposes a practical choice: how many histogram bins to use. Fewer bins favor fairness but increase error, reflecting a trade-off involving statistical bias and variance. Thus, the distribution-estimation step directly influences the balance between prediction error and fairness in the resulting post-processed model.
summary.tldr: The method privately estimates prediction distributions and remaps them toward a shared distribution, with an analyzed fairness–error trade-off.

title: Differentially Private Post-Processing for Fair Regression

abstract: Imitation learning heavily relies on the quality of provided demonstrations. In scenarios where demonstrations are imperfect and rare, a prevalent approach for refining policies is through online fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, in which a Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization is often employed to stabilize the learning process. However, our investigation reveals that on the one hand, imperfect demonstrations can bias the online learning process, the KL regularization will further constrain the improvement of online policy exploration. To address the above issues, we propose Iterative Regularized Policy Optimization (IRPO), a framework that involves iterative offline imitation learning and online reinforcement exploration. Specifically, the policy learned online is used to serve as the demonstrator for successive learning iterations, with a demonstration boosting to consistently enhance the quality of demonstrations. Experimental validations conducted across widely used benchmarks and a novel fixed-wing UAV control task consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of IRPO in improving both the demonstration quality and the policy performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/GongXudong/IRPO.

paragraphs: Imitation learning inherits weaknesses from its demonstrations, especially when examples are scarce and imperfect. Online reinforcement learning can refine the resulting policy, often with KL regularization to stabilize updates. This paper finds that imperfect demonstrations can bias that refinement, while regularization can further restrict the exploration needed to improve.

Iterative Regularized Policy Optimization, or IRPO, alternates offline imitation learning with online reinforcement exploration. The policy produced by online learning becomes the demonstrator for subsequent iterations. A demonstration-boosting process improves the examples used for later learning, allowing the source of imitation guidance to evolve along with the policy.

The key idea is to repeatedly refresh the demonstrations instead of leaving the initial examples as a persistent source of bias. Experiments on widely used benchmarks and a new fixed-wing UAV control task show improvements in both demonstration quality and policy performance. These results support the iterative interaction between imitation and exploration as a way to learn more effectively from imperfect starting demonstrations.
summary.tldr: IRPO alternates imitation and reinforcement learning, using improved online policies to strengthen demonstrations for subsequent iterations.

title: Iterative Regularized Policy Optimization with Imperfect Demonstrations

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) show significant strides in general-propose multimodal applications such as visual dialogue and embodied navigation. However, existing multimodal evaluation benchmarks cover a limited number of multimodal tasks testing rudimentary capabilities, falling short in tracking LVLM development. In this study, we present MMT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to assess LVLMs across massive multimodal tasks requiring expert knowledge and deliberate visual recognition, localization, and reasoning. MMT-Bench comprises $31,325$ meticulously curated multi-choice visual questions from various multimodal scenarios such as vehicle driving and embodied navigation, covering $32$ core meta-tasks and $162$ subtasks in multimodal understanding. Due to its extensive task coverage, MMT-Bench enables the evaluation of LVLMs using a task map, facilitating the discovery of in- and out-of-domain tasks. Evaluation results involving $20$ publicly available LVLMs such as the proprietary GeminiProVision model, underscore the significant challenges posed by MMT-Bench. We anticipate that MMT-Bench will inspire the community to develop next-generation multimodal foundation models aimed at achieving general-purpose multimodal intelligence.

The paper argues that existing benchmarks cover too few tasks and emphasize basic capabilities. MMT-Bench expands evaluation to tasks requiring expert knowledge as well as careful visual recognition, localization, and reasoning.

The benchmark contains 31,325 curated multiple-choice visual questions across 32 broad task categories and 162 subtasks. Its scenarios include vehicle driving and embodied navigation. This breadth supports a task map for examining model capabilities and identifying tasks that fall inside or outside a model's domain.

The results show that MMT-Bench poses substantial challenges for the evaluated systems. The task map makes the variety of abilities part of the assessment, supporting the stated goal of tracking progress toward more general-purpose multimodal models.
summary.tldr: MMT-Bench evaluates vision-language models with 31,325 visual questions spanning 162 subtasks and reveals substantial challenges for current evaluated systems.

title: MMT-Bench: A Comprehensive Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating Large Vision-Language Models Towards Multitask AGI

abstract: This paper introduces RaLMSpec, a framework that accelerates iterative retrieval-augmented language model (RaLM) with speculative retrieval and batched verification. RaLMSpec further introduces several important systems optimizations, including prefetching, optimal speculation stride scheduler, and asynchronous verification. The combination of these techniques allows RaLMSPec to significantly outperform existing systems. For document-level iterative RaLM serving, evaluation over three LLMs on four QA datasets shows that RaLMSpec improves over existing approaches by $1.75$-$2.39\times$, $1.04$-$1.39\times$, and $1.31$-$1.77\times$ when the retriever is an exact dense retriever, approximate dense retriever, and sparse retriever respectively. For token-level iterative RaLM (KNN-LM) serving, RaLMSpec is up to $7.59\times$ and $2.45\times$ faster than existing methods for exact dense and approximate dense retrievers, respectively.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented language models consult external information while generating answers. When retrieval happens repeatedly, serving the model involves coordinating many retrieval and generation operations. RaLMSpec targets this repeated work with speculative retrieval and batched verification: it anticipates retrieval work and checks speculative results together, making the interaction between retrieval and generation more efficient.

The framework combines this approach with several systems optimizations. Prefetching prepares information ahead of use, a speculation stride scheduler controls how far speculation proceeds, and asynchronous verification allows checking to happen without making every operation wait in sequence. These components address the execution of iterative retrieval, with evaluations covering both document retrieval and token-level retrieval in KNN language models.

Across three language models and four question-answering datasets, document-level speedups range from 1.75–2.39 times for exact dense retrieval, 1.04–1.39 times for approximate dense retrieval, and 1.31–1.77 times for sparse retrieval. Token-level serving reaches speedups of up to 7.59 and 2.45 times for exact and approximate dense retrieval, respectively. The differing gains show that the benefit depends on the retrieval setting.
summary.tldr: RaLMSpec accelerates repeated retrieval during language-model serving by combining speculative retrieval, batched verification, and coordinated systems optimizations.

title: Accelerating Iterative Retrieval-augmented Language Model Serving with Speculation

abstract: In this paper, we investigate how randomness and uncertainty influence learning in games. Specifically, we examine a perturbed variant of the dynamics of “follow-the-regularized-leader” (FTRL), where the players’ payoff observations and strategy updates are continually impacted by random shocks. Our findings reveal that, in a fairly precise sense, “uncertainty favors extremes”: in any game, regardless of the noise level, every player’s trajectory of play reaches an arbitrarily small neighborhood of a pure strategy in finite time (which we estimate). Moreover, even if the player does not ultimately settle at this strategy, they return arbitrarily close to some (possibly different) pure strategy infinitely often. This prompts the question of which sets of pure strategies emerge as robust predictions of learning under uncertainty. We show that (a) the only possible limits of the FTRL dynamics under uncertainty are pure Nash equilibria; and (b) a span of pure strategies is stable and attracting if and only if it is closed under better replies. Finally, we turn to games where the deterministic dynamics are recurrent—such as zero-sum games with interior equilibria—and show that randomness disrupts this behavior, causing the stochastic dynamics to drift toward the boundary on average.
