paragraphs: This paper examines follow-the-regularized-leader learning when random shocks continually affect payoff observations and strategy updates. In the studied dynamics, randomness pushes play toward pure strategies, where a player concentrates on one action. Every player reaches arbitrarily small neighborhoods of pure strategies in finite time and revisits such neighborhoods infinitely often.

Randomness disrupts that recurrence and produces an average drift toward the boundary. These results distinguish repeated movement toward extreme strategies from actual convergence, while explaining how uncertainty changes the long-run structure of regularized learning.
summary.tldr: Randomly perturbed FTRL repeatedly approaches pure strategies, with pure Nash equilibria as its only possible limits.

title: The impact of uncertainty on regularized learning in games

abstract: Benchmark contamination has become a significant concern in the LLM evaluation community. Previous Agents-as-an-Evaluator address this issue by involving agents in the generation of questions. Despite their success, the biases in Agents-as-an-Evaluator methods remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we present a theoretical formulation of evaluation bias, providing valuable insights into designing unbiased evaluation protocols. Furthermore, we identify two type of bias in Agents-as-an-Evaluator through carefully designed probing tasks on a minimal Agents-as-an-Evaluator setup. To address these issues, we propose the Unbiased Evaluator, an evaluation protocol that delivers a more comprehensive, unbiased, and interpretable assessment of LLMs. Extensive experiments reveal significant room for improvement in current LLMs. Additionally, we demonstrate that the Unbiased Evaluator not only offers strong evidence of benchmark contamination but also provides interpretable evaluation results.

paragraphs: Generating evaluation questions with agents offers a response to benchmark contamination, where test material may have appeared in model training. However, the process used to generate and administer those questions can introduce its own biases. This paper examines that problem in methods that use agents as evaluators.

The authors develop a theoretical formulation of evaluation bias to guide protocol design. They then use carefully constructed probing tasks in a minimal agent-evaluator setup to identify two types of bias. Building on those findings, they propose the Unbiased Evaluator, a protocol intended to provide a more comprehensive, unbiased, and interpretable assessment of language models.

Extensive experiments reveal significant remaining room for improvement in current models. The protocol also provides strong evidence of benchmark contamination and produces interpretable evaluation results. The contribution is to make the evaluation procedure itself an object of analysis: generating new questions is only one part of the problem, and the authors use their bias formulation and probes to guide a revised assessment protocol.
summary.tldr: The Unbiased Evaluator uses a theoretical analysis of agent-evaluation bias to improve interpretability and expose evidence of benchmark contamination.

title: Unbiased Evaluation of Large Language Models from a Causal Perspective

abstract: Deep learning models often struggle when deployed in real-world settings due to distribution shifts between training and test data. While existing approaches like domain adaptation and test-time training (TTT) offer partial solutions, they typically require additional data or domain-specific auxiliary tasks. We present Idempotent Test-Time Training (IT3), a novel approach that enables on-the-fly adaptation to distribution shifts using only the current test instance, without any auxiliary task design. Our key insight is that enforcing idempotence—where repeated applications of a function yield the same result—can effectively replace domain-specific auxiliary tasks used in previous TTT methods. We theoretically connect idempotence to prediction confidence and demonstrate that minimizing the distance between successive applications of our model during inference leads to improved out-of-distribution performance. Extensive experiments across diverse domains (including image classification, aerodynamics prediction, and aerial segmentation) and architectures (MLPs, CNNs, GNNs) show that IT3 consistently outperforms existing approaches while being simpler and more widely applicable. Our results suggest that idempotence provides a universal principle for test-time adaptation that generalizes across domains and architectures.

Our key insight is that enforcing idempotence—where repeated applications of a function yield the same result—can effectively replace domain-specific auxiliary tasks used in previous TTT methods. Extensive experiments across diverse domains (including image classification, aerodynamics prediction, and aerial segmentation) and architectures (MLPs, CNNs, GNNs) show that IT3 consistently outperforms existing approaches while being simpler and more widely applicable. paragraphs: Models can lose accuracy when deployment data differs from their training data. Test-time training addresses this by adapting during inference, but existing methods often need extra data or a specially designed auxiliary task. IT3 proposes adaptation using only the current test instance and a consistency principle that does not require domain-specific auxiliary-task design.

That principle is idempotence: applying a function again should leave its result unchanged. IT3 adapts the model by reducing the distance between successive applications during inference. The paper theoretically connects this property to prediction confidence, giving a rationale for using repeated-application consistency as the signal that drives adaptation.

Experiments cover image classification, aerodynamics prediction, and aerial segmentation, using architectures including multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and graph neural networks. IT3 consistently outperforms existing approaches in the reported experiments while offering a simpler adaptation setup. The authors interpret these results as evidence that idempotence may provide a broadly applicable adaptation principle; the empirical breadth supports that possibility without establishing success for every domain.
summary.tldr: IT3 adapts models on a single test instance by encouraging repeated applications to agree, improving performance across several domains and architectures.

title: IT$^3$: Idempotent Test-Time Training

abstract: Removing unwanted concepts from large-scale text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models while maintaining their overall generative quality remains an open challenge. This difficulty is especially pronounced in emerging paradigms, such as Stable Diffusion (SD) v3 and Flux, which incorporate flow matching and transformer-based architectures. These advancements limit the transferability of existing concept-erasure techniques that were originally designed for the previous T2I paradigm (e.g., SD v1.4). In this work, we introduce EraseAnything, the first method specifically developed to address concept erasure within the latest flow-based T2I framework. We formulate concept erasure as a bi-level optimization problem, employing LoRA-based parameter tuning and an attention map regularizer to selectively suppress undesirable activations. Furthermore, we propose a self-contrastive learning strategy to ensure that removing unwanted concepts does not inadvertently harm performance on unrelated ones. Experimental results demonstrate that EraseAnything successfully fills the research gap left by earlier methods in this new T2I paradigm, achieving state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of concept erasure tasks.

EraseAnything addresses this challenge in newer systems that combine flow-based generation with transformer architectures. EraseAnything formulates the task as a bi-level optimization problem, coupling two levels of optimization. It uses LoRA-based parameter tuning together with a regularizer on attention maps to selectively suppress unwanted activations. A self-contrastive learning strategy is intended to protect performance on concepts unrelated to the removal target, making preservation part of the method rather than only an evaluation concern.

The paper presents the approach as the first specifically developed for concept erasure in this newer flow-based framework. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of erasure tasks. These findings support adapting the optimization and preservation mechanisms to the model architecture, with the reported success covering selective concept removal as well as the goal of maintaining broader generative quality.
summary.tldr: EraseAnything adapts concept erasure to flow-based text-to-image transformers using targeted parameter updates, attention regularization, and self-contrastive learning.

title: EraseAnything: Enabling Concept Erasure in Rectified Flow Transformers

abstract: Offline-to-online Reinforcement Learning (O2O RL) aims to perform online fine-tuning on an offline pre-trained policy to minimize costly online interactions. Existing work used offline datasets to generate data that conform to the online data distribution for data augmentation. However, generated data still exhibits a gap with the online data, limiting overall performance. To address this, we propose a new data augmentation approach, Classifier-Free Diffusion Generation (CFDG). Without introducing additional classifier training overhead, CFDG leverages classifier-free guidance diffusion to significantly enhance the generation quality of offline and online data with different distributions. Additionally, it employs a reweighting method to enable more generated data to align with the online data, enhancing performance while maintaining the agent’s stability. Experimental results show that CFDG outperforms replaying the two data types or using a standard diffusion model to generate new data. Our method is versatile and can be integrated with existing offline-to-online RL algorithms. By implementing CFDG to popular methods IQL, PEX and APL, we achieve a notable 15% average improvement in empirical performance on the D4RL benchmark such as MuJoCo and AntMaze.

title: Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning with Classifier-Free Diffusion Generation

abstract: Multi-view clustering (MVC) leverages complementary information from diverse data sources to enhance clustering performance. However, its practical deployment in distributed and privacy-sensitive scenarios remains challenging. Federated multi-view clustering (FMVC) has emerged as a potential solution, but existing approaches suffer from substantial limitations, including excessive communication overhead, insufficient privacy protection, and inadequate handling of missing views. To address these issues, we propose Efficient Federated Incomplete Multi-View Clustering (EFIMVC), a novel framework that introduces a localized optimization strategy to significantly reduce communication costs while ensuring theoretical convergence. EFIMVC employs both view-specific and shared anchor graphs as communication variables, thereby enhancing privacy by avoiding the transmission of sensitive embeddings. Moreover, EFIMVC seamlessly extends to scenarios with missing views, making it a practical and scalable solution for real-world applications. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of EFIMVC in clustering accuracy, communication efficiency, and privacy preservation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tracesource/EFIMVC.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups data using complementary information from several sources. Applying it across distributed participants creates additional challenges: communication can be costly, shared representations can expose sensitive information, and some participants or examples may lack certain views. EFIMVC is designed to address these concerns together within a federated clustering framework.

The method uses localized optimization to reduce communication, accompanied by a theoretical convergence result. For the information that must be exchanged, it uses both view-specific and shared anchor graphs. This choice avoids sending sensitive embeddings and provides a way to communicate structure relevant to clustering. The framework also accommodates missing views, so its operation does not require every source of information to be present.

Benchmark experiments report advantages in clustering accuracy, communication efficiency, and privacy preservation. The contribution is the combination of these properties within one approach: reducing exchanges while retaining useful information across views and supporting incomplete data. Its privacy benefit is tied to avoiding embedding transmission; the abstract does not frame that design choice as an absolute guarantee against disclosure.
summary.tldr: EFIMVC combines local optimization and anchor-graph communication to improve federated clustering efficiency, privacy preservation, and handling of missing views.

title: Efficient Federated Incomplete Multi-View Clustering

abstract: With the integration of image modality, the semantic space of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is more complex than text-only models, making their interpretability more challenging and their alignment less stable, particularly susceptible to low-quality data, which can lead to inconsistencies between modalities, hallucinations, and biased outputs. As a result, developing interpretability methods for MLLMs is crucial for improving alignment quality and efficiency. In text-only LLMs, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have gained attention for their ability to interpret latent representations. However, extending SAEs to multimodal settings presents new challenges due to modality fusion and the difficulty of isolating cross-modal representations. To address these challenges, we introduce SAE-V, a mechanistic interpretability framework that extends the SAE paradigm to MLLMs. By identifying and analyzing interpretable features along with their corresponding data, SAE-V enables fine-grained interpretation of both model behavior and data quality, facilitating a deeper understanding of cross-modal interactions and alignment dynamics. Moreover, by utilizing cross-modal feature weighting, SAE-V provides an intrinsic data filtering mechanism to enhance model alignment without requiring additional models. Specifically, when applied to the alignment process of MLLMs, SAE-V-based data filtering methods could achieve more than 110% performance with less than 50% data. Our results highlight SAE-V’s ability to enhance interpretability and alignment in MLLMs, providing insights into their internal mechanisms.

paragraphs: Adding images to a language model makes its internal representations harder to interpret and its alignment more sensitive to data quality. Poor examples can contribute to disagreements between modalities, hallucinations, and biased outputs. SAE-V addresses these connected problems by extending sparse autoencoders to multimodal language models, where separating cross-modal representations is challenging.

The framework identifies interpretable features and examines the data associated with them. This links analysis of model behavior to analysis of training-data quality, providing a finer-grained view of how modalities interact. SAE-V then uses cross-modal feature weighting to filter alignment data through the model’s own representations, without requiring an additional model.

The authors report that SAE-V-based filtering could achieve more than 110% performance using less than 50% of the data. This is a relative performance claim, rather than an accuracy exceeding 100%. The result connects interpretability to a practical training benefit: understanding internal features can help select data that supports more effective and data-efficient alignment in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: SAE-V interprets multimodal features and uses them to filter alignment data, reporting improved relative performance with less than half the data.

title: SAE-V: Interpreting Multimodal Models for Enhanced Alignment

abstract: Current video-language models struggle with long-video understanding due to limited context lengths and reliance on sparse frame subsampling, which often leads to information loss. In this paper, we introduce $\infty$-Video, which is able to process arbitrarily long videos through a continuous-time long-term memory (LTM) consolidation mechanism. Our framework augments video Q-formers by making them able to process unbounded video contexts efficiently and without requiring additional training. Through continuous attention, our approach dynamically allocates higher granularity to the most relevant video segments, forming "sticky" memories which evolve over time. Experiments with Video-LLaMA and VideoChat2 demonstrate improved performance in video question-answering tasks, showcasing the potential of continuous-time LTM mechanisms to enable scalable and training-free comprehension of long videos.

paragraphs: Video-language models face a context limit when processing long recordings. Selecting only a sparse set of frames can fit that limit but lose information needed to understand the video. This paper introduces ∞-Video, a framework that uses continuous-time long-term memory consolidation to process arbitrarily long video inputs without additional training.

The framework augments video Q-formers with a mechanism for handling unbounded video context. Continuous attention assigns finer detail to segments judged most relevant. The resulting sticky memories evolve over time, allowing the representation of the video to change as processing continues. This provides a way to allocate memory detail selectively across a long sequence.

Experiments with Video-LLaMA and VideoChat2 show improved performance on video question answering. These results support the usefulness of the memory mechanism within existing video-language systems. The contribution combines a way to handle inputs beyond a fixed context window with a training-free integration, demonstrating the potential of continuous-time memory for scalable long-video understanding.
summary.tldr: ∞-Video adds evolving continuous-time memory to video-language models, improving long-video question answering without additional training.

title: $∞$-Video: A Training-Free Approach to Long Video Understanding via Continuous-Time Memory Consolidation

abstract: As machine learning-based prediction systems are increasingly used in high-stakes situations, it is important to understand how such predictive models will perform upon deployment. Distribution-free uncertainty quantification techniques such as conformal prediction provide guarantees about the loss black-box models will incur even when the details of the models are hidden. However, such methods are based on frequentist probability, which unduly limits their applicability. We revisit the central aspects of conformal prediction from a Bayesian perspective and thereby illuminate the shortcomings of frequentist guarantees. We propose a practical alternative based on Bayesian quadrature that provides interpretable guarantees and offers a richer representation of the likely range of losses to be observed at test time.

paragraphs: The paper examines how to describe the losses a predictive model is likely to incur after deployment. Conformal prediction addresses this problem with distribution-free guarantees and can work even when the model’s internal details are unavailable. The authors argue that the frequentist interpretation underlying these guarantees restricts how they can be used.

Their approach revisits the central ingredients of conformal prediction from a Bayesian perspective. This changes the way uncertainty about future losses is represented and interpreted. The proposed practical alternative uses Bayesian quadrature, placing that method at the center of a framework for describing a model’s likely test-time behavior.

The stated contribution is both conceptual and methodological: a critique of how existing guarantees should be understood, together with an alternative that offers interpretable guarantees and a richer picture of possible losses. This matters when a deployment decision requires understanding the range of likely outcomes, beyond the particular assurance supplied by a conventional conformal procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper reinterprets conformal prediction through Bayesian reasoning and proposes Bayesian quadrature for richer, interpretable descriptions of test-time losses.

title: Conformal Prediction as Bayesian Quadrature

abstract: Developing autonomous agents that quickly explore an environment and adapt their behavior online is a canonical challenge in robotics and machine learning. While humans are able to achieve such fast online exploration and adaptation, often acquiring new information and skills in only a handful of interactions, existing algorithmic approaches tend to rely on random exploration and slow, gradient-based behavior updates. How can we endow autonomous agents with such capabilities on par with humans? Taking inspiration from recent progress on both in-context learning and large-scale behavioral cloning, in this work we propose behavioral exploration: training agents to internalize what it means to explore and adapt in-context over the space of ”expert” behaviors. To achieve this, given access to a dataset of expert demonstrations, we train a long-context generative model to predict expert actions conditioned on a context of past observations and a measure of how ”exploratory” the expert’s behaviors are relative to this context. This enables the model to not only mimic the behavior of an expert, but also, by feeding its past history of interactions into its context, to select different expert behaviors than what have been previously selected, thereby allowing for fast online adaptation and targeted, ”expert-like” exploration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in both simulated locomotion and manipulation settings, as well as on real-world robotic manipulation tasks, illustrating its ability to learn adaptive, exploratory behavior.

paragraphs: Autonomous agents need to discover useful behavior while interacting with an environment. Random exploration and slow behavioral updates can make this difficult. This paper proposes learning exploration itself from expert demonstrations, so an agent can use its interaction history to choose purposeful behaviors and adapt online.

Given a dataset of expert demonstrations, the method trains a long-context generative model to predict expert actions. Its inputs include past observations and a measure of how exploratory an expert behavior would be relative to that context. This makes the learning objective sensitive to what the agent has already experienced, rather than treating every expert action as equally informative at every moment.

During deployment, the agent feeds its growing interaction history back into the model. That context lets it select expert behaviors different from those previously chosen, supporting targeted exploration and fast adaptation. Experiments cover simulated locomotion, simulated manipulation, and real robotic manipulation. The findings support learning an adaptive exploration strategy over available expert behaviors, with access to demonstrations central to the approach.
summary.tldr: Behavioral exploration trains agents to use interaction history to select informative expert-like behaviors and adapt online.

title: Behavioral Exploration: Learning to Explore via In-Context Adaptation

abstract: Large transformer models are known to produce high-norm tokens. In vision transformers (ViTs), such tokens have been mathematically modeled through the singular vectors of the linear approximations of layers. However, in large language models (LLMs), the underlying causes of high-norm tokens remain largely unexplored, and their different properties from those of ViTs require a new analysis framework. In this paper, we provide both theoretical insights and empirical validation across a range of recent models, leading to the following observations: i) The layer-wise singular direction predicts the abrupt explosion of token norms in LLMs. ii) The negative eigenvalues of a layer explain its sudden decay. iii) The computational pathways leading to high-norm tokens differ between initial and noninitial tokens. iv) High-norm tokens are triggered by the right leading singular vector of the matrix approximating the corresponding modules. We showcase two practical applications of these findings: the improvement of quantization schemes and the design of LLM signatures. Our findings not only advance the understanding of singular defects in LLMs but also open new avenues for their application. We expect that this work will stimulate further research into the internal mechanisms of LLMs. Code is released at https://github.com/haoqiwang/singular_defect.

paragraphs: Large language models sometimes produce token representations with unusually large magnitudes. This paper studies the mechanisms behind those high-norm tokens, combining mathematical analysis with empirical checks across recent models. Although related behavior has been studied in vision transformers, the authors argue that language models exhibit different properties requiring their own analytical framework.

The analysis links abrupt growth in token magnitude to singular directions of layer approximations and sudden decay to negative eigenvalues. It also finds that initial tokens and later tokens reach high magnitudes through different computational pathways. More specifically, the leading right singular vector of a matrix approximating the relevant module is identified as triggering high-norm behavior.

These findings connect an observable internal anomaly to particular mathematical properties of model computations. The paper demonstrates applications in improving quantization schemes and designing LLM signatures. Its contribution therefore includes both an explanation of where unusually large activations arise and examples of how that explanation can inform practical model techniques. The evidence combines theoretical insights with observations across multiple models.
summary.tldr: The paper links unusually large token representations to spectral properties of LLM layers and demonstrates applications in quantization and model signatures.

title: Demystifying Singular Defects in Large Language Models

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are increasingly recognized for their biological plausibility and energy efficiency, positioning them as strong alternatives to Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) in neuromorphic computing applications. SNNs inherently process temporal information by leveraging the precise timing of spikes, but balancing temporal feature utilization with low energy consumption remains a challenge. In this work, we introduce Temporal Shift module for Spiking Neural Networks (TS-SNN), which incorporates a novel Temporal Shift (TS) module to integrate past, present, and future spike features within a single timestep via a simple yet effective shift operation. A residual combination method prevents information loss by integrating shifted and original features. The TS module is lightweight, requiring only one additional learnable parameter, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing architectures with minimal additional computational cost. TS-SNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like CIFAR-10 (96.72%), CIFAR-100 (80.28%), and ImageNet (70.61%) with fewer timesteps, while maintaining low energy consumption. This work marks a significant step forward in developing efficient and accurate SNN architectures.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks represent information through spikes over time, creating opportunities for energy-efficient computation. Making good use of temporal features while keeping energy consumption low remains difficult. TS-SNN introduces a lightweight temporal shift module intended to improve the information available within each timestep without adding substantial computational cost.

The module shifts spike features so that past, present, and future features are integrated within a single timestep. A residual combination preserves the original features alongside the shifted ones to prevent information loss. The module adds only one learnable parameter and is designed to fit into existing architectures with minimal additional computation.

These findings connect a small architectural change to improved temporal feature use. The contribution is a simple mechanism for bringing information across time into the network's processing while retaining the efficiency goals that motivate spiking architectures.
summary.tldr: TS-SNN shifts and combines spike features across time to improve accuracy with fewer timesteps and little added computation.

title: TS-SNN: Temporal Shift Module for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Causal inference is a key research area in machine learning, yet confusion reigns over the tools needed to tackle it. There are prevalent claims in the machine learning literature that you need a bespoke causal framework or notation to answer causal questions. In this paper, we make it clear that you can answer any causal inference question within the realm of probabilistic modelling and inference, without causal-specific tools or notation. Through concrete examples, we demonstrate how causal questions can be tackled by writing down the probability of everything. We argue for the advantages of the generality of the probabilistic modelling lens, when compared to bespoke causal frameworks. Lastly, we reinterpret causal tools as emerging from standard probabilistic modelling and inference, elucidating their necessity and utility.

paragraphs: This position paper addresses a disagreement about the mathematical tools needed for causal inference. The authors argue that any causal inference question can be formulated and answered within probabilistic modeling and inference, without requiring a separate causal notation or specialized framework. Their claim is about the expressive and inferential sufficiency of the probabilistic approach.

The paper develops this position through concrete examples that describe the relevant situation probabilistically in full. By making the modeled quantities and their relationships explicit, the authors show how causal questions can be handled within a general modeling language. They argue that this generality offers advantages over using frameworks designed specifically for causal reasoning.

The authors also reinterpret causal tools as arising from standard probabilistic modeling and inference. This gives those tools a place within the broader approach and helps explain their necessity and usefulness. The paper’s message concerns how causal reasoning is represented and carried out: specialized causal tools can be understood through ordinary probabilistic machinery, even when they remain useful ways to organize the reasoning.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that probabilistic modeling and inference are sufficient for causal questions and can explain the role of specialized causal tools.

title: Position: Probabilistic Modelling is Sufficient for Causal Inference

abstract: Reasoning Large Language Models (R-LLMs) have significantly advanced complex reasoning tasks but often struggle with factuality, generating substantially more hallucinations than their non-reasoning counterparts on long-form factuality benchmarks. However, extending online Reinforcement Learning (RL), a key component in recent R-LLM advancements, to the long-form factuality setting poses several unique challenges due to the lack of reliable verification methods. Previous work has utilized automatic factuality evaluation frameworks such as FActScore to curate preference data in the offline RL setting, yet we find that directly leveraging such methods as the reward in online RL leads to reward hacking in multiple ways, such as producing less detailed or relevant responses. We propose a novel reward function that simultaneously considers the factual precision, response detail level, and answer relevance, and applies online RL to learn high quality factual reasoning. Evaluated on six long-form factuality benchmarks, our factual reasoning model achieves an average reduction of 23.1 percentage points in hallucination rate, a 23% increase in answer detail level, and no degradation in the overall response helpfulness.

paragraphs: Stronger reasoning does not automatically produce more factual long answers. The authors report that reasoning language models can hallucinate substantially more than their non-reasoning counterparts on long-form factuality benchmarks. Applying online reinforcement learning is challenging because these answers lack the reliable verification available for some other reasoning tasks.

The paper finds that directly using automatic factuality evaluators as online rewards invites reward hacking. A model can improve its reward by giving less detail or becoming less relevant. The proposed reward therefore combines factual precision, response detail, and answer relevance, so training considers whether a response remains informative and responsive alongside whether its claims are accurate.

Across six long-form factuality benchmarks, the resulting model reduces hallucination rate by an average of 23.1 percentage points and increases answer detail by 23%, with no degradation in overall helpfulness. The joint result matters because a lower hallucination rate alone could reflect evasive or sparse answers. Here, the reported improvement accompanies greater detail and preserved helpfulness.
summary.tldr: An online RL reward balancing factual precision, detail, and relevance reduces hallucinations while producing more detailed answers.

title: Learning to Reason for Factuality

abstract: Decoding-based regression, which reformulates regression as a sequence generation task, has emerged as a promising paradigm of applying large language models for numerical prediction. However, its progress is hindered by the misalignment between discrete token-level objectives (e.g., cross-entropy) and continuous numerical values. Existing approaches relying on token-level constraints often fail to capture the global magnitude of the target value, limiting their precision and generalization. In this paper, we propose to unlock the potential of decoding-based regression via reinforcement learning. We formulate the generation process as a Markov decision process, utilizing sequence-level rewards to enforce global numerical coherence.Under this framework, we present GenRe$^2$, which combines policy gradient methods and on-policy distillation to provide dense expert supervision while preserving error magnitudes, thereby resolving the temporal credit assignment challenge. Extensive experiments across tabular regression, code metric prediction and generative reward modeling demonstrate that GenRe$^2$ consistently outperforms traditional baselines, establishing a robust paradigm for general-purpose numerical prediction.

Extensive experiments across tabular regression, code metric prediction and generative reward modeling demonstrate that GenRe$^2$ consistently outperforms traditional baselines, establishing a robust paradigm for general-purpose numerical prediction.

paragraphs: Decoding-based regression asks a language model to generate a number as a sequence of tokens. Standard token prediction objectives do not directly reflect numerical distance: learning which token should come next does not by itself capture how far the completed prediction is from the target. The paper identifies this mismatch as a barrier to precision and generalization.

The authors formulate number generation as a Markov decision process and use rewards attached to complete sequences to encourage numerical coherence. Their method, GenRe², combines policy gradients with on-policy distillation. The distillation component supplies dense expert supervision while retaining information about error magnitude, addressing the difficulty of assigning responsibility for a final numerical error to earlier generation decisions.

Experiments cover tabular regression, code metric prediction, and generative reward modeling. GenRe² consistently outperforms traditional baselines in these evaluations. The findings support training generated numerical answers according to their overall values, with intermediate guidance helping the model learn from that sequence-level objective. This connects the mechanics of token generation more closely to the quantity the regression task actually evaluates.
summary.tldr: GenRe² combines sequence-level reinforcement learning and expert distillation to align generated numerical predictions with their actual error magnitudes.

title: Beyond Token-level Supervision: Unlocking the Potential of Decoding-based Regression via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The specification of the action space plays a pivotal role in imitation-based robotic manipulation policy learning, fundamentally shaping the optimization landscape of policy learning. While recent advances have focused heavily on scaling training data and model capacity, the choice of action space remains guided by ad-hoc heuristics or legacy designs, leading to an ambiguous understanding of robotic policy design philosophies. To address this ambiguity, we conducted a large-scale and systematic empirical study, confirming that the action space does have significant and complex impacts on robotic policy learning. We dissect the action design space along temporal and spatial axes, facilitating a structured analysis of how these choices govern both policy learnability and control stability. Based on 13,000+ real-world rollouts on a bimanual robot and evaluation on 500+ trained models over four scenarios, we examine the trade-offs between absolute vs. delta representations, and joint-space vs. task-space parameterizations. Our large-scale results suggest that properly designing the policy to predict delta actions consistently improves performance, while joint-space and task-space representations offer complementary strengths, favoring control stability and generalization, respectively.

paragraphs: A robot policy must express its decisions in some action representation, and that choice influences how readily it learns from demonstrations. This paper studies action design as a substantive part of policy learning. It asks how different representations affect both the learning problem and the stability of the resulting robot control, addressing choices often inherited from convention or selected heuristically.

The study organizes action choices along temporal and spatial axes. It compares absolute targets with delta actions, which describe changes, and joint-space commands with task-space commands. The evidence comes from more than 13,000 physical robot rollouts on a bimanual platform and evaluations of over 500 trained models across four scenarios.

The results suggest that properly designing a policy to predict delta actions consistently improves performance in the study. Spatial representations show complementary strengths: joint-space actions favor control stability, while task-space actions favor generalization. These findings make action representation a practical design consideration alongside training data and model capacity, while preserving the empirical nature of the conclusions.
summary.tldr: A large robot study finds benefits from properly designed delta actions and complementary stability and generalization strengths across spatial representations.

title: Demystifying Action Space Design for Robotic Manipulation Policies

abstract: Without incurring significant computational overhead, train-free long video generation aims to enable foundation video generation models to produce longer videos. Frame-level autoregressive frameworks, e.g., FIFO-diffusion, offer the advantage of generating infinitely long videos with constant memory consumption. However, the mismatch between training and inference, coupled with the challenge of maintaining long-term consistency, limits the effective utilization of foundation models. To mitigate these concerns, we propose MIGA, a novel infinite-frame long video generation method. Firstly, we propose an effective two-stage alignment mechanism that mitigates the training-inference gap by reducing the excessive noise span fed to the model. We then introduce an innovative dual consistency enhancement mechanism, where the self-reflection approach corrects early high-noise frames and the long-range frame guidance approach leverages later low-noise frames with broad coverage to steer generation, jointly improving temporal consistency. Extensive experiments on VBench and NarrLV demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of MIGA. Our project page is available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/miga_homepage/.

paragraphs: Extending a pretrained video generator to produce long sequences requires more than repeatedly producing additional frames. Frame-level autoregressive methods can continue indefinitely with constant memory, but their inference conditions differ from training, and consistency becomes difficult to maintain over time. MIGA addresses these problems within train-free long-video generation, aiming to make better use of existing foundation models.

Its first component is a two-stage alignment mechanism. This reduces the excessive spread of noise levels presented to the model, narrowing the training–inference gap. The second component combines two forms of consistency enhancement. Self-reflection corrects early frames that still contain substantial noise, while long-range guidance uses later, less noisy frames with broad coverage to steer generation.

These components address different sources of difficulty: alignment improves the conditions under which the pretrained model operates, while the paired guidance mechanisms improve temporal consistency. Experiments on VBench and NarrLV report state-of-the-art performance for MIGA. The contribution concerns the quality and coherence of continued generation; the ability to keep producing frames alone does not establish long-term consistency.
summary.tldr: MIGA improves train-free long-video generation by aligning noise conditions and combining early-frame correction with long-range guidance.

title: Enhancing Train-Free Infinite-Frame Generation for Consistent Long Videos

abstract: Data attribution has become an important component of pricing, auditing, and governance in machine learning pipelines, yet most attribution methods implicitly assume that attribution values faithfully reflect participants’ contributions. We show that this assumption can fail: a single participant in a standard distributed training workflow can substantially inflate its measured attribution value while preserving global utility. Our attribution-first attack uses latent optimization to inject small synthetic batches that preserve utility while exploiting non-IID label coverage and evaluator sensitivities. Across datasets, models, and multiple marginal-utility evaluators, the attack consistently increases the adversary’s attribution value and reshapes the relative attribution structure among benign clients without degrading accuracy or triggering geometry-based defenses. These results show that attribution itself forms a new attack surface and motivate the development of attribution-robust and incentive-compatible scoring mechanisms.

paragraphs: Data attribution assigns value to participants’ contributions to a trained model, informing pricing, audits, and governance. Its usefulness depends on those scores reflecting contribution faithfully. This paper shows that a participant in distributed training can manipulate its measured attribution while leaving the global model’s predictive utility intact.

The attack optimizes latent representations to construct small synthetic batches. It exploits uneven label coverage across participants and sensitivities in the evaluators that measure marginal utility. The objective centers on increasing the participant’s assigned value while preserving the usefulness of the trained model, making attribution manipulation distinct from an attack whose visible effect is lower accuracy.

Across the tested datasets, models, and several marginal-utility evaluators, the attack consistently raises the adversary’s attribution and changes the relative scores of benign clients. It does so without degrading accuracy or triggering the geometry-based defenses evaluated. These findings identify contribution scoring as an attack surface and motivate scoring mechanisms that remain reliable when participants have incentives to manipulate their measured value.
summary.tldr: A distributed-learning participant can inflate its measured data contribution with synthetic batches while preserving model accuracy.

title: On the Fragility of Data Attribution When Learning Is Distributed

abstract: Despite the ubiquity of multiway data across scientific domains, there are few performant and user-friendly methods that fit non-standard nonnegative tensor factorization models tailored to the data at-hand. Researchers may use gradient-based automatic differentiation, which often struggles under nonnegative constraints, choose between a limited set of methods with mature implementations, or implement their own model from scratch. As an alternative, we introduce NNEinFact, an einsum-based multiplicative update algorithm that fits any nonnegative tensor factorization expressible as a tensor contraction by minimizing one of many user-specified loss functions, including the $(\alpha,\beta)$-divergence. To use NNEinFact, the researcher specifies their model with a string. NNEinFact converges to a stationary point of the loss, supports missing data, and fits to tensors with hundreds of millions of entries in seconds. Empirically, NNEinFact fits custom models which outperform standard ones in prediction tasks on real-world tensor data by over 37% and attains less than half the test loss of gradient-based methods while converging up to 90 times faster. Software is publicly available at github.com/jhood3/einfact.

title: Near-Universal Multiplicative Updates for Nonnegative Einsum Factorization

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning aims to construct world models for efficient sampling. Current mainstream algorithms can be broadly categorized into two paradigms: maximum likelihood and value-aware world models. The former employs structured Recurrent/Transformer State-Space Models to capture environmental dynamics but overlooks task-relevant features. The latter prioritizes decision-critical states but suffers from sub-optimal performance. While recent efforts have sought to integrate these approaches, they typically rely on auxiliary modules or heavy external priors that significantly increase computational complexity. In this work, we propose a Value-Aligned World Model, a minimalist framework designed to synergize these two paradigms with negligible overhead. Specifically, We introduce an intrinsic latent-space value-alignment regularization that compels the world model to prioritize task-relevant features while maintaining the structural integrity of stochastic dynamics. To ensure stable optimization, we develop an adaptive weighting mechanism that acts as a self-regulating curriculum, balancing reconstruction fidelity with decision-making utility. Extensive experiments on Atari 100k and DeepMind Control benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm consistently boosts existing methods with minimal added code and computational overhead. Code is available at supplementary material.

paragraphs: A world model helps a reinforcement-learning agent learn how its environment behaves. The paper describes a tension between accurately modeling environmental dynamics and emphasizing the features that matter for decisions. Models optimized for likelihood can overlook task relevance, while approaches focused on value can deliver suboptimal performance.

The proposed Value-Aligned World Model combines these priorities through a regularization term inside the model’s latent representation. This term encourages attention to task-relevant features while preserving the structure of stochastic dynamics. An adaptive weighting mechanism adjusts the balance between reconstruction fidelity and decision usefulness, functioning as a curriculum that regulates itself during optimization.

Experiments on Atari 100k and DeepMind Control show consistent improvements to existing methods, with minimal additional code and computational overhead. The significance is the simplicity of the integration: the framework brings decision relevance into world-model learning without the auxiliary modules or heavy external priors described in earlier combinations. The results support treating predictive fidelity and usefulness for control as objectives that can be trained together efficiently.
summary.tldr: Value-Aligned World Models improve existing reinforcement-learning methods by adaptively balancing faithful dynamics modeling with task-relevant latent representations.

title: Boosting World Models Learning via Latent-Space Value Alignment

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision modules, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of long-horizon, adversarial interaction while faithfully acting on human instructions. We introduce a long-horizon Red Alert RTS benchmark with a hierarchical interface in which LLMs output budgeted, low-frequency macro/tactical intents that are executed deterministically for standardized comparison. The benchmark evaluates (i) robustness to “rules-as-variable” perturbations via rule-style shifts , (ii) competitive strength via Elo-style ratings from head-to-head matches, and (iii) human steerability via standardized language interventions. Beyond win/loss, we log economy growth/spending, combat loss ratio, and visibility coverage to diagnose long-horizon failure modes. Overall, the benchmark provides a reproducible and diagnostic testbed for robustness and controllability in long-horizon adversarial decision making.

paragraphs: A language model making decisions over a long game must compete with an opponent, adapt to changing rules, and respond to human instructions. This paper introduces a Red Alert real-time strategy benchmark designed to examine these capabilities together. Its emphasis is on diagnosing behavior across extended interactions, with winning serving as one part of the evaluation.

The interface separates the model’s decisions from their execution. Models issue budgeted, low-frequency strategic or tactical intentions, which are executed deterministically for standardized comparisons. Evaluation covers robustness to changes in rule style, competitive strength through Elo-style ratings from head-to-head matches, and steerability through standardized language interventions.

The benchmark also records economic growth and spending, combat loss ratios, and visibility coverage. These measurements provide additional evidence about long-horizon failure modes that a final win or loss can conceal. The stated contribution is a reproducible diagnostic testbed for robustness and controllability, connecting competitive outcomes to intermediate behavior and responses to human direction.
summary.tldr: A Red Alert benchmark evaluates long-horizon LLM competition, rule robustness, and human steerability while logging behavior beyond wins and losses.

title: From Winning to Understanding: A Diagnostic Long-Horizon RTS Benchmark for LLMs

abstract: Post-training Large Vision-and-Language Models (LVLMs) typically involves Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for knowledge injection or Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) for performance enhancement. However, SFT often leads to sub-optimal performance, while RLVR remains constrained by the model’s internal knowledge base. While a sequential SFT $\rightarrow$ RLVR pipeline can be used, it introduces significant computational overhead and suffers from catastrophic forgetting. To address these limitations, we propose ViSurf (Visual Supervised-and-Reinforcement Fine-Tuning), a unified, single-stage paradigm that integrates the strengths of both SFT and RLVR. By analyzing their training objectives, we establish a unified framework that injects ground-truth labels directly into RLVR rollouts, facilitating simultaneous external supervision and internal reinforcement. Furthermore, we introduce three novel reward control strategies to ensure training stability and optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ViSurf consistently outperforms standalone SFT, RLVR, and the traditional two-stage pipeline across diverse benchmarks. In-depth analysis corroborates these findings, validating the derivation and design principles of ViSurf.

paragraphs: Vision-language post-training commonly uses supervised examples to add knowledge or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to improve performance. Each has a weakness in the paper’s account: supervised tuning can yield suboptimal performance, while reward-based tuning is constrained by existing model knowledge. Running them sequentially adds substantial computation and can lead to catastrophic forgetting.

ViSurf combines the two forms of learning in one stage. After analyzing their objectives, the authors construct a framework that injects ground-truth labels into reinforcement-learning rollouts. This lets external supervision and internal reinforcement operate together. Three additional reward-control strategies are introduced to support stable training and optimization.

Experiments report consistent improvements over supervised fine-tuning alone, reinforcement learning alone, and the conventional two-stage pipeline across diverse benchmarks. Further analysis supports the framework’s derivation and design. The central contribution is a way to connect learning from known answers with learning from rewards during the same training process, addressing the separation that can make sequential post-training expensive and prone to losing previously acquired knowledge.
summary.tldr: ViSurf combines ground-truth supervision and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning in a single vision-language post-training stage.

title: ViSurf: Visual Supervised-and-Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for Large Vision-and-Language Models

abstract: Sparse camera-conditioned image-to-video generation presents a pivotal challenge: synthesizing geometrically consistent 3D motion from minimal pose cues. Existing methods, which largely rely on dense supervision or naive interpolation, suffer from severe pose drift and motion discontinuities due to the lack of robust 3D priors. In this paper, we introduce CamGeo, a novel framework that distills rich 3D geometric knowledge from a pre-trained video-to-3D model (VGGT) directly into the diffusion backbone. To achieve this without incurring inference latency, we propose a training-only distillation strategy. Specifically, CamGeo incorporates: (1) keyframe trajectory distillation that enforces cycle-consistency with sparse input poses, (2) cross-frame consistency distillation with both camera trajectory and depth constraints to generate consistent structure across unsupervised frames, and (3) a three-stage coarse-to-fine curriculum learning, progressively scales geometric complexity, from global structure coherence to fine-grained refinement, achieving stable optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CamGeo achieves consistent improvements under various sparsity ratios.

paragraphs: CamGeo tackles image-to-video generation when only a small number of camera poses are supplied. Sparse instructions leave much of the motion between specified views unconstrained. The paper identifies pose drift and discontinuous motion as problems in existing methods and attributes them to insufficient three-dimensional geometric guidance.

The framework transfers geometric knowledge from a pretrained video-to-3D model, VGGT, into the video diffusion backbone during training. One distillation component enforces cycle consistency between keyframe trajectories and the provided poses. Another applies camera-trajectory and depth constraints across frames, including those without direct supervision. Together, these objectives encourage generated views to describe a consistent underlying structure.

Training follows a three-stage curriculum that moves from overall geometric coherence toward finer refinement as complexity increases. Because the distillation machinery is used only during training, it does not add inference latency. Experiments report consistent improvements across different levels of pose sparsity. The approach therefore targets the missing geometric guidance between sparse camera instructions while preserving the inference-time generation pipeline.
summary.tldr: CamGeo distills 3D knowledge into a video generator during training to improve motion consistency under sparse camera guidance without adding inference latency.

title: CamGeo: Sparse Camera-Conditioned Image-to-Video Generation with 3D Geometry Priors

abstract: We study the correlation clustering problem in the node-arrival data stream model. Unlike previous work, where the stream consists of the graph’s edges, we focus on the setting in which the stream contains only the nodes. This model better reflects many real-world scenarios in which the data stream naturally consists of raw objects (e.g., images, tweets), and the similar/dissimilar edges are derived through a similarity function. We present C$^4$Approx, a streaming algorithm that approximates the cost of correlation clustering using sublinear space in the number of nodes and a constant number of passes. We further complement this result with lower bounds. Experiments on real-world datasets show that by storing only 2% of the nodes, our algorithm achieves performance comparable to the classic Pivot algorithm and the more recent PrunedPivot algorithm, even on sparse graphs.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimating correlation clustering cost when data arrives as a stream of objects. The objects might be images or tweets, with a similarity function supplying their similar or dissimilar relationships. This differs from a stream that directly supplies graph edges, and better matches settings where relationships must be derived from incoming raw objects.

The proposed C⁴Approx algorithm approximates clustering cost while using space that grows sublinearly with the number of nodes. It also requires only a constant number of passes over the stream. These guarantees address the central storage challenge: estimating the cost without retaining the entire collection of objects. The paper complements the algorithm with lower bounds on the problem.

On real-world datasets, storing only 2% of the nodes produces performance comparable to Pivot and PrunedPivot, including on sparse graphs. This empirical result supports the usefulness of the node-arrival formulation under tight storage constraints. The contribution concerns approximation of clustering cost, so its stated guarantee should be understood in terms of that estimation objective.
summary.tldr: C⁴Approx estimates correlation clustering cost from streaming objects using sublinear storage and a constant number of passes.

title: Estimating Correlation Clustering Cost in Node-Arrival Stream

abstract: Foundation models have transformed machine learning for language and vision, but achieving comparable impact in physical simulation remains a challenge. Data heterogeneity and unstable long-term dynamics inhibit learning from sufficiently diverse dynamics, while varying resolutions and dimensionalities challenge efficient training on modern hardware. Through empirical and theoretical analysis, we incorporate new approaches to mitigate these obstacles, including a harmonic-analysis–based stabilization method, load-balanced distributed 2D-3D training strategies, and compute-adaptive tokenization. Using these tools, we develop Walrus, a transformer-based foundation model developed primarily for fluid-like continuum dynamics. Walrus is pretrained on nineteen diverse scenarios spanning astrophysics, geoscience, rheology, plasma physics, acoustics, and classical fluids. Experiments show that Walrus outperforms prior foundation models on both short- and long-term prediction horizons on downstream tasks and across the breadth of pretraining data, while ablation studies confirm the value of our contributions to forecast stability, training throughput, and transfer performance over conventional approaches.

Differences in spatial resolution and dimensionality also complicate efficient training, so the paper addresses computational organization alongside the forecasting problem.

Experiments show better short-term and long-term predictions than prior foundation models on downstream tasks and across the pretraining data. The findings connect improvements in numerical behavior and training efficiency to the broader objective of a reusable model for diverse continuum systems, particularly those with fluid-like dynamics.
summary.tldr: Walrus combines stabilized forecasting and efficient heterogeneous training to improve continuum-dynamics predictions across diverse physical scenarios.

title: Walrus: A Cross-domain Foundation Model for Continuum Dynamics

abstract: Shampoo is attracting considerable attention for its superior performance on large-scale optimization benchmarks; yet it faces a significant practical bottleneck: the prohibitive computational overhead of matrix inversion. To mitigate this, practitioners typically rely on stale preconditioner updates, creating a fundamental trade-off between computational efficiency and optimization fidelity. In this work, we provide a theoretical study of staleness through the complementary lenses of convergence and stability. While staleness improves computational efficiency, it inherently degrades performance and introduces numerical instability. Crucially, we identify that damping, acting as a numerical stabilizer, can effectively suppress these negative effects. Guided by this analysis, we propose FOAM, an adaptive algorithm that stabilizes training by dynamically controlling both the damping factor and the eigendecomposition frequency based on an approximation of the staleness-oriented error. Experimental results demonstrate that FOAM reduces wall-clock time compared to standard Shampoo while maintaining robust convergence.

Crucially, we identify that damping, acting as a numerical stabilizer, can effectively suppress these negative effects. Guided by this analysis, we propose FOAM, an adaptive algorithm that stabilizes training by dynamically controlling both the damping factor and the eigendecomposition frequency based on an approximation of the staleness-oriented error. Experimental results demonstrate that FOAM reduces wall-clock time compared to standard Shampoo while maintaining robust convergence.

paragraphs: Shampoo is an optimizer with strong results on large-scale optimization benchmarks, but its matrix computations can be expensive. A common practical response is to reuse an older preconditioner instead of recomputing it at every update. This saves computation while introducing staleness, creating a tradeoff between inexpensive updates and how faithfully the optimizer follows current information.

The paper analyzes this tradeoff through convergence and numerical stability. Its analysis identifies harmful effects of staleness and shows that damping, used as a numerical stabilizer, can suppress them. This makes damping a means of addressing the errors associated with reusing outdated preconditioners, alongside deciding how often to refresh them.

FOAM turns that analysis into an adaptive algorithm. It approximates staleness-oriented error and uses the estimate to control both the damping factor and the frequency of eigendecomposition. Experiments show lower wall-clock training time than standard Shampoo while maintaining robust convergence. The contribution is a coordinated way to adjust stabilization and expensive matrix updates, tying computational savings to an estimate of optimization error.
summary.tldr: FOAM adapts Shampoo's damping and matrix-update frequency to reduce training time while controlling errors from stale preconditioners.

title: FOAM: Frequency and Operator-Error Based Adaptive Damping Method for Reducing Staleness-Oriented Error for Shampoo

abstract: Document visual question answering requires models not only to answer questions correctly, but also to precisely localize answers within complex document layouts. While large vision-language models (VLMs) achieve strong spatial grounding, their inference cost and latency limit real-world deployment; on the other hand, compact VLMs are efficient but suffer substantial localization degradation under standard fine-tuning or distillation. To address this gap, we propose DocVAL, a validated chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation framework that transfers explicit spatial reasoning from large teacher models to compact, deployable student VLMs. DocVAL combines (1) teacher-generated spatial CoT supervision, (2) a rule-based dual-mode validator that filters low-quality training signals and provides fine-grained, pixel-level corrective feedback, and (3) a validation-driven two-stage training procedure with iterative refinement. Text detection is used only as training-time scaffolding for supervision and validation, enabling the final student to operate as a pure VLM without OCR or detection at inference. Across multiple document understanding benchmarks, the proposed DocVAL yields consistent improvements of up to 6-7 ANLS points over comparable compact VLMs. We further introduce mean Average Precision (mAP) as a localization metric for document question answering and report strong spatial grounding performance under this new evaluation. We release 95K validator-verified CoT traces and show that high-quality, validated supervision is more effective than scaling unfiltered data, enabling efficient and trustworthy document grounding. Code/Data: GitHub.

title: DocVAL: Validated Chain-of-Thought Distillation for Grounded Document VQA

abstract: In adaptive experiments, statistical inference is essential for reliable decision-making and scientific discovery. Often in these settings, collecting labeled data is expensive, but decision-makers have access to large unlabeled datasets and strong pretrained AI models that can generate outcome predictions. Effectively leveraging these predictions in online experiments poses fundamental challenges for statistical inference: AI models may be misspecified, and data collected under adaptive policies are inherently non-i.i.d., invalidating classical inference techniques. To address these challenges, we propose a Prediction-Powered Adaptive Inference (PPAI) estimator that integrates unlabeled data, predicted labels, and adaptively collected labeled data through a single estimating equation. We establish asymptotic normality of the PPAI estimator under mild conditions on the data-collection policy, enabling valid confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for a broad class of Z-functionals. The method incorporates a data-driven tuning mechanism that adaptively weights AI predictions according to their informativeness, guaranteeing that the resulting asymptotic variance is no worse than that of the labeled-only baseline, and is strictly smaller when predictions are informative. Numerical experiments further support the theory, illustrating efficiency gains with informative AI predictions and robust performance when predictions are inaccurate.

paragraphs: Adaptive experiments can collect expensive labeled outcomes while also having access to abundant unlabeled data and AI predictions. Using those predictions for statistical inference is challenging because they may be inaccurate, and adaptive data collection violates the independent, identically distributed setting of classical methods. PPAI combines these information sources in a single estimating equation.

The authors establish asymptotic normality under mild conditions on the data-collection policy, supporting confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for a broad class of quantities described by estimating equations. A data-driven tuning mechanism adjusts the weight given to AI predictions according to how informative they are. This makes prediction usefulness part of the estimator's operation.

The resulting asymptotic variance is guaranteed to be no worse than that of a labeled-only baseline and strictly smaller when predictions are informative. Numerical experiments support efficiency gains with useful predictions and robustness when predictions are inaccurate. The guarantee concerns asymptotic inference under the stated policy conditions, providing a principled route for incorporating pretrained predictions into adaptive experimentation.
summary.tldr: PPAI combines AI predictions with adaptive experiment data to improve asymptotic inference efficiency when predictions help, without worsening baseline asymptotic variance.

title: Prediction-Powered Adaptive Inference with Pretrained AI Models for Contextual Bandits

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated exceptional general reasoning capabilities. However, their performance in embodied navigation remains hindered by a scarcity of aligned open-world vision and robot control data. Despite simulators providing a cost-effective alternative for data collection, the inherent reliance on photorealistic simulations often limits the transferability of learned policies. To this end, we propose S*andbox-Abstracted Grounded Experience (SAGE), a framework that enables agents to learn within a physics-grounded semantic abstraction rather than a photorealistic simulation, mimicking the human capacity for mental simulation where plans are rehearsed in simplified physics abstractions before execution. SAGE operates via three synergistic phases: (1) Genesis: constructing diverse, physics-constrained semantic environments to bootstrap experience; (2) Evolution: distilling experiences through Reinforcement Learning (RL), utilizing a novel asymmetric adaptive clipping mechanism to stabilize updates; (3) Navigation: bridging the abstract policy to open-world control. We demonstrate that SAGE* significantly improves planner-assisted embodied navigation, achieving a 53.21% LLM-Match Success Rate on A-EQA (+9.7% over baseline), while showing encouraging transfer to physical indoor robot deployment. Project page is available at: https://frankzxshen.github.io/SAGE.

SAGE explores learning through simplified semantic environments that preserve physical constraints, resembling rehearsal of a plan in an abstract mental simulation.

The framework has three phases. Genesis creates varied semantic environments constrained by physics. title: Plan in Sandbox, Navigate in Open Worlds: Learning Physics-Grounded Abstracted Experience for Embodied Navigation

abstract: We present a fine-grained theoretical analysis of the performance gap between two-stage reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and direct preference optimization (DPO). Our study decomposes this gap into two sources: the explicit representation gap under exact optimization and the implicit representation gap under finite samples. In the exact optimization setting, we characterize how the relative capacities of the reward and policy model classes influence the final policy qualities. We show that RLHF, DPO, or online DPO can outperform one another depending on type of model mis-specifications. Notably, online DPO can outperform both RLHF and standard DPO when the reward and policy model classes are isomorphic and both mis-specified. In the approximate optimization setting, we provide a concrete construction where the ground-truth reward is sparse and show that RLHF requires significantly fewer samples than DPO to recover an effective reward model, highlighting a statistical advantage of two-stage learning. Together, these results provide a comprehensive understanding of the performance gap between RLHF and DPO under various settings, and offer practical insights into when each method is preferred.

paragraphs: This paper theoretically examines why two-stage reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization can produce different policy quality. It separates the gap into two sources: differences in what the model classes can represent under exact optimization, and differences that arise when learning from finite samples.

For exact optimization, the relative capacities of reward and policy model classes determine which method has an advantage. RLHF, standard DPO, and online DPO can each outperform the others under different forms of model misspecification. In particular, online DPO can beat both alternatives when reward and policy classes are isomorphic and both are misspecified.

For approximate optimization, the authors construct a setting with a sparse ground-truth reward in which RLHF needs significantly fewer samples than DPO to recover an effective reward model. Together, the results make method choice conditional on representation and data conditions, rather than supporting a universal ranking of preference-learning approaches.
summary.tldr: The analysis shows that RLHF, DPO, and online DPO have different advantages depending on model misspecification and finite-sample conditions.

title: Understanding the Performance Gap in Preference Learning: A Dichotomy of RLHF and DPO

abstract: Concept erasure has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate undesired or unsafe content in diffusion models, yet existing methods still face significant limitations. While training-based methods are effective, their high computational cost limits scalability. Editing-based methods are more efficient and deployment-friendly, yet they struggle to simultaneously achieve precise concept erasure and preserve overall generative capacity. We identify this core limitation of the editing-based methods as reliance on additive parameter updates. Our empirical analysis reveals that concept semantics primarily depend on neuron direction rather than neuron magnitude, while overall generative capacity relies on the angular geometry of neurons. As additive updates inherently entangle direction, magnitude, and angular geometry, they inevitably introduce unintended interference between concept erasure and overall generation performance. To address this, we propose Orthogonal Concept Erasure (OCE), which reformulates editing-based erasure as multiplicative parameter updates from a geometric perspective. Specifically, OCE applies layer-wise orthogonal transformations derived from a closed-form solution to the parameters, enabling precise concept erasure while preserving the neuron magnitude and angular geometry. Furthermore, to address conflicting constraints in multi-concept erasure, OCE introduces a subspace-level objective with structured subspace manipulation, yielding a more effective and scalable erasure. Extensive experiments on single- and multi-concept erasure demonstrate that OCE outperforms existing methods in concept erasure and non-target preservation, erasing up to 100 concepts in 4.3 s. Code: https://github.com/HansSunY/OCE.

The paper focuses on efficient parameter editing, where existing methods struggle to balance precise removal with preservation. Its empirical analysis links concept semantics mainly to neuron directions and general generation capacity to the angular relationships among neurons.

Conventional additive edits change direction, magnitude, and angular geometry together. OCE instead applies multiplicative, layer-wise orthogonal transformations obtained from a closed-form solution. These results support the efficiency and selectivity of the proposed editing approach.
summary.tldr: OCE removes concepts through orthogonal parameter transformations that preserve neuron magnitudes and angular geometry.

title: Orthogonal Concept Erasure for Diffusion Models

abstract: To address the increasing long-context compute limitations of softmax attention, several subquadratic recurrent operators have been developed. This work includes models such as Mamba-2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). As the space of recurrences grows, a parallel line of work has arisen to taxonomize them. One compelling view is the test-time regression (TTR) framework, which interprets recurrences as performing online least squares updates that learn a linear map from the keys to values. Existing delta-rule recurrences can be seen as first-order approximations to this objective, but notably ignore the curvature of the least-squares loss during optimization. In this work, we address this by introducing preconditioning to these recurrences. Starting from the theory of online least squares, we derive equivalences between linear attention and the delta rule in the exactly preconditioned case. Next, we realize this theory in practice by proposing a diagonal approximation: this enables us to introduce preconditioned variants of DeltaNet, GDN, and KDA alongside efficient chunkwise parallel algorithms for computing them. Empirically, we find that our preconditioned delta-rule recurrences yield consistent performance improvements across synthetic recall benchmarks and language modeling at the 340M and 1B scale.

paragraphs: Recurrent sequence models offer alternatives to the growing compute cost of full attention on long inputs. One way to understand these recurrences is as an online regression process: at each step, the model updates a linear mapping from keys to values. Existing delta-rule updates approximate this process using first-order information while ignoring the curvature of the regression objective.

This paper introduces preconditioning, which adjusts updates to account for that curvature. Starting with online least-squares theory, the authors derive equivalences between linear attention and delta-rule updates in the exactly preconditioned case.
