The results support curvature-aware updates as a way to improve these recurrent models, while distinguishing the exact theoretical equivalence from the diagonal approximation used in practice.
summary.tldr: Preconditioned delta-rule recurrences incorporate regression curvature through efficient diagonal approximations, improving recall and language-modeling results.

title: Preconditioned DeltaNet: Curvature-aware Sequence Modeling for Linear Recurrences

abstract: Language models acquire syntax and world knowledge together, entangling the two in ways that limit efficiency and controllability. We show that syntax can be learned while suppressing semantic plausibility and world-knowledge cues, yielding more efficient and controllable models. We train tiny LMs on grammatical nonsense — syntactically well-formed text with semantic content ablated via constrained relexicalization (SAMBAL). Models trained on this data perform comparably to standard pretraining on syntactic benchmarks (BLiMP, SyntaxGym) while scoring at chance on world knowledge probes (EWoK). On targeted grammar-plausibility conflict probes, content-neutral models prefer grammaticality where standard models prefer plausibility, and their representations show more syntactic vs lexical alignment. On efficiency, disentanglement yields substantial sample and parameter gains: in low-resource regimes, a 5M-parameter model matches a 30M-parameter baseline at the same data budget. On controllability, content-neutral models adapt rapidly to a new domain with minimal exposure, suggesting the feasibility of modular post-hoc knowledge specialization.

paragraphs: Language-model training usually mixes learning grammar with learning meaning and facts about the world. This paper investigates whether small models can acquire syntax when semantic plausibility and world-knowledge cues are suppressed. The authors train on grammatical nonsense created through SAMBAL, a constrained word-replacement procedure that preserves syntactic structure while ablating semantic content.

The resulting models perform comparably to standard pretraining on BLiMP and SyntaxGym, while scoring at chance on EWoK world-knowledge probes. When targeted tests put grammaticality in conflict with plausibility, these models favor grammaticality where standard models favor plausible content. Their internal representations also align more strongly with syntax relative to lexical information, supporting the intended separation.

The approach brings efficiency gains in the studied low-resource regimes: a five-million-parameter model matches a thirty-million-parameter baseline using the same data budget. The models also adapt rapidly to a new domain with limited exposure. This suggests the possibility of learning a compact grammatical foundation and subsequently specializing its knowledge, while leaving that broader modular-training prospect as a suggested direction.
summary.tldr: Tiny models trained on grammatical nonsense retain strong syntax performance while showing efficiency gains and reduced reliance on semantic plausibility.

title: Learning syntax without semantics: Disentangled tiny language models

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) links gene expression with tissue morphology but remains expensive and low-throughput, motivating surrogates that infer expression from routine histology. Whole-slide H&E-to-ST inference pairs a gigapixel image with gene measurements at a sparse, irregular set of locations, making multiscale modeling challenging without incurring dense-grid overhead or quadratic token mixing. We propose HiST, a hierarchical sparse transformer that treats measured locations as a lattice-indexed sparse field and builds a dyadic encoder–decoder directly on the active tissue footprint. HiST combines sparse window attention for local geometric correspondence with resolution-changing operators for rapid multiscale context integration. For a fixed window size, the dominant runtime and memory scale with the number of observed locations rather than the dense slide area. To mitigate slide-specific acquisition variation, HiST adds a bottlenecked global conditioning pathway via a slide calibration token that summarizes slide-level context and conditions local representations. On a multi-organ benchmark spanning diverse tissues and acquisition sources, HiST improves predictive performance over recent baselines while reducing runtime and peak memory.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression at locations in tissue, but its expense and limited throughput motivate predicting expression from routine histology images. The computational challenge is uneven: a whole-slide image can be enormous, while gene measurements occupy only a sparse, irregular set of positions. HiST builds its representation around those observed locations.

The model uses a hierarchical sparse encoder–decoder operating on the active tissue footprint. Local attention windows capture nearby geometric relationships, while changes in resolution combine context across scales. With window size fixed, the dominant runtime and memory costs follow the number of observed locations rather than the full slide area. This directly addresses the overhead of processing an otherwise mostly unobserved grid.

HiST also uses a compact slide calibration token to summarize slide-wide context and condition local representations, aiming to reduce variation associated with acquisition. On a benchmark covering multiple organs and acquisition sources, it improves prediction over recent baselines while reducing runtime and peak memory. The results connect efficient sparse processing with stronger cross-modal tissue modeling.
summary.tldr: HiST predicts spatial gene expression from histology using a sparse multiscale transformer whose main costs track observed tissue locations.

title: HiST: A Hierarchical Sparse Transformer for Cross-Modal Spatial Transcriptomics Modeling

abstract: Diffusion models have recently set new benchmarks in Speech Enhancement (SE). However, most existing score-based models treat speech spectrograms merely as generic 2D images, applying uniform processing that ignores the intrinsic structural sparsity of audio, which results in inefficient spectral representation and prohibitive computational complexity. To bridge this gap, we propose DVPD, an extremely lightweight Dual-View Predictive Diffusion model, which uniquely exploits the dual nature of spectrograms as both visual textures and physical frequency-domain representations across both training and inference stages. Specifically, during training, we optimize spectral utilization via the Frequency-Adaptive Non-uniform Compression (FANC) encoder, which preserves critical low-frequency harmonics while pruning high-frequency redundancies. Simultaneously, we introduce a Lightweight Image-based Spectro-Awareness (LISA) module to capture features from a visual perspective with minimal overhead. During inference, we propose a Training-free Lossless Boost (TLB) strategy that leverages the same dual-view priors to refine generation quality without any additional fine-tuning. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks demonstrate that DVPD achieves state-of-the-art performance while requiring only 35% of the parameters and 40% of the inference MACs compared to SOTA lightweight model, PGUSE. These results highlight DVPD’s superior ability to balance high-fidelity speech quality with extreme architectural efficiency. Code and audio samples are available at https://github.com/ke12345213/dvpd_demo

paragraphs: DVPD improves speech enhancement by treating a spectrogram as both a visual pattern and a representation of audio frequencies. The paper argues that processing every region uniformly, as if the spectrogram were a generic image, overlooks useful audio structure and wastes computation. Its design uses these two views during both training and generation.

The frequency-adaptive encoder compresses different spectral regions differently, retaining important low-frequency harmonics while removing high-frequency redundancy. A lightweight visual module contributes features drawn from the spectrogram's image-like appearance. At inference time, a further refinement strategy uses the same complementary information to improve generation without additional fine-tuning. Each component contributes to using spectral structure more efficiently.

Across the evaluated benchmarks, DVPD achieves state-of-the-art performance while using 35% of the parameters and 40% of the inference multiply-accumulate operations of PGUSE, the lightweight comparison model. These results indicate that incorporating audio-specific structure alongside visual features can improve the balance between enhanced speech quality and computational requirements.
summary.tldr: DVPD combines frequency-aware compression and visual spectrogram features to enhance speech with substantially fewer parameters and computations.

title: Dual-View Predictive Diffusion: Lightweight Speech Enhancement via Spectrogram-Image Synergy

abstract: Hyperspectral Image Single Image Super-Resolution (HSI-SISR) faces a conflict between computational efficiency and global non-local modeling. Existing Transformers suffer from quadratic complexity, while window-based methods compromise global capture. To address this, we propose the Spatial-Spectral Dual-Clustering-based Network (SSDCN). Our method introduces three innovations. First, we design a Spatial-Spectral Dual-Cluster Block (SSDCB). Replacing expensive point-to-point attention, it uses content-driven clustering to learn low-rank structural bases, achieving global modeling with linear complexity $\mathcal{O}(KN)$. Second, we propose a pyramid progressive hierarchical architecture with a Feature Reuse Reconstruction Block (FRRB). It reuses the core tensor and spectral factors from coarse levels, updating only spatial factors to minimize redundancy. Third, we propose a Pyramid Hierarchical Reconstruction Joint Loss to supervise intermediate levels, ensuring structural accuracy and preventing error accumulation. Experiments demonstrate that SSDCN surpasses SOTA methods in metrics and visual quality with significantly fewer parameters and FLOPs, achieving an optimal efficiency-performance balance.

paragraphs: Hyperspectral image super-resolution needs to capture relationships across spatial locations and spectral information while controlling computation. Full attention is expensive, but restricting processing to windows weakens access to global relationships. SSDCN addresses this tradeoff through content-driven clustering that provides a compact basis for modeling structure across the image.

Its spatial-spectral dual-cluster block replaces point-to-point attention with learned low-rank structural bases, giving global modeling with O(KN) complexity. A progressive pyramid architecture then reuses the core tensor and spectral factors from coarser levels. Updating only the spatial factors reduces redundant reconstruction work as the model moves through the hierarchy.

A joint reconstruction loss supervises intermediate pyramid levels to maintain structural accuracy and prevent accumulated errors. Experiments report better quantitative metrics and visual quality than state-of-the-art methods while using substantially fewer parameters and floating-point operations. The gains combine a cheaper global modeling mechanism with reuse across reconstruction levels, addressing efficiency in both feature processing and progressive image reconstruction.
summary.tldr: SSDCN combines spatial-spectral clustering and hierarchical feature reuse for more efficient, higher-quality hyperspectral super-resolution.

title: SSDCN: Spatial-Spectral Dual-Clustering-based Network for Hyperspectral Image Super-resolution

abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable scaling LLM parameters under a fixed inference budget by activating only a small subset of experts via top-$k$ routing. While this preserves causality and suits autoregressive language models, the discrete top-$k$ operator is not differentiable, forcing a fixed number of active experts per input and resulting in inefficient use of computation. We propose SoftMoE, which replaces discrete routing with a truncated soft top-$k$ LapSum relaxation, allowing gradient-based optimization of expert routing. We further parameterize the mean number of active experts per layer and impose a global budget constraint, enabling the model to learn how to allocate expert capacity across layers. SoftMoE remains fully compatible with autoregressive modeling and achieves performance comparable to or better than sparse MoE on language modeling and downstream tasks, while activating significantly fewer experts. Notably, the learned allocation is highly non-uniform, with later layers activating more experts. The source code is publicly available$^\dagger$.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models limit computation by activating only some expert modules for each input. Standard top-k routing makes a discrete selection and fixes how many experts are used, restricting how computation can be allocated. SoftMoE replaces this selection with a truncated soft top-k LapSum relaxation that allows routing to be optimized through gradients.

The method also learns the mean number of active experts in each layer under a global budget constraint. This gives training control over where expert capacity is spent across the network. The routing design remains compatible with autoregressive generation, so it can be used when tokens must be generated according to their preceding context.

Experiments on language modeling and downstream tasks show performance comparable to or better than sparse MoE while activating significantly fewer experts. The learned distribution is highly uneven, with later layers using more experts. This finding supports allowing the model to discover layer-specific computational needs. The contribution combines differentiable routing with budgeted allocation, making expert usage itself a learned part of the architecture's behavior.
summary.tldr: SoftMoE learns differentiable expert routing and layer-specific allocations, matching or improving performance while activating fewer experts.

title: SoftMoE: Soft Differentiable Routing for Mixture-of-Experts in LLMs

abstract: Recent work has sought to understand Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning, yet a principled, model-intrinsic signal that captures its layer-wise reasoning dynamics remains underexplored. We bridge this gap by demonstrating that the $\ell_2$ norm of hidden states serves as an endogenous signal of the model’s reasoning intensity. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a diagnostic probe, we observe that LLMs’ internal reasoning is marked by a sharp increase in reasoning feature activations concentrated in late layers. Motivated by this pattern, we establish a formal link between reasoning intensity and the model’s latent geometry and theoretically prove that the $\ell_2$ norm of hidden states bounds the activation strength of SAE reasoning features. Empirical correlation analysis and causal interventions further prove $\ell_2$ norm as a faithful indicator, where heightened norms consistently correspond to critical reasoning steps. We then introduce three test-time scaling techniques guided by $\ell_2$ norms: Adaptive Layer-wise Reasoning Recursion, (ii) Endogenous Reasoning State Steering, and (iii) $\ell_2$-guided Response Selection, which requires no additional training or data and is compatible with advanced inference engines. Experiments across model architectures and benchmarks show that $\ell_2$-norm-based techniques significantly improve reasoning performance, offering a principled yet simple lens to perceive and control LLM latent reasoning dynamics. Our codes are available at https://github.com/zjy1298/The-Tell-Tale-Norm.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a simple quantity inside a language model can reveal how its reasoning changes across layers. The proposed signal is the Euclidean magnitude, or L2 norm, of hidden states. Using sparse autoencoders as diagnostic probes, the authors observe a sharp increase in reasoning-feature activations concentrated in later layers.

They connect this pattern to the geometry of internal representations and theoretically prove that hidden-state norms bound the activation strength of reasoning features identified by the autoencoders. Correlation analyses and causal interventions further support the norm as an indicator of reasoning intensity, with heightened norms consistently associated with critical reasoning steps in their analyses.

The authors then use this signal in three inference-time techniques: adaptive layer-wise reasoning recursion, steering of internal reasoning states, and response selection guided by norms. The approach requires no additional training or data and is compatible with advanced inference engines. Experiments across architectures and benchmarks show significant reasoning improvements, linking a measurable internal signal to practical methods for directing computation during inference.
summary.tldr: Hidden-state L2 norms indicate reasoning intensity and guide inference-time techniques that improve reasoning without additional training or data.

title: The Tell-Tale Norm: $\ell_2$ Magnitude as a Signal for Reasoning Dynamics in Large Language Models

abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) introduce a new paradigm for language generation, which in turn presents new challenges for aligning them with human preferences. In this work, we aim to improve the policy optimization for dLLMs by reducing the cost of the trajectory probability calculation, thereby enabling scaled-up offline policy training. We prove that: (i) under reference policy regularization, the probability ratio of the newly unmasked tokens is an unbiased estimate of that of intermediate diffusion states, and (ii) the probability of the full trajectory can be effectively estimated with a single forward pass of a re-masked final state. By integrating these two trajectory reduction strategies into a policy optimization objective, we propose Trajectory Reduction Policy Optimization (dTRPO). We evaluate dTRPO on 7B dLLMs across instruction-following and reasoning benchmarks. Results show that it substantially improves the core performance of state-of-the-art dLLMs, achieving gains of up to 9.6% on STEM tasks, up to 4.3% on coding tasks, and up to 3.0% on instruction-following tasks. Moreover, dTRPO exhibits strong training efficiency due to its offline, single-forward nature, and achieves improved generation efficiency through high-quality outputs.

paragraphs: Aligning diffusion language models requires policy optimization suited to their generation process. A costly part is calculating probabilities along the sequence of intermediate diffusion states. dTRPO reduces this calculation to make larger-scale offline policy training more practical.

The paper establishes two trajectory reductions. Under reference policy regularization, the probability ratio for newly unmasked tokens is an unbiased estimate of the ratio for intermediate diffusion states. It also shows that full-trajectory probability can be effectively estimated using one forward pass on a final state that has been masked again. These results support an optimization objective that avoids evaluating the full trajectory in the usual way.

Evaluations on 7B diffusion language models report gains of up to 9.6% on STEM tasks, 4.3% on coding, and 3.0% on instruction following. These are maximum reported gains rather than uniform improvements across every task. The authors also report strong training efficiency from offline, single-forward computation and improved generation efficiency associated with higher-quality outputs, linking the probability reductions to practical training and generation benefits.
summary.tldr: dTRPO reduces diffusion-language-model trajectory calculations to enable efficient offline policy training and improve reasoning and instruction following.

title: dTRPO : Trajectory Reduction in Policy Optimization of Diffusion Large Language Models

abstract: kernel functions built using quantum-mechanical principles and have emerged as a centerpiece of quantum machine learning. The initial enthusiasm for quantum kernel machines has been tempered by recent studies suggesting that quantum kernels could not offer significant computational or statistical advantages when learning from classical data. However, most of the research in this area has been devoted to scalar-valued kernels in standard classification or regression settings for which classical kernel methods are efficient and effective, leaving very little room for improvement with quantum kernels. In this position paper, we argue that progress in this field requires moving beyond scalar-valued kernels toward more expressive kernel frameworks. Scalar-valued kernels lack the degrees of freedom necessary to fully exploit intrinsically quantum resources such as entanglement and are not rich enough to deal with complex learning tasks where classical learning methods struggle. Building on recent advances in operator-valued kernel learning and $C^*$-algebraic kernel representations, we propose a roadmap for designing quantum kernels capable of leveraging entanglement and non-commutative structures to tackle complex structured prediction problems. To support this viewpoint, we present an initial proof-of-concept illustrating how quantum operator-valued kernel formulations can reveal structural dependencies that remain difficult to access for scalar-valued kernel methods. This shift in focus could open a pathway toward a new generation of quantum kernel machines and a more faithful exploration of their potential advantages.

paragraphs: This paper argues that quantum kernel research has concentrated on a restrictive setting: scalar-valued kernels for standard classification and regression on classical data. Classical methods already work effectively there, leaving limited room for improvement. The authors suggest that disappointing results in this setting do not settle the potential of richer quantum kernel approaches.

Their proposed direction uses operator-valued kernels and C*-algebraic representations. These offer more expressive mathematical structures than kernels returning a single scalar. The aim is to exploit quantum features such as entanglement and non-commutative structure when learning complex, structured predictions. The authors argue that scalar kernels lack the degrees of freedom needed to make full use of these resources.

An initial proof of concept illustrates how operator-valued quantum kernels can expose structural dependencies that scalar-valued approaches find difficult to access. The paper builds a research roadmap around that observation. It presents a possible path toward advantages in more demanding tasks, rather than a general demonstration of computational or statistical superiority for quantum kernel machines.
summary.tldr: Richer quantum kernels may reveal useful structural dependencies and create opportunities that scalar-valued kernels leave unexplored.

title: Position: Quantum Kernel Machines Should Move Beyond Scalar-Valued Kernels to Realize Their Potential

abstract: As endangered languages disappear, Machine Learning (ML) increasingly frames their revitalization as a problem of scale, emphasizing more data, larger models, and broader coverage. We posit that scale is not the limiting constraint in endangered language revitalization, and that progress lies in methodological and evaluative reorientation. Evidence from Language Identification (LID), Optical Character Recognition (OCR), and synthetic data generation shows that benchmark-driven scaling produces brittle or culturally misaligned outcomes, as evaluation and modeling lack epistemic fit. Advancement in this domain lies in rethinking methodology, by grounding evaluation in cultural fidelity, community trust, and situated use rather than abstract accuracy. The revitalization of endangered languages is not about the universality of success, but the specificity of care afforded to each language and community.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the idea that endangered-language revitalization primarily needs larger datasets, larger models, and broader language coverage. The authors argue that the main constraint lies in how researchers formulate methods and evaluate success. A system can improve an abstract score without adequately serving the language and community it is meant to support.

They draw evidence from language identification, optical character recognition, and synthetic data generation. Across these areas, they describe benchmark-driven scaling as producing brittle or culturally misaligned outcomes when modeling and evaluation do not fit the knowledge and context of the community. The problem concerns the relationship between what a system measures and what meaningful language support requires.

The proposed reorientation places cultural fidelity, community trust, and situated use at the center of evaluation. Progress would be assessed in relation to the particular language and its users. The paper’s broader message is that technical success in revitalization needs community-specific care and appropriate methods, rather than an expectation that greater scale will resolve these mismatches.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that endangered-language technology needs culturally grounded methods and evaluation because scale does not resolve misalignment with community needs.

abstract: We study the problem of learning a classification task in which only a dissimilarity function of the objects is accessible. That is, data are not represented by feature vectors but in terms of their pairwise dissimilarities. We investigate the suﬃcient conditions for dissimilarity functions to allow building accurate classifiers. Our results have the advantages that they apply to unbounded dissimilarities and are invariant to order-preserving transformations. The theory immediately suggests a learning paradigm: construct an ensemble of decision stumps each depends on a pair of examples, then find a convex combination of them to achieve a large margin. We next develop a practical algorithm called Dissimilarity based Boosting (DBoost) for learning with dissimilarity functions under the theoretical guidance. Experimental results demonstrate that DBoost compares favorably with several existing approaches on a variety of databases and under diﬀerent conditions.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when objects are accessible only through their pairwise dissimilarities. There are no feature vectors to use directly. The theoretical question is what properties of a dissimilarity function are sufficient to support accurate classifiers, allowing learning to proceed from relationships between objects.

The authors derive sufficient conditions that accommodate unbounded dissimilarities and remain invariant under order-preserving transformations. This means the results do not require a fixed upper limit on dissimilarity values and are unchanged by transformations that preserve their ordering. The theory suggests building an ensemble of decision stumps, each depending on a pair of examples, and combining them with a convex weighting to obtain a large margin.

Guided by that construction, the paper introduces Dissimilarity based Boosting, or DBoost. Experiments across several databases and different conditions show that it compares favorably with existing approaches. The work links a theoretical account of when dissimilarity information can suffice with a practical ensemble method. Its conditions are sufficient for the stated learning results, rather than presented as requirements every useful dissimilarity must satisfy.
summary.tldr: DBoost turns pairwise dissimilarities into a large-margin ensemble, guided by sufficient conditions for learning without feature vectors.

title: On learning with dissimilarity functions

abstract: This paper addresses exact learning of Bayesian network structure from data and expert's knowledge based on score functions that are decomposable. First, it describes useful properties that strongly reduce the time and memory costs of many known methods such as hill-climbing, dynamic programming and sampling variable orderings. Secondly, a branch and bound algorithm is presented that integrates parameter and structural constraints with data in a way to guarantee global optimality with respect to the score function. It is an any-time procedure because, if stopped, it provides the best current solution and an estimation about how far it is from the global solution. We show empirically the advantages of the properties and the constraints, and the applicability of the algorithm to large data sets (up to one hundred variables) that cannot be handled by other current methods (limited to around 30 variables).

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network's structure means selecting relationships among variables from data and any available expert knowledge. This paper studies exact structure learning with decomposable scoring functions. It first identifies properties that reduce time and memory requirements for several search approaches, including hill-climbing, dynamic programming, and sampling variable orderings.

The authors then present a branch-and-bound algorithm that combines data with constraints on both parameters and structure. It guarantees global optimality with respect to the score function. It is also an anytime procedure: if interrupted, it returns the best solution found so far and an estimate of its distance from the global solution.

Experiments demonstrate benefits from the proposed properties and constraints. They also show applicability to datasets with up to one hundred variables, compared with the roughly thirty-variable limit described for other contemporary methods. This is an empirical scalability result, not a guarantee for every problem of that size. The combination of constraints, search reductions, and an optimality-gap estimate makes exact learning more usable when full search is expensive.
summary.tldr: Constraint-aware branch-and-bound supports exact Bayesian network structure learning and returns a current solution with a gap estimate if interrupted.

title: Structure learning of Bayesian networks using constraints

abstract: We consider the problem of rank loss minimization in the setting of multilabel classification, which is commonly tackled by means of convex surrogate losses defined on pairs of labels. Very recently, this approach was put into question by the negative result showing that any such loss function is necessarily inconsistent. In this paper, we show a positive result which is arguably surprising in light of the previous one: despite being simpler, common convex surrogates for binary classification, defined on single labels instead of label pairs, are consistent for rank loss minimization. Instead of directly proving convergence, we give a much stronger result by deriving regret bounds and convergence rates. The proposed losses suggest efficient and scalable algorithms, which are tested experimentally.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of rank loss minimization in the setting of multilabel classification, which is commonly tackled by means of convex surrogate losses defined on pairs of labels. Very recently, this approach was put into question by the negative result showing that any such loss function is necessarily inconsistent. In this paper, we show a positive result which is arguably surprising in light of the previous one: despite being simpler, common convex surrogates for binary classification, defined on single labels instead of label pairs, are consistent for rank loss minimization. Instead of directly proving convergence, we give a much stronger result by deriving regret bounds and convergence rates. The proposed losses suggest efficient and scalable algorithms, which are tested experimentally.

paragraphs: In multilabel classification, an example can have several relevant labels, and the goal here is to rank those labels appropriately. A common training strategy replaces ranking loss with an easier convex objective defined over pairs of labels. The paper starts from a negative theoretical result showing inconsistency of that pairwise surrogate approach.

The authors establish a positive result for a simpler alternative: common convex binary-classification losses applied to individual labels can be consistent for ranking-loss minimization. This means that optimizing an appropriate single-label surrogate can remain aligned with the desired ranking objective, despite avoiding direct training on label pairs.

The analysis goes beyond establishing eventual consistency. It derives regret bounds and convergence rates, giving a quantitative relationship between learning progress and ranking performance. The resulting losses suggest efficient, scalable algorithms, which the authors evaluate experimentally. The central finding is that a seemingly more direct pairwise formulation need not offer the stronger theoretical foundation; simpler individual-label losses can provide the consistency and quantitative guarantees sought for this task.
summary.tldr: Common convex losses applied to individual labels can consistently optimize multilabel rankings, with regret bounds and convergence rates.

title: Consistent Multilabel Ranking through Univariate Losses
